mem.t: with good will doing service as to the Lord and not to men.

lessons.title: As to the Lord
lessons.theme: I work for my boss, but I truly serve the Lord

v: Servants, be obedient to those who according to the flesh are your masters, with fear and trembling, in singleness of your heart, as to Christ,
not in the way of service only when eyes are on you, as men pleasers, but as servants of Christ, doing the will of God from the heart,
with good will doing service as to the Lord and not to men,
knowing that whatever good thing each one does, he will receive the same good again from the Lord, whether he is bound or free.

lessons.still: Before you walk into work or open your laptop, place your boss’s name before the Lord. Pray: “Lord, today I work for them, but I am serving you. Make my heart willing — not just putting on a show for people.”
teach: Paul wrote these words to slaves in the Roman Empire — people in a far harder position than any employee today. Here Paul doesn’t address the institution of slavery itself, but he gives them a perspective that turns everything around: “with good will doing service as to the Lord and not to men”. Not “service only when eyes are on you, as men pleasers”, but “doing the will of God from the heart”. For in the end the reward comes not from an earthly master but from the Lord himself.

Offices have a familiar ‘CCTV effect’: when the manager is around, everyone sits up straighter and types faster; when the manager is away on a trip, the pace slackens. What Paul calls service “only when eyes are on you” is working for the camera. But a Christian’s work has another audience — the Lord, unseen yet all-seeing. When you know your real ‘boss’ never goes on a business trip, work stops being a performance and becomes worship.

“Good will” is the key phrase. Forced compliance builds resentment; willing service brings freedom. This doesn’t mean suppressing your feelings or pretending your boss is always right. It means setting your faithfulness free from your boss’s performance. Whether my boss is good is between them and the Lord; whether I am faithful is between me and the Lord. Change your thinking and you change your life: from “I’m slaving away for them” to “I’m offering this to the Lord”.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Humility means laying down power and returning to my proper place. Serving as to the Lord means not competing in my heart with my boss over who is king, but letting Jesus be King. Humility breeds humility, and both sides win.
lessons.scene: Wenjun is a team leader in a telecoms call centre. The new supervisor watches only the numbers and publicly names people in the group chat whose call times run long. Wenjun resents it; she feels the supervisor has no idea what the front line is like. Today the supervisor is away. The team start chatting and scrolling, and someone laughs: “Day off for good behaviour! You take a break too, boss!”
q: Who is God? — “Whatever good thing each one does, he will receive the same good again from the Lord.” How does this rewarding Lord change what you expect from your work?
Who am I? — Is your attitude at work shaped more by whether your boss is present, or by the Lord’s presence?
How shall I respond? — How could Wenjun lead her team right now, and let go of her resentment towards the supervisor?
lessons.jesus: Jesus said, “The Son of Man also came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many” (Mark 10:45). He is Lord of lords, yet he willingly took the form of a servant. Our strength to serve others comes from the Lord who served us first and gave his life for us.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, thank you for willingly giving your life for me. As I work for my boss today, help me remember that it is you I truly serve. When they are away, keep me just as diligent; when they are unfair, help me hand my hurt to you. Take the resentment out of my heart and give me a willing spirit. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Finish one important task while your boss is away
Treat one task you dread as a gift to the Lord
Say in your heart: “I serve you for the Lord’s sake”
lessons.noon: “With good will doing service as to the Lord and not to men” — Lord, right now I offer this work to you.

lessons.title: The Corner of the Robe
lessons.theme: Don’t take matters into your own hands; leave judgement to God

v: When Saul had returned from following the Philistines, he was told, “Behold, David is in the wilderness of En Gedi.”
Then Saul took three thousand chosen men out of all Israel, and went to seek David and his men on the rocks of the wild goats.
He came to the sheep pens by the way, where there was a cave; and Saul went in to relieve himself. Now David and his men were staying in the innermost parts of the cave.

David’s men said to him, “Behold, the day of which the LORD said to you, ‘Behold, I will deliver your enemy into your hand, and you shall do to him as it shall seem good to you.’” Then David arose and cut off the skirt of Saul’s robe secretly.
Afterward, David’s heart struck him because he had cut off Saul’s skirt.
He said to his men, “The LORD forbid that I should do this thing to my lord, the LORD’s anointed, to stretch out my hand against him, since he is the LORD’s anointed.”
So David checked his men with these words, and didn’t allow them to rise against Saul. Saul rose up out of the cave, and went on his way.

lessons.still: Clench your fists for ten seconds, then slowly open them. Pray: “Lord, I let go of the urge to strike back myself. The one who hurt me — I place them in your hands.”
teach: Saul was hunting David with three thousand chosen men, and walked alone into the very cave where David was hiding. David’s men told him that the day the LORD had spoken of had come. It looked like a door God had opened. David secretly cut off a corner of Saul’s robe — and afterwards “David’s heart struck him”. He said, “The LORD forbid that I should do this thing to my lord, the LORD’s anointed, to stretch out my hand against him.” He knew Saul was in the wrong; he also knew judgement was not his to carry out.

Workplaces have their own ‘cave moments’. You hold something on your boss: an anonymous letter, a screenshot, a ‘casual’ remark to the CEO that could bring them down. People around you say, “Now’s your chance!” But there is a thin line between cutting a robe and drawing a sword. David’s conscience struck him even over the robe, because he knew that humiliating someone with a small move and wounding them with a blade come from the same heart that wants to be king.

Not striking back doesn’t mean doing nothing. David later openly explained the truth to Saul, and kept himself out of harm’s way. Today, if a boss is acting illegally or bullying people, you can — and should — raise it through proper channels, and seek help from trusted people or legal advice where needed. The difference lies in motive: is it for justice and to protect people, or for revenge and to settle a score? Let God be God, let people be people; my part is to walk in the light.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Pride is leaving my place to grab power; humility is laying power down and returning to my place. David put down the sword and let God be God. Pride provokes pride, but humility leaves a door open for reconciliation.
lessons.scene: Mere teaches at a primary school in Wellington. The principal regularly presents her classroom results to parents as his own ideas, and marked her down in her appraisal. Today a colleague forwards her a recording of the principal mocking parents in private. “Just send this to the school board,” the colleague says. “He’s finished.” She looks at the file, finger hovering over “Forward”.
q: Who is God? — David called Saul “the LORD’s anointed”. How do you see God’s sovereignty behind those in authority?
Who am I? — Are you holding a ‘corner of the robe’ that you want to use to prove yourself or shame someone?
How shall I respond? — How can Mere tell the difference between what should go through proper channels and what is simply the urge for revenge?
lessons.jesus: When Jesus was arrested he could have asked his Father for more than twelve legions of angels, yet he did not lift a hand. Peter says, “When he was cursed, he didn’t curse back. When he suffered, he didn’t threaten, but committed himself to him who judges righteously” (1 Peter 2:23). His refusal to strike back became the way of our salvation.
lessons.pray: Righteous Lord, you know the wrongs I have suffered at work. Heal the anger in my heart, and keep me from taking revenge with my own hands. If injustice needs to be exposed, give me wisdom to go through proper channels; if I just want to get my own back, let my heart strike me and bring me back to you. I leave judgement with you. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Delete one screenshot or draft kept only for revenge
Write down your hurt about your boss and pour it out to God
If something illegal is happening, record facts and consult someone you trust
lessons.noon: “The LORD forbid that I should do this thing to my lord” — Lord, right now I lower my hand and place them in yours.

lessons.title: Where Submission Stops
lessons.theme: Submit for the Lord’s sake — and for his sake, say no

v: Therefore subject yourselves to every ordinance of man for the Lord’s sake: whether to the king, as supreme,
or to governors, as sent by him for vengeance on evildoers and for praise to those who do well.
For this is the will of God, that by well-doing you should put to silence the ignorance of foolish men.
Live as free people, yet not using your freedom for a cloak of wickedness, but as bondservants of God.
Honour all men. Love the brotherhood. Fear God. Honour the king.
But Peter and John answered them, “Whether it is right in the sight of God to listen to you rather than to God, judge for yourselves,
for we can’t help telling the things which we saw and heard.”

lessons.still: Draw a line on your desk with your finger. Pray: “Lord, within this line I want to submit wholeheartedly. Show me clearly where you have drawn the boundary, and give me courage not to cross it.”
teach: On the one hand Peter writes, “Subject yourselves to every ordinance of man for the Lord’s sake,” and even “Honour the king” — and the emperor of his day was no friend of Christians. On the other hand, the same Peter told the council, “Whether it is right in the sight of God to listen to you rather than to God, judge for yourselves.” These don’t contradict each other. We submit “for the Lord’s sake”; so when a human command requires us to go against the Lord, that very same reason becomes our reason to say no.

A company’s lines of authority are like a building’s evacuation routes. On a normal day everyone follows the signs and listens to the building manager. But when there’s a fire, anyone has the right — and the duty — to push open the door marked ‘Emergency Exit’. Your boss can decide your hours, your projects and how you work. They cannot require you to falsify records, break the law, harm people, or betray the core of your faith. The key question is: is this “I don’t like it”, or “God doesn’t permit it”?

Say no like a Christian. Check the facts first and make sure it isn’t a misunderstanding. Then explain your reasons respectfully and privately, and offer an alternative. Keep a record of the conversation. Where needed, use internal or legal channels and seek help from trusted people or professionals. After saying no, keep being faithful in everything else, so people can see you are not rebelling against authority but fearing God. As Peter says, “by well-doing you should put to silence the ignorance of foolish men.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Scripture is my standard. Submission has limits, and those limits are drawn by God’s word, not by feelings or self-interest. Humble submission within the line and gentle firmness beyond it — both are ways of letting Jesus be King.
lessons.scene: Guanlin is site manager for a construction firm. The project is behind schedule, and his boss wants him to sign today’s safety checklist stating the scaffolding has been ‘reinforced’ — though the materials won’t arrive until next week. On the phone the boss says, “Just sign it. If anything happens, it’s on me.” Tomorrow morning twenty workers will be up on that scaffolding. He picks up the pen, then puts it down.
q: Who is God? — Why is “for the Lord’s sake” both the reason to submit and the reason to say no?
Who am I? — Do you tend to cross the line in order to comply, or refuse too quickly to submit?
How shall I respond? — How can Guanlin say no while respecting his boss, protecting the workers and offering an alternative?
lessons.jesus: Jesus paid the temple tax and respected those in authority, yet he would not yield an inch on his Father’s will. He cleansed the temple, and he stood silent before Pilate. He knew when to submit and when to stand firm, because his heart had one focus: “My food is to do the will of him who sent me” (John 4:34).
lessons.pray: Lord, give me wisdom to know when to submit and when to say no. Keep me from compromising out of fear, and from resisting out of pride. If today I must refuse an unjust request, give me gentle words, a clear position, and your peace to face the consequences. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Write down two lines you will never cross at work
Look up one verse that speaks to a request troubling you
Before you say no, prepare an alternative
lessons.noon: “Subject yourselves to every ordinance of man for the Lord’s sake” — Lord, right now both my yes and my no are for you.

lessons.title: Apples of Gold
lessons.theme: Disagreeing upward with fitting words, patience and respect

v: A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in settings of silver.
As an earring of gold, and an ornament of fine gold, so is a wise reprover to an obedient ear.
As the cold of snow in the time of harvest, so is a faithful messenger to those who send him; for he refreshes the soul of his masters.
As clouds and wind without rain, so is he who boasts of gifts deceptively.
By patience a ruler is persuaded. A soft tongue breaks the bone.
So, then, my beloved brothers, let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger;

lessons.still: Before a meeting or a reply, take a deep breath and count to five. Pray: “Lord, make me swift to hear and slow to speak. May every word I say today be like apples of gold in settings of silver.”
teach: Proverbs says, “A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in settings of silver.” A fitting word is not only right in content but right in timing, tone and setting. It also says, “By patience a ruler is persuaded. A soft tongue breaks the bone.” In the ancient world, contradicting a king could cost your life. The wise did not meet force with force; they used patience and gentleness. Abigail, in today’s longer reading, stopped David in exactly this way when he was about to draw his sword.

Communicating upward is like using satnav in an unfamiliar city. You know where you want to end up, but the satnav first works out where you are now. What pressure is your boss under right now? Do they care most about results, risk or reputation? Understand them first, then share your view, with an alternative ready. A single sentence — “Can I check I’ve understood you correctly?” — often lowers defences more than ten pages of objections.

Respecting a boss who disagrees with you doesn’t mean abandoning your view; it means trading ‘winning the argument’ for ‘winning the person’. The self-centred want to prove they are right; the self-emptied care that the work is right and the relationship is right. People matter more than tasks — don’t hurt people for the sake of a project. Once you have spoken, if your boss still doesn’t agree, and nothing goes against faith or law, cooperate willingly before the Lord and leave the outcome to God. Patience is not weakness; it is trusting that God can persuade a ruler’s heart.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Humility breeds humility; pride provokes pride. When you speak up the line, first lay down the need to win and return to your place. Relationships matter more than things — and more than winning a meeting.
lessons.scene: Pinyu is a senior designer at a branding agency. Her creative director insists on changing a client’s new packaging to bold red and gold; she believes it will ruin the brand’s identity. At the internal meeting before tomorrow’s pitch, the director says, “That’s settled. Any objections?” The room goes quiet. In Pinyu’s hands is the alternative design she stayed up all night to finish.
q: Who is God? — God can use patience to persuade a ruler. How does that change the way you see your boss’s heart?
Who am I? — When you disagree, do you tend to clash head-on, or go silent?
How shall I respond? — Should Pinyu speak up in the meeting, or talk to the director privately afterwards? How might she begin?
lessons.jesus: As a boy in the temple, Jesus was found “sitting in the middle of the teachers, both listening to them and asking them questions” (Luke 2:46). His words were always full of grace and truth; when challenged, he often answered with a question that made people think. His gentleness never weakened his truthfulness.
lessons.pray: Lord of wisdom, guard my mouth. When I disagree with my boss, make me swift to hear, slow to speak and slow to anger. Give me fitting words and fitting timing, and a patient heart. If my idea is accepted, may the glory be yours; if not, make me willing to cooperate and leave the outcome with you. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Before giving your view, restate your boss’s view first
Prepare an alternative, not just an objection
If overruled, sincerely say, “I’ll give it my full support”
lessons.noon: “A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in settings of silver.” — Lord, right now please guard my tongue.

lessons.title: Holding Up the Leader’s Hands
lessons.theme: Good team members don’t just finish tasks; they strengthen their boss

v: Then Amalek came and fought with Israel in Rephidim.
Moses said to Joshua, “Choose men for us, and go out to fight with Amalek. Tomorrow I will stand on the top of the hill with God’s rod in my hand.”
So Joshua did as Moses had told him, and fought with Amalek; and Moses, Aaron, and Hur went up to the top of the hill.
When Moses held up his hand, Israel prevailed. When he let down his hand, Amalek prevailed.

But Moses’ hands were heavy; so they took a stone, and put it under him, and he sat on it. Aaron and Hur held up his hands, the one on the one side, and the other on the other side. His hands were steady until sunset.
Joshua defeated Amalek and his people with the edge of the sword.

lessons.still: Raise both hands and hold them up for ten seconds. Feel your arms grow heavy. Lower them slowly and pray: “Lord, my boss gets tired too. Today make me someone who holds up their hands.”
teach: Israel was fighting Amalek. Joshua fought in the valley; Moses stood on the hilltop with raised hands. “When Moses held up his hand, Israel prevailed. When he let down his hand, Amalek prevailed.” But Moses was only human: “Moses’ hands were heavy.” So Aaron and Hur brought a stone for him to sit on and held up his hands, one on each side. “His hands were steady until sunset.” Part of that victory was won by two men quietly holding up someone else’s arms.

In a relay race, the baton is most often dropped not on the straight but in the changeover zone. Many of a boss’s struggles happen in unseen changeover zones too: papers not ready before a meeting, figures not checked in time, a key chart missing from a presentation to senior leadership. Good team members don’t just run their own leg well; they run a couple of extra strides through the changeover so their boss can take the baton cleanly. That isn’t flattery; it’s seeing what someone needs.

Holding up your boss’s hands is a humble yet powerful kind of service. It seeks no credit — Scripture records the names of Aaron and Hur but not a single word they said. Through the 321 lens, your boss is also one of your ‘2’ — in 920, the people God has placed around you, with whom you practise the self-emptied ‘0’ and bear the ‘9’ fruits of the Spirit. When you pour yourself out for them, you are pouring yourself out for God’s kingdom, and letting Jesus receive all the glory.
lessons.light: 321 Light: 920 — my boss is one of my ‘2’. Self-denial means living for Jesus and for others, not for myself. Holding up a leader’s hands is the self-emptied life at its most practical in the workplace.
lessons.scene: Tomasi is a team leader at a distribution centre in Auckland. His manager has just taken over two warehouses, often works late into the night, and has become short-tempered. On Friday the stocktake results are due at head office, but the data is still a mess. Tomasi could leave on time. He looks at the light still on in his manager’s office, then at his jacket on the back of his chair.
q: Who is God? — God gave Israel victory through both Moses’ raised hands and those who held them up. What does that show you about how God designs teams?
Who am I? — Are you someone who only runs your own leg, or someone who notices what your boss needs?
How shall I respond? — What one practical thing could Tomasi do today to strengthen his manager?
lessons.jesus: In Gethsemane Jesus said to his disciples, “Stay here and watch with me” (Matthew 26:38). He longed for company, but they fell asleep. Yet he did not give up on them; instead he gave his life for them. Today he invites us to be the ones who stay awake and hold others up.
lessons.pray: Lord, thank you for giving me a boss. I confess I often see their faults and overlook their burdens. Open my eyes today to where their hands are growing heavy, and let me hold them up like Aaron and Hur — not for credit, not for show, but so that your name is glorified. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Ask your boss: “Is there anything I can take off your plate this week?”
Prepare something your boss will need, ahead of time
Speak well of your boss in front of others
lessons.noon: “Aaron and Hur held up his hands” — Lord, right now make me someone who holds others up.

mem.t: I exhort therefore, first of all, that petitions, prayers, intercessions, and givings of thanks be made for all men.

lessons.title: First of All, Pray
lessons.theme: Interceding for bosses and those in authority opens the way for peace and the gospel

v: I exhort therefore, first of all, that petitions, prayers, intercessions, and givings of thanks be made for all men,
for kings and all who are in high places, that we may lead a tranquil and quiet life in all godliness and reverence.
For this is good and acceptable in the sight of God our Saviour,
who desires all people to be saved and come to full knowledge of the truth.

lessons.still: Think of the first manager you will meet today and say their name in your heart. Pray: “Lord, I place them in your hands. Give them wisdom, and give me a heart to love them.”
teach: Paul writes to Timothy, who was pastoring in Ephesus: “I exhort therefore, first of all, that petitions, prayers, intercessions, and givings of thanks be made for all men,” and he names a group in particular: “for kings and all who are in high places”. The emperor of the day was hardly kind to Christians. “First of all” means this is not optional. Paul gives two reasons: “that we may lead a tranquil and quiet life in all godliness and reverence”, and because God “desires all people to be saved and come to full knowledge of the truth”.

Praying for your boss is like changing the filter in the office air conditioning. You never see it, yet it affects the air everyone breathes. Complaining clouds the air; prayer slowly freshens it. Many of us spend ages in the staff kitchen discussing our manager’s failings, yet rarely spend a minute praying for them. Of the four kinds of prayer Paul lists — petitions, prayers, intercessions and thanksgiving — notice that thanksgiving is one: giving thanks for your boss.

Praying for those in authority changes us too. It is hard to resent someone while you are praying for them; when you ask God to give them wisdom, you begin to see them through God’s eyes. That is how changing your thinking changes your life: from “they are my problem” to “they are someone God loves and wants to save”. Whether your boss is a believer, whether they are fair — neither affects this instruction. First of all, pray for them.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The order of relationships is God → myself → others → tasks. Bring your boss before God first, then deal with the relationship and the work. People matter more than tasks — even the hardest boss is someone God wants to save.
lessons.scene: Xiufeng is a clerk in a city government office in southern Taiwan. Her new section chief is heavy-handed and routinely shoots down everyone’s proposals; behind his back, colleagues call him ‘King Veto’. At lunch today, the team is tearing into him again in the staff canteen. Xiufeng remembers this morning’s reading. Her chopsticks stop mid-air — should she join in, or say something?
q: Who is God? — God “desires all people to be saved”. Does that include the manager you find hardest to work with?
Who am I? — Roughly how does the time you spend complaining about your boss compare with the time you spend praying for them?
How shall I respond? — How could Xiufeng respond at the table without pretending to agree or joining in the criticism?
lessons.jesus: On the cross Jesus prayed for those who crucified him: “Father, forgive them, for they don’t know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34). He is the greatest intercessor, and he still intercedes for us at God’s right hand (Romans 8:34). When we pray for others, we join in his work.
lessons.pray: King of kings, I place my boss in your hands. Give them wisdom in their decisions, health and peace, and help them come to know your truth. Take away the complaining in my heart, so that in the staff kitchen I say one less criticism, and in prayer I offer one more blessing. May our office know peace because you are present. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Offer one petition, intercession and thanks for your boss today
When others criticise your boss, don’t join in — pray silently
Write down one thing about your boss to thank God for
lessons.noon: “For kings and all who are in high places” — Lord, right now I ask your blessing on my boss.

lessons.title: Seek the Peace of the City
lessons.theme: In an imperfect company, be someone who brings peace

v: The LORD of Armies, the God of Israel, says to all the captives whom I have caused to be carried away captive from Jerusalem to Babylon:
“Build houses and dwell in them. Plant gardens and eat their fruit.
Take wives and father sons and daughters. Take wives for your sons, and give your daughters to husbands, that they may bear sons and daughters. Multiply there, and don’t be diminished.
Seek the peace of the city where I have caused you to be carried away captive, and pray to the LORD for it; for in its peace you will have peace.”

lessons.still: Look around your place of work — an office, a factory, a shop, a desk at home. Pray: “Lord, this is where you have placed me. Today I pray not only for my own peace, but for peace in this place.”
teach: What the exiles in Babylon most wanted to hear was, “You’ll be home soon.” But the letter Jeremiah sent from God said: “Build houses and dwell in them. Plant gardens and eat their fruit.” More than that: “Seek the peace of the city where I have caused you to be carried away captive, and pray to the LORD for it.” Babylon was the city that had taken them captive, yet God told them to pray for it, “for in its peace you will have peace”. It was a call to put down roots in a foreign place and become a blessing there.

Many people treat their company like a hotel: I’m only passing through, so if the room is messy or something breaks, it’s not my problem — I’ll just check out. But God calls us to take responsibility for where we are, as if it were our own home. Even if you plan to leave in two years, you can still plant a tree today: improve a process, train a new colleague well, pray for the company’s operations. You are not a guest; you are someone who has been sent.

Seeking the peace of your company doesn’t mean endorsing every decision it makes, nor making the company your whole life. It means being a channel of blessing where you stand. This is where building God’s order begins: not escaping an imperfect world, but living out the ways of his kingdom within it. Shift your perspective — from “this place doesn’t deserve my effort” to “God has placed me here to bring peace”.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Our one purpose is to build God’s order. God’s people do not flee Babylon; they bless the city from within it. Our focus is not on our surroundings but on the Lord who sends us.
lessons.scene: Weilun is a production line supervisor at an electronic components factory in Penang. Revenue is down this year and rumours of redundancies are circulating. Staff are anxious; some have started coasting, others are busy job-hunting. Weilun himself has had a message from a headhunter. Before this morning’s briefing, the plant manager takes him aside: “Can you hold this line together?”
q: Who is God? — God told the exiles to pray for Babylon. What does that show you about his heart?
Who am I? — In your company, are you more like a hotel guest, or someone who has been sent?
How shall I respond? — How could Weilun answer the plant manager, and seek the peace of the factory during this uncertain season?
lessons.jesus: As Jesus drew near Jerusalem and saw the city, he wept over it (Luke 19:41), because it did not know the things that belonged to its peace. He wept for a city that would reject him, and he gave his life for it. His heart is the heart that seeks the peace of the place where we are.
lessons.pray: Lord, thank you for placing me in this company. Even though it is imperfect, and has sometimes disappointed me, make me someone who brings peace. I pray for the business, for my employer’s decisions and for my colleagues’ families. Because your children are here, may there be a little more justice and a little more hope. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Pray for one minute for the company’s business and decisions
Improve one small process or tidy one shared space
Encourage a colleague who is feeling anxious
lessons.noon: “Seek the peace of the city” — Lord, right now I seek the peace of my company.

lessons.title: Nehemiah’s Arrow Prayer
lessons.theme: Before you speak, pray silently to the God of heaven

v: In the month Nisan, in the twentieth year of Artaxerxes the king, when wine was before him, I picked up the wine, and gave it to the king. Now I had not been sad before in his presence.
The king said to me, “Why is your face sad, since you are not sick? This is nothing else but sorrow of heart.” Then I was very much afraid.
I said to the king, “Let the king live forever! Why shouldn’t my face be sad, when the city, the place of my fathers’ tombs, lies waste, and its gates have been consumed with fire?”
Then the king said to me, “What is your request?” So I prayed to the God of heaven.
I said to the king, “If it pleases the king, and if your servant has found favour in your sight, I ask that you would send me to Judah, to the city of my fathers’ tombs, that I may build it.”
The king said to me (the queen was also sitting by him), “How long will your journey be? When will you return?” So it pleased the king to send me, and I set a time for him.
Moreover I said to the king, “If it pleases the king, let letters be given me to the governors beyond the River, that they may let me pass through until I come to Judah;

and a letter to Asaph the keeper of the king’s forest, that he may give me timber to make beams for the gates of the citadel by the temple, for the wall of the city, and for the house that I will occupy.” The king granted my requests, because of the good hand of my God on me.

lessons.still: Before today’s first important conversation, count silently to three. Use those three seconds to pray: “God of heaven, give me the right words.” Practise turning this tiny prayer into a habit.
teach: Nehemiah was cupbearer to the Persian king, one of the people closest to him and most trusted. For months he had grieved over the ruin of Jerusalem (see Nehemiah 1:1; 2:1), until one day his sadness showed on his face before the king. The king asked, “What is your request?” In that moment, “I prayed to the God of heaven,” and only then did he speak. The prayer was so short its words weren’t even recorded, yet it changed his life — and the life of a city.

This kind of prayer is often called an ‘arrow prayer’: short, swift, shot straight towards heaven. The most critical moments at work rarely leave time to kneel: bumping into the CEO in the lift, being suddenly put on the spot in a meeting, an angry customer on the line. But there is always time to loose an arrow. It’s like a keyboard shortcut — once you know it well, one press takes you straight there when it matters most.

Arrow prayers are powerful because of the long prayer behind them. Before Nehemiah ever spoke to the king, he had “fasted and prayed before the God of heaven” (Nehemiah 1:4). So an arrow prayer is not a lucky shot; it is the natural overflow of a long relationship. And Nehemiah did more than pray: he already knew how long he needed and which letters to ask for. Prayer and preparation go together — that is relying on the Spirit with your heart. Afterwards he said it was “because of the good hand of my God on me”. The glory goes to God, not to himself.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Rely on the Spirit with your heart, not on yourself with your head. Arrow prayers bring us back to the Spirit’s guidance at every critical moment; and after success, “the good hand of my God” reminds us to let Jesus receive all the glory.
lessons.scene: Priya is a claims officer at an insurance company in Singapore. Her father in India is seriously ill and she needs a month’s leave, but it’s year-end close and her manager hates anyone taking leave now. This afternoon she is called into his office for a performance review. Suddenly he asks, “You seem to have a lot on your mind lately. What’s going on?”
q: Who is God? — How was “the good hand of my God” at work in Nehemiah’s story? Have you seen that hand in your own work?
Who am I? — In moments of pressure, is your first reaction to pray, or to panic?
How shall I respond? — How could Priya send up an arrow prayer right now, and then speak to her manager honestly and with preparation?
lessons.jesus: At Lazarus’ tomb, Jesus lifted up his eyes and said, “Father, I thank you that you listened to me” (John 11:41). His relationship with the Father was so close that prayer was as natural as breathing. Through him, we too can come to the Father at any moment, anywhere.
lessons.pray: God of heaven, thank you for always hearing my prayers. At every critical moment today — before a meeting, before I reply, when I’m put on the spot — remind me to send an arrow to you first. Make me like Nehemiah, close to you in ordinary days and well prepared beforehand. If things go well, may all the glory be yours. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Pray silently for three seconds before every reply to your manager
Write down the key points of a request before you make it
When it works out, say: “Thank God for his good hand”
lessons.noon: “So I prayed to the God of heaven.” — Lord, right now I pray to you first, before I speak.

lessons.title: A Prayer List for Work
lessons.theme: Pray for your company with intention and become a source of blessing

v: The LORD was with Joseph, and he was a prosperous man. He was in the house of his master the Egyptian.
His master saw that the LORD was with him, and that the LORD made all that he did prosper in his hand.
Joseph found favour in his sight. He ministered to him, and Potiphar made him overseer over his house, and all that he had he put into his hand.

From the time that he made him overseer in his house, and over all that he had, the LORD blessed the Egyptian’s house for Joseph’s sake. The LORD’s blessing was on all that he had, in the house and in the field.
In nothing be anxious, but in everything, by prayer and petition with thanksgiving, let your requests be made known to God.

lessons.still: Open the notes app on your phone and create a new page titled “Praying for my company”. Write down three names or three matters. Then pray quietly: “Lord, I hand this list to you.”
teach: Joseph was sold into Egypt and became a slave in Potiphar’s house. But “the LORD was with Joseph, and he was a prosperous man” — and even his master noticed. Scripture says, “the LORD blessed the Egyptian’s house for Joseph’s sake.” One man who feared God brought blessing to an entire household and its fields. Joseph did not choose where he worked, yet he became the source of blessing in that place.

Many of us keep a to-do list for work, but never a prayer list for our company. Try treating your company like a project Gantt chart: every department, every major project, every manager, even every client can become a ‘prayer item’. Paul says, “In nothing be anxious, but in everything, by prayer and petition with thanksgiving, let your requests be made known to God.” “Everything” surely includes next quarter’s orders, the new system going live, and the audit coming up.

A prayer list changes how you see your company. Where you once saw only problems, you begin to see needs; where you once thought only of your own appraisal, you begin to pray for the whole team’s wellbeing. This is change from the inside out: first our thinking, then our life, and then fruit in our relationships and ministry. No need for fanfare. Like Joseph, be quietly faithful and quietly prayerful, and in his time God will let people see that he is present.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Letting Jesus be King includes letting him be King over the company. Praying for your company is the quietest yet most powerful way to build God’s order. What matters is not the size of the company, but whether God is present.
lessons.scene: Guodong is sales manager at a small textile mill in Tainan. The mill has just landed a big order with a tight deadline, and production and sales are fighting every day, with the owner caught in the middle and at his wits’ end. Guodong has only ever prayed about his own sales figures. Tonight he opens his notebook, wanting to write a prayer list for the whole mill, but doesn’t know where to start.
q: Who is God? — God blessed a whole household “for Joseph’s sake”. What does that show you about how God uses his children?
Who am I? — Do your prayers mostly revolve around your own needs, or do they include your whole company?
How shall I respond? — How could Guodong write his first prayer list for the company? Write three items for your own company too.
lessons.jesus: After the Last Supper, Jesus prayed a long prayer for his disciples (John 17). He interceded for them one by one, and then prayed “for those also who will believe in me through their word” (John 17:20). His heart holds a very long prayer list, and your name is on it.
lessons.pray: Lord, thank you for placing me in this company. Today I put it on my prayer list: give the owner wisdom, help the departments work together, protect my colleagues’ health and families, and may our products and services truly bless our customers. Make me, like Joseph, a blessing in this place. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Write a company prayer list: three people, three matters
At lunch, pray for one item on the list
Ask God for peace in a department that is in conflict
lessons.noon: “The LORD was with Joseph, and he was a prosperous man.” — Lord, right now please be with our company.

lessons.title: The Thirty-Day Prayer Challenge
lessons.theme: Keep praying for your boss and let God change them — and you

v: He also spoke a parable to them that they must always pray and not give up,
Moreover, as for me, far be it from me that I should sin against the LORD in ceasing to pray for you; but I will instruct you in the good and the right way.

lessons.still: In your calendar, count thirty days from today and make a small mark. Pray: “Lord, for these thirty days I will pray for my boss every day. Give me perseverance, so that I don’t give up.”
teach: Jesus told the parable of the widow and the judge, and Scripture states its purpose up front: “that they must always pray and not give up”. The widow went back to the unjust judge again and again, and in the end she received justice. When the people demanded a king and grieved Samuel’s heart, he still said, “Far be it from me that I should sin against the LORD in ceasing to pray for you.” For Samuel, giving up on intercession was not mere laziness; it was sin against God.

Personal trainers will tell you that muscle isn’t built in a single session; it grows through weeks of steady training. Intercession is the same. Praying for your boss once is easy. The hard part is day ten, day twenty, when nothing has changed — or things have got worse — and you have to decide whether to carry on. Today you are invited to take the ‘Thirty-Day Prayer Challenge’: one minute a day, praying for your boss.

After thirty days, your boss may have changed, or may not. But one thing will almost certainly change: you. You’ll notice less resentment and more understanding. You’ll begin to pray about their family, their pressures and their health, and to see them as someone who needs grace. This is 920: every person connected to me is one of my ‘2’; through intercession I practise the self-emptied ‘0’ and bear the ‘9’ fruits of the Spirit.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Among the eight steps for changing our thinking, repetition is key. Thirty days of prayer turns ‘praying for my boss’ from a one-off piece of information into a repeated practice, then a habit — and even something to multiply among colleagues.
lessons.scene: Huimin is a teller at a bank branch in Taipei. The branch manager is especially hard on her and often corrects her in front of customers, which leaves her humiliated. This week she read Samuel’s words and was struck to the heart. This morning she set up a thirty-day reminder on her phone for eight o’clock. Just as she is about to tap “Save”, she remembers the look on her manager’s face yesterday, and hesitates.
q: Who is God? — Jesus says we must “always pray and not give up”. What kind of God encourages us to keep praying?
Who am I? — On which day of praying for someone are you most likely to give up? What discourages you?
How shall I respond? — Should Huimin tap “Save”? Will you begin your own thirty-day prayer challenge too?
lessons.jesus: Jesus said to Peter, “I prayed for you, that your faith wouldn’t fail” (Luke 22:32). He knew Peter would deny him, yet he still prayed for him. He intercedes for us every day and never gives up. Our persistent prayer for our boss is an echo of his enduring love.
lessons.pray: Lord, I admit that praying for my boss isn’t easy, especially when they have hurt me. But I accept these thirty days. Give me perseverance, and work in their heart; give them peace and wisdom. Above all, change me, so that I see them through your eyes. As for me, far be it from me to stop praying for them. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Set a daily thirty-day prayer reminder
Pray one sentence today for your boss’s family or health
Note down what you prayed on day one
lessons.noon: “They must always pray and not give up” — Lord, right now I won’t give up; I will keep praying for them.

mem.t: For it is commendable if someone endures pain, suffering unjustly, because of conscience towards God.

lessons.title: Suffering Unjustly
lessons.theme: Enduring injustice for the sake of conscience towards God is commendable in his sight

v: Servants, be in subjection to your masters with all respect, not only to the good and gentle, but also to the wicked.
For it is commendable if someone endures pain, suffering unjustly, because of conscience towards God.
For what glory is it if, when you sin, you patiently endure beating? But if when you do well, you patiently endure suffering, this is commendable with God.
For you were called to this, because Christ also suffered for us, leaving you an example, that you should follow his steps,

lessons.still: Sit down and rest your open hands on your knees, as if handing back a report that was never yours. Pray quietly: “Lord, if I am wronged today, let my conscience be clear before you first.”
teach: Many of the people Peter wrote to were household servants. They had no employment law, no grievance procedure, and if their master was harsh, they simply had to bear it. Peter did not tell them to revolt, nor did he pretend the pain was not real. Instead he wrote something startling: “For it is commendable if someone endures pain, suffering unjustly, because of conscience towards God.” He distinguished two kinds of suffering. Being punished for wrongdoing is your own doing; but enduring suffering when you have done well “is commendable with God.” The key is not the pain itself but the phrase “conscience towards God.” People may misjudge you, but God sees clearly.

Workplace injustice is like a doctored attendance record. You clocked in on time, yet the system says you were late. The decision was your manager’s mistake, yet the meeting minutes record it as your poor execution. You can explain the facts, and sometimes you should, but often that record cannot be corrected straight away. In that moment the question is not only “What do people think of me?” but “What does heaven’s record say?” Human appraisals get things wrong; God’s ledger never does. You do not need office opinion to tell you who you are.

Peter goes on: “For you were called to this, because Christ also suffered for us, leaving you an example, that you should follow his steps.” Enduring injustice is not weakness; it is following. The self-centred life rushes to secure its own justice, to be its own king and judge. The self-emptied life still tells the truth, but leaves the final verdict to God. This does not mean tolerating wrongdoing or letting people walk all over you. If you face ongoing bullying or unlawful treatment, please seek help from someone you trust or from a professional. Endurance never means giving up protecting yourself.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Jesus is my example: he left footsteps for us to follow. My focus is on Jesus, not on my manager’s mood. My perspective shifts from the human to the divine: human verdicts are temporary; God’s approval is eternal.
lessons.scene: Zhiruo is an auditor at an accounting firm. When an engagement goes wrong, her manager tells the partner, “Zhiruo missed the note in the accounts.” In fact, the manager had told her not to check that note. As soon as the meeting ends, Zhiruo opens her phone. The message thread is still there, and her finger hovers, ready to forward the screenshot to the whole team chat…
q: Who is God? — “This is commendable with God.” What does this tell you about how God regards those who suffer for conscience’s sake?
Who am I? — When you are wronged, is your first thought “get justice now” or “keep my conscience clear before God”?
How shall I respond? — If you were Zhiruo, how could you set the record straight without a spirit of revenge?
lessons.jesus: The greatest miscarriage of justice in history happened at the place called The Skull. The only truly innocent man was executed as a criminal. He did not use heaven’s authority to overturn the verdict; he willingly bore the injustice in order to carry the guilt of people like us. When you are wronged, you are not alone: the one who left “an example” walks ahead of you.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, you know the injustice I faced at work today. Part of me wants to prove right now that I was right and let everyone know whose fault it was. Please quiet my heart first, and let my conscience be clear before you. Give me wisdom: to explain calmly when I should, and to wait and trust you when I should. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Write down one grievance and label it “handed to God”
Before replying to a message today, delete the barbed sentence
Silently pray a blessing over the person who wronged you
lessons.noon: “it is commendable if someone endures pain, suffering unjustly, because of conscience towards God” — Lord, right now I hand you this injustice and choose a clear conscience before you.

lessons.title: The Boss Who Changed the Pay Ten Times
lessons.theme: People can change your wages, but not God’s care for you

v: You know that I have served your father with all of my strength.
Your father has deceived me, and changed my wages ten times, but God didn’t allow him to hurt me.
If he said, ‘The speckled will be your wages,’ then all the flock bore speckled. If he said, ‘The streaked will be your wages,’ then all the flock bore streaked.
Thus God has taken away your father’s livestock, and given them to me.
These twenty years I have been in your house. I served you fourteen years for your two daughters, and six years for your flock, and you have changed my wages ten times.

Unless the God of my father, the God of Abraham, and the fear of Isaac, had been with me, surely now you would have sent me away empty. God has seen my affliction and the labour of my hands, and rebuked you last night.”

lessons.still: Open today’s calendar, but before you look at the meetings, look at your hands. Say to the Lord: “Lord, you see all my labour. Today I will work with all my strength and leave the outcome in your hands.”
teach: Jacob worked for his uncle Laban for twenty years: fourteen for two wives, six for a flock, consumed by drought by day and frost by night (Genesis 31:40). Worse still, Laban “changed my wages ten times.” One day the speckled animals were Jacob’s pay, the next it was the streaked. Yet Jacob’s testimony was this: “God didn’t allow him to hurt me.” Whatever the terms, the flock kept producing exactly what Jacob had been promised. Laban could rewrite the contract, but he could not outpace God’s blessing.

Today’s Laban might be the boss who keeps adjusting the bonus scheme. Just as you near your target, the target moves up; the commission you agreed is recalculated at year end. It is like chasing a carrot tied to the front of a treadmill. Jacob was not perfect: he had his own clever trick with peeled branches (Genesis 30:37–39). But in the end he admitted that what protected him was not cunning but God. He could say, “I have served your father with all of my strength.” He did his part, kept honest accounts, and left the case with the God who “has seen my affliction and the labour of my hands.”

When the self-centred life meets unfairness, it either schemes like Laban or smoulders with resentment while doing the bare minimum. Over those twenty years God slowly reshaped Jacob. The deceiver learned what it was to be deceived; he learned that real security lay not in contract terms but in “the God of Abraham” being with him. This is not a call to stop asking for what is fair; negotiate well when you need to. It is a call to move your security from the contract to God. Change your thinking and your life changes: from “I must get it back” to “God has seen.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: The Bible is my standard: serve with all your strength and do not answer scheming with scheming. People matter more than tasks: Jacob did not burn every relationship over his wages. Life first, then relationships, then ministry: God was shaping Jacob’s life in an unfair place.
lessons.scene: Yongchang is a production supervisor at an electronics factory in Penang. This year the owner has changed the performance bonus formula for the third time, and by his calculations his whole team’s year-end bonus has dropped another twenty per cent. At lunch his team start egging him on: “Boss, let’s just slow down. Working harder gets us nothing anyway!” Seven or eight pairs of eyes turn to him, waiting…
q: Who is God? — “God has seen my affliction and the labour of my hands.” What kind of God is he in your unfair situation?
Who am I? — Faced with rules that keep changing, are you more like scheming Laban or like Jacob, working hard and trusting?
How shall I respond? — How can Yongchang respond to his team without dismissing their real frustration or leading them into a go-slow?
lessons.jesus: Jesus was valued at thirty pieces of silver (Matthew 26:15), the price the law set as compensation for a slave. The Lord of all creation was grossly undervalued, yet he did not love one bit less. He let himself be undervalued so that we, who owed so much, could be bought back at the cost of his own precious blood. In God’s eyes, your worth was settled long ago.
lessons.pray: Righteous God, you see my labour at work, and you see the changes that are not fair. I admit I am resentful and have been tempted to do the bare minimum. Help me, like Jacob, to serve with all my strength, and to remember that my protection is not a contract but you. Give me courage and gentleness for what I should ask for, and peace for what I should let go. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Put this month’s work results in order and file them
Choose one task today and do it with all your strength
Hear a complaining colleague out fully before replying
lessons.noon: “God has seen my affliction and the labour of my hands” — Lord, right now I trust that you see it all, and I don’t need to get it back myself.

lessons.title: Cursed, He Did Not Curse Back
lessons.theme: Entrust yourself to him who judges righteously

v: who didn’t sin, “neither was deceit found in his mouth.”
When he was cursed, he didn’t curse back. When he suffered, he didn’t threaten, but committed himself to him who judges righteously.
When they came to the place that is called “The Skull”, they crucified him there with the criminals, one on the right and the other on the left.
Jesus said, “Father, forgive them, for they don’t know what they are doing.” Dividing his garments amongst them, they cast lots.

lessons.still: Turn your phone face down and close your eyes for ten seconds. Say to yourself: “When he was cursed, he didn’t curse back.” Then pray: “Lord, today my mouth and my fingers are yours to govern.”
teach: Peter had seen it with his own eyes. In the high priest’s courtyard he himself denied his Lord three times, while his Lord stood trial, spat upon, mocked and flogged. Years later Peter wrote: “When he was cursed, he didn’t curse back. When he suffered, he didn’t threaten, but committed himself to him who judges righteously.” Jesus was not powerless to strike back; he said he could ask his Father for “more than twelve legions of angels” (Matthew 26:53). He chose not to retaliate, not out of weakness, but because he had handed his case to a higher court.

At work, the cursing often happens in the group chat. Your manager calls you out in front of dozens of colleagues. Your fingers are already on the keyboard, a rebuttal typed, one tap from sending. In that moment you are like a surgeon holding a scalpel: the same blade can heal or wound. Not answering back does not mean never speaking; it means not swinging the same blade back. You can explain later, privately and calmly. But you need not turn a misunderstanding into a war in the heat of anger.

The word translated “committed” carries the sense of handing over, like formally transferring a case file to a judge. The self-centred life wants to be prosecutor, judge and enforcer all at once. The self-emptied life hands judgement back to God and lets God be God. Strangely, this sets your heart free: you no longer have to rehearse arguments in your head all night. Humility draws out humility; pride provokes pride. When you do not answer back, you often give the other person room to calm down too.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Let Jesus be King, and let him be my judge too. Humility means laying down power and returning to my proper place. Not answering back means laying down my “right” to win the round, and letting God be God. Rely on the Spirit with your heart rather than rehearsing counter-attacks in your head.
lessons.scene: Farah is the front office manager at a hotel chain in Singapore. After a guest complaint, the area manager posts in the all-staff group: “Farah’s team has messed up again. This standard is not fit for a supervisor.” Over twenty colleagues have seen it. Farah’s finger hovers over the screen; she has already typed three lines in reply…
q: Who is God? — Jesus entrusted himself to “him who judges righteously.” What is this God worthy of being entrusted with in your life?
Who am I? — When criticised in public, do you usually answer back, go cold, or entrust it to God?
How shall I respond? — Should Farah delete those three lines, rewrite them, or say it at another time and in another way?
lessons.jesus: On the cross, with the crowd jeering and the soldiers mocking, Jesus opened his mouth and said, “Father, forgive them, for they don’t know what they are doing.” He did not merely refrain from cursing back; he prayed for those who cursed him. That prayer includes me. I too have wounded others with my words, and he has opened the door of forgiveness to me.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, you did not curse back, but I so often insist on the last word. If someone criticises me publicly today, please guard my fingers and my lips. I hand this matter over to you, for you judge righteously. Help me to explain calmly what needs explaining, and to pray for the person who criticised me. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: When angry, wait ten minutes before pressing send
Write your rebuttal on paper, pray, then decide
Pray for whoever upset you today: “Father, forgive them”
lessons.noon: “When he was cursed, he didn’t curse back” — Lord, right now I give you the words I want to say.

lessons.title: Raising a Concern in the Right Spirit
lessons.theme: Seeking justice and fearing God can go hand in hand

v: But Daniel purposed in his heart that he would not defile himself with the king’s delicacies, nor with the wine which he drank. Therefore he requested of the prince of the eunuchs that he might not defile himself.
Now God made Daniel find kindness and compassion in the sight of the prince of the eunuchs.

The prince of the eunuchs said to Daniel, “I fear my lord the king, who has appointed your food and your drink. For why should he see your faces worse looking than the youths who are of your own age? Then you would endanger my head with the king.”
Then Daniel said to the steward whom the prince of the eunuchs had appointed over Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah:
“Test your servants, I beg you, ten days; and let them give us vegetables to eat and water to drink.

But Paul said to them, “They have beaten us publicly without a trial, men who are Romans, and have cast us into prison! Do they now release us secretly? No, most certainly, but let them come themselves and bring us out!”
The sergeants reported these words to the magistrates, and they were afraid when they heard that they were Romans,
and they came and begged them. When they had brought them out, they asked them to depart from the city.

lessons.still: Write today’s difficult conversation in one line and place it on your desk. Rest both hands on it and pray: “Lord, I want to speak the truth with reverence. Give me courage, and give me gentleness.”
teach: Peter calls us to endure injustice, yet Scripture also shows God’s servants raising concerns in proper ways. In the Babylonian court Daniel did not want to eat the king’s food. He did not stage a hunger strike; he “requested of the prince of the eunuchs” and offered a workable proposal: “Test your servants, I beg you, ten days.” In Philippi, Paul was beaten and jailed without trial. When the magistrates wanted to release him quietly, he replied, “Do they now release us secretly? No, most certainly.” He used his lawful rights as a Roman citizen, not to vent his anger, but perhaps to secure fair treatment for the young church in that city.

A formal complaint is like a hospital’s incident reporting system. It exists not to settle scores but to stop the same error from harming the next patient. When you face unreasonable overtime, unlawful demands or harassment, raising it through proper channels is responsible towards your company, your colleagues and God. But how you report matters. Bring facts, not humiliation. Offer solutions, not just anger. Respect the other person’s position, and do not spread gossip. Daniel’s ten-day test was a proposal that gave his superior a way to say yes without losing face.

Endurance and raising concerns are not opposites; the question is motive. Is it for a clear conscience before God, or to win? A self-centred complaint wants the other side to look bad; a self-emptied complaint wants things put right. Obedience has limits: “We must obey God rather than men” (Acts 5:29). If something involves illegality, safety or bullying, please do not struggle on alone; speak to someone you trust, to HR, or to a professional. Letting Jesus be King includes letting him reign over the email you write.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The Bible is my standard: Daniel had resolve and courtesy; Paul had principle and restraint. The order of relationships is God, self, others, tasks. Seek justice in the matter, but never wound people for the sake of the matter.
lessons.scene: Yuxuan is a firmware engineer at a tech company in Hsinchu. For three months the project has demanded overtime until midnight, with no overtime pay at all. In a private chat his teammates rage about the boss, and someone suggests leaking it anonymously online. Yuxuan has a complete record of his clock-in times. He stares at the screen: leak it, put up with it, or find another way?
q: Who is God? — “God made Daniel find kindness and compassion in the sight of the prince of the eunuchs.” How does God work as we raise our concerns?
Who am I? — When you have stood up for your rights before, was your motive to put things right, or to make the other side look bad?
How shall I respond? — How could Yuxuan, like Daniel, raise a concern with facts, a proposal and respect?
lessons.jesus: At his trial an officer struck Jesus in the face. Jesus said, “If I have spoken evil, testify of the evil; but if well, why do you beat me?” (John 18:23). He did not hit back, yet he calmly named the injustice. His gentleness was not silent weakness but strength with truth and restraint. And still he went on to the cross, to save the very people who treated him unjustly.
lessons.pray: Lord, you see what is unreasonable in our workplace. I do not want simply to swallow it, nor to wreck things in anger. Give me Daniel’s wisdom to speak with grace, facts and a proposal, and Paul’s courage not to shrink back when I need to stand up. Let even my complaint become an act of worship to you. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Write the relevant facts as a timeline, no adjectives
Draft one concrete improvement to go with your concern
Talk first with a trusted senior colleague or HR
lessons.noon: “Test your servants, I beg you, ten days” — Lord, right now give me a proposal full of wisdom and gentleness.

lessons.title: Pulling Up the Root of Bitterness
lessons.theme: Don’t let bitterness take root; be kind and forgive one another

v: Follow after peace with all men, and the sanctification without which no man will see the Lord,
looking carefully lest there be any man who falls short of the grace of God, lest any root of bitterness springing up trouble you and many be defiled by it,
Let all bitterness, wrath, anger, outcry, and slander be put away from you, with all malice.
And be kind to one another, tender hearted, forgiving each other, just as God also in Christ forgave you.

lessons.still: Take three deep breaths. Each time you breathe out, picture gently pulling out a splinter. Say to the Lord: “Lord, search my heart. If there is a root of bitterness, help me pull it up today.”
teach: The writer to the Hebrews uses a gardener’s image: “lest any root of bitterness springing up trouble you and many be defiled by it.” A root lives underground, out of sight, but it grows, spreads and can eventually ruin the whole garden. Bitterness usually begins with a real hurt: an unfair appraisal, credit taken from you, a cutting remark. Being hurt is not a sin. But if someone “falls short of the grace of God” and lets that wound ferment in the dark, it grows into bitterness.

Bitterness is like a forgotten lunch box at the back of the office fridge. At first there is just a faint smell, and nobody bothers to deal with it. A few weeks later, everything in the fridge has picked up that sour odour. Resentment towards your manager eventually seeps into your tone with colleagues, your patience with customers, even the way you speak to your children at home. Paul says: “Let all bitterness, wrath, anger, outcry, and slander be put away from you, with all malice.” Putting away does not mean pressing it down; it means bringing it out and handing it over.

This week we have learned to endure injustice, to entrust ourselves to God, and to raise concerns rightly. The last lesson goes deepest: the heart. The self-emptied life does not pretend it was never hurt; it lets grace flow into the deepest part of the wound. Paul gives the remedy: “be kind to one another, tender hearted, forgiving each other, just as God also in Christ forgave you.” Forgiveness does not say the other person was right, nor does it restore trust overnight. It hands God the right to collect the debt. Rely on the Spirit with your heart instead of replaying it in your head, and you will find that the first person set free is you.
lessons.light: 321 Light: A changed life changes daily living: once bitterness is cleared out, the whole atmosphere of life changes. 920: the manager who hurt you is also one of your “2”, the people God has placed around you. Practising the self-emptied “0” towards him is how the “9”, the fruit of the Spirit such as kindness and patience, grows.
lessons.scene: Huiling has taught at an independent Chinese secondary school in Kuala Lumpur for twelve years. This year the deputy head of department post went to a colleague who joined only three years ago and is close to the principal. Huiling offered her congratulations, then lay awake all night. Tomorrow’s department meeting is the new deputy’s first time chairing, and Huiling is first on the agenda to present…
q: Who is God? — “Just as God also in Christ forgave you.” How has God treated everything you owed him?
Who am I? — Is there a forgotten lunch box at the back of your heart that you have never dealt with?
How shall I respond? — At tomorrow’s meeting, what concrete step could Huiling take to refuse bitterness a place to take root?
lessons.jesus: Jesus was betrayed, denied and deserted by his closest friends. After his resurrection he prepared a charcoal fire and fish for Peter on the shore. He did not rake over the past; he simply asked Peter whether he loved him. That fire was the warmest forgiveness the world has known. Because he forgave us first, we have strength to pull up the root of bitterness.
lessons.pray: Loving Father, you know the wounded place in my heart. I do not want it to grow into bitterness that poisons my work and my family. Water me with the forgiveness of Christ, so that I can show kindness to the person who hurt me. I hand you the right to collect this debt. Please heal me, and bless them. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Write down the name that stirs bitterness, and pray for them
Don’t bring up that old matter behind anyone’s back today
Give that colleague one sincere word of appreciation
lessons.noon: “be kind to one another, tender hearted, forgiving each other” — Lord, right now pull up the root of bitterness in my heart.

mem.t: As for you, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good, to save many people alive, as is happening today.

lessons.title: Steward in Potiphar’s House
lessons.theme: The LORD was with him, and even a slave’s work was blessed

v: Joseph was brought down to Egypt. Potiphar, an officer of Pharaoh’s, the captain of the guard, an Egyptian, bought him from the hand of the Ishmaelites that had brought him down there.
The LORD was with Joseph, and he was a prosperous man. He was in the house of his master the Egyptian.
His master saw that the LORD was with him, and that the LORD made all that he did prosper in his hand.
Joseph found favour in his sight. He ministered to him, and Potiphar made him overseer over his house, and all that he had he put into his hand.

From the time that he made him overseer in his house, and over all that he had, the LORD blessed the Egyptian’s house for Joseph’s sake. The LORD’s blessing was on all that he had, in the house and in the field.
He left all that he had in Joseph’s hand. He didn’t concern himself with anything, except for the food which he ate. Joseph was well-built and handsome.

lessons.still: Before you push open the office or shop door, pause with your hand on the handle. Say to the Lord: “Lord, you were with Joseph, and you are with me. Bless this place today for my sake.”
teach: At seventeen Joseph was sold by his own brothers, passed from hand to hand down to Egypt, and became a slave in the house of Potiphar, captain of the guard. The latest line on his CV read “slave”. Yet by verse two the chapter’s great refrain appears: “The LORD was with Joseph, and he was a prosperous man.” Even his master, who did not know the LORD, could see it: “His master saw that the LORD was with him.” Perhaps Joseph missed his father and wept at night. But by day he did the work in front of him, until his master put “all that he had” into his hand.

Picture a manager posted to an unfashionable branch. Head office seems to have forgotten the shop; customers are few. Yet every day she straightens the shelves, scrubs the toilets and treats each customer like an honoured guest. Six months later the branch quietly climbs the sales report. The corners people overlook, God sees. Joseph’s prosperity was not luck; it was the fruit of God’s presence and faithful work: “the LORD blessed the Egyptian’s house for Joseph’s sake.” A Christian at work can become a channel of blessing to a whole team.

This week’s theme is being used by God in adversity. The first lesson of adversity is not escape but staying with God where you are. The self-centred life says, “Once I get a better position, I’ll really try.” The self-emptied life says, “The Lord is here, so I will be faithful here.” Life first, then relationships, then ministry: God built life in Joseph first, and only then entrusted him with a household, a prison and a nation. Your present post may be the very training ground God has prepared for you.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The Holy Spirit is my guide: God’s presence is the source of every true success. Let Jesus receive all the glory: Joseph’s good work made his master see that “the LORD was with him”, not how capable Joseph was.
lessons.scene: Guanlin is a new graduate with a business degree, but he has been posted to the property management office of a building in Taichung, handling repair requests, recycling and parking disputes all day. In the class group chat his friends are sharing job offers from multinationals. He looks at his seventh repair slip of the day and thinks, “What am I even doing here?” At the counter, the next resident is already banging on the desk…
q: Who is God? — “The LORD was with Joseph.” What did this mean for a slave who had been sold? What does it mean for you?
Who am I? — Are you also waiting for a better position before you give your best?
How shall I respond? — How can Guanlin face the resident banging on the desk in a way that shows God is with him?
lessons.jesus: Jesus “emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Philippians 2:7). The Lord of heaven came to earth as servant of all, stooping to wash his disciples’ feet. Joseph was forced into slavery; Jesus chose to become a servant. Because of him, our humblest work is lifted up and becomes an altar of service to God.
lessons.pray: Lord who was with Joseph, thank you that you are with me today. I confess I often feel my work is insignificant, and I compare and complain. Help me to be faithful in this post, and to receive every task and every customer as coming from your hand. For my sake, bless this team. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Before going in, pray: “Lord, you are with me”
Do your least noticed task to the highest standard
Ask God once today to bless your manager and company
lessons.noon: “The LORD was with Joseph, and he was a prosperous man” — Lord, right now I rely not on luck but on your presence.

lessons.title: How Can I Do This Great Wickedness?
lessons.theme: Refusing temptation because I live before God

v: After these things, his master’s wife set her eyes on Joseph; and she said, “Lie with me.”
But he refused, and said to his master’s wife, “Behold, my master doesn’t know what is with me in the house, and he has put all that he has into my hand.
No one is greater in this house than I am, and he has not kept back anything from me but you, because you are his wife. How then can I do this great wickedness, and sin against God?”
As she spoke to Joseph day by day, he didn’t listen to her, to lie by her, or to be with her.
About this time, he went into the house to do his work, and there were none of the men of the house inside.
She caught him by his garment, saying, “Lie with me!” He left his garment in her hand, and ran outside.

lessons.still: Stand up and plant your feet firmly, as though standing on a clear boundary line. Pray: “Lord, in every place no one else can see today, remind me that you are here.”
teach: Joseph’s temptation came daily, came close, and came with power behind it. His master’s wife “set her eyes on Joseph”, and she spoke to him “day by day”. His answer is worth memorising: “How then can I do this great wickedness, and sin against God?” First he spoke of his master’s trust: “he has put all that he has into my hand.” Then of the boundary: “he has not kept back anything from me but you.” Finally of the root issue: sinning against God. He was not merely afraid of being caught; he knew he lived before God. On the day the house was empty, he left his garment and ran.

Workplace temptation often appears when “there were none of the men of the house inside”: the hotel on a business trip, the late-night private message, the envelope a client slips you, the expense claim no one will check. It is like a cyber-security firewall. Real protection is not set up when the hacker arrives; the rules are written in advance: which connections are always refused, which ports are never opened. Joseph would not “lie by her, or be with her”. He refused not only the act but even the proximity. Running away is not shameful; it is wise.

Joseph said “How can I?”, not merely “I mustn’t.” This is a matter of identity, not only of rules. The self-centred life asks, “What happens if I do it? Will I get caught?” The self-emptied life asks, “Is this worthy of the God who is with me?” After obeying, Joseph lost his garment, lost his job, and was falsely accused and imprisoned. Doing right does not guarantee an immediate reward. But God values a pure heart above a respectable title. Guarding your heart is the deepest foundation for being an overcomer at work.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The order of relationships is God, self, others, tasks. Joseph looked to God first, before his master’s trust and his own desires. With our focus on Jesus we find strength to flee temptation, our perspective shifting from passing pleasure to eternal glory.
lessons.scene: Samuel is a sales manager for a building supplies company in Auckland, and he is married. For six months he has often travelled with a saleswoman from a partner firm, and lately she has started messaging him late at night to share personal troubles. Tonight in Wellington, after a client dinner, she says in the hotel lift, “Come to my room for another drink? We can go over tomorrow’s presentation.” The lift doors are about to open…
q: Who is God? — “Sin against God?” How did Joseph know the God who sees in secret?
Who am I? — Where no one can see, what are your boundaries? Who is your firewall?
How shall I respond? — When the lift doors open, what should Samuel say, and which way should he walk?
lessons.jesus: When Jesus was tempted in the wilderness, he answered each time with “It is written.” Hebrews tells us he is one “who has been in all points tempted like we are, yet without sin” (Hebrews 4:15). He overcame temptation, and he feels our weakness. When we fall, his cross opens the way home.
lessons.pray: Holy Lord, you know where I am weak. When I travel, work late, am alone, or face temptation, remind me that you are right here. Give me Joseph’s courage to refuse what must be refused and to run when I must run. Guard my heart, my family and my integrity, and let me live before you even in hidden places. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Write down one boundary you will keep today
End one flirtatious or inappropriate conversation today
Ask a spiritual companion to hold you accountable
lessons.noon: “How then can I do this great wickedness, and sin against God?” — Lord, right now remind me that you are here.

lessons.title: Faithful in Prison
lessons.theme: Even at the lowest point, God is present and service is possible

v: Joseph’s master took him, and put him into the prison, the place where the king’s prisoners were bound, and he was there in custody.
But the LORD was with Joseph, and showed kindness to him, and gave him favour in the sight of the keeper of the prison.
The keeper of the prison committed to Joseph’s hand all the prisoners who were in the prison. Whatever they did there, he was responsible for it.
The keeper of the prison didn’t look after anything that was under his hand, because the LORD was with him; and that which he did, the LORD made it prosper.
Joseph came in to them in the morning, and saw them, and saw that they were sad.
He asked Pharaoh’s officers who were with him in custody in his master’s house, saying, “Why do you look so sad today?”
They said to him, “We have dreamt a dream, and there is no one who can interpret it.” Joseph said to them, “Don’t interpretations belong to God? Please tell it to me.”

lessons.still: On your commute, notice one weary stranger near you. Pray silently: “Lord, even if I am low today, let me notice the sadness on other people’s faces.”
teach: Joseph fell from steward to prisoner, and on a false charge. Yet the refrain returns: “But the LORD was with Joseph.” The place changed and his status changed, but God did not. Before long the keeper of the prison “committed to Joseph’s hand all the prisoners”. More beautiful still, Joseph did not wallow in his own injustice. One morning he noticed that two of Pharaoh’s officers “were sad”, and asked, “Why do you look so sad today?” A man full of his own grievances could still see other people’s sorrow. That is God’s work within him.

Being demoted, moved to a forgotten department, or taking casual work after redundancy is like a phone switching to low-power mode. Many features shut down, the screen dims, only the basics keep running. But the most important functions stay on: you can still call and still connect. The low point of a career is the same.
