Your connection with God, your care for people, your faithfulness in small things are all still there. Joseph did not say, “I’ll help once I’m out.” He said, “Don’t interpretations belong to God? Please tell it to me.”

When the cupbearer was released, he forgot Joseph for two full years (Genesis 41:1). Faithfulness does not guarantee being remembered, but God does not forget. At the lowest point the self-centred life sees only its own wrongs and shrinks; the self-emptied life still asks others, “Are you all right today?” and somehow grows larger. Change your thinking and your life changes: the low point is not where God is absent but the workshop where he most often shapes us. If you are facing unemployment or demotion, let people you trust walk with you; you need not carry it alone.
lessons.light: 321 Light: People matter more than tasks: in prison Joseph still kept people in his heart. 920: the officers in custody were Joseph’s “2”, people God placed near him; at his lowest point he practised the self-emptied “0” and bore the “9”, fruit like goodness and kindness. Focus on Jesus, not on circumstances.
lessons.scene: Yongqing was a purchasing supervisor at a logistics company in Shenzhen. Because she refused to tamper with a quotation, she was moved to the warehouse to do stock counts, and her pay grade dropped. This morning she sees an older warehouse worker crouched in a corner between the shelves, quietly wiping away tears. Yongqing’s own heart is in turmoil. She stands still, wondering whether to go over…
q: Who is God? — “But the LORD was with Joseph.” How did God show his presence in the prison?
Who am I? — When you are low, do you mostly see your own wrongs, or can you still see other people’s needs?
How shall I respond? — Should Yongqing go over? What could she say or do?
lessons.jesus: On the cross, in terrible agony, Jesus still turned to the criminal beside him and promised, “Assuredly I tell you, today you will be with me in Paradise” (Luke 23:43). At the very lowest point he still saw a desperate man. This same Lord sees you in your low place today.
lessons.pray: Lord, sometimes I feel thrown into prison and forgotten. Thank you that you never leave me. When I am low, help me still to do the small things well and to notice the sorrowful people around me. I trust your timing. Guard my heart from turning bitter in this low place. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Ask one colleague today: “Are you all right?”
Finish one small assigned task fully and on time
Write on a sticky note: God has not forgotten me
lessons.noon: “But the LORD was with Joseph” — Lord, right now in this low place, I still believe you are with me.

lessons.title: From Prison to Prime Minister
lessons.theme: When God’s time comes, he opens the door himself

v: Then Pharaoh sent and called Joseph, and they brought him hastily out of the dungeon. He shaved himself, changed his clothing, and came in to Pharaoh.
Pharaoh said to Joseph, “I have dreamt a dream, and there is no one who can interpret it. I have heard it said of you, that when you hear a dream you can interpret it.”
Joseph answered Pharaoh, saying, “It isn’t in me. God will give Pharaoh an answer of peace.”
Pharaoh said to his servants, “Can we find such a one as this, a man in whom is the Spirit of God?”
Pharaoh said to Joseph, “Because God has shown you all of this, there is no one so discreet and wise as you.
You shall be over my house. All my people will be ruled according to your word. Only in the throne I will be greater than you.”
Pharaoh said to Joseph, “Behold, I have set you over all the land of Egypt.”

lessons.still: Glance at the time on your phone, then put the phone down. Pray: “Lord, my times are in your hands. Today I will not rush ahead, and I will not give up.”
teach: Joseph was seventeen when he was sold (Genesis 37:2) and thirty when he stood before Pharaoh (Genesis 41:46): thirteen years in between. When Pharaoh called, “they brought him hastily out of the dungeon”. Thirteen years of waiting were reversed in a single day. Standing before the most powerful man in Egypt, Joseph’s first words were, “It isn’t in me. God will give Pharaoh an answer of peace.” He did not seize the chance to sell himself or plead his case; he pointed to God. So Pharaoh said, “Can we find such a one as this, a man in whom is the Spirit of God?”

God’s timing is like a baker proving dough. It must rest and rise; rush it into the oven and you get a brick. Through those thirteen years God was proving Joseph, turning a boy who carried tales about his brothers into a leader who understood service, humility and the human heart. Looking for work, waiting for promotion, waiting for a business breakthrough, you may feel you have been left on the shelf. But the real question is not “Why is it taking so long?” but “What is God making of me in this season?”

The moment of promotion is the moment pride most easily slips in. Yet Joseph said, “It isn’t in me.” Humility means laying down power and returning to your proper place. The self-centred life, once promoted, rushes to prove itself; the self-emptied life, once promoted, sees more clearly who promoted it. Pharaoh entrusted all Egypt to Joseph because those thirteen years had already formed in him “a man in whom is the Spirit of God”. Success is not proof, and failure is not condemnation. On God’s timetable, waiting is part of the work.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Let Jesus receive all the glory: “It isn’t in me.” Among the eight steps, this is repetition: through waiting after waiting, God engraved a new way of thinking into Joseph’s life. Our perspective turns from the temporary to the eternal.
lessons.scene: Jianjun is forty-five. He was a structural engineer at a design institute in Chengdu until a department merger; he has now been out of work for almost two years, getting by on freelance drawing checks. Today he finally sits in an interview room at a large construction firm. The interviewer flips through his CV and asks, “How do you explain this two-year gap?” He doesn’t know whether to tell it as failure, or as a different kind of story…
q: Who is God? — From Joseph’s thirteen years of waiting, what do you learn about God’s timing?
Who am I? — While waiting, do you more often ask “Why so long?” or “What is God making of me?”
How shall I respond? — How could Jianjun answer the interviewer honestly and with hope?
lessons.jesus: Jesus “was about thirty years old” when he began his ministry (Luke 3:23). At the wedding in Cana he said, “My hour has not yet come.” All his life he submitted to his Father’s timetable, even to the cross. His journey from the tomb to the throne is the greatest reversal in history, and every reversal in our lives is hidden in his resurrection.
lessons.pray: God who holds time in your hands, you know how long I have waited and how anxious I feel. In these days, shape me into a vessel after your own heart. If you open the door, let me say “It isn’t in me” and give you the glory. If I must wait longer, let me rest content in your hands while you work in me. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Write down one thing God has done in you while waiting
Do one small thing to prepare for the future today
When someone praises you, reply: “Thank God”
lessons.noon: “It isn’t in me. God will give Pharaoh an answer of peace.” — Lord, right now I turn my focus from myself back to you.

lessons.title: God Meant It for Good
lessons.theme: Above every harm and injustice, God has a greater purpose

v: When Joseph’s brothers saw that their father was dead, they said, “It may be that Joseph will hate us, and will fully pay us back for all the evil which we did to him.”
They sent a message to Joseph, saying, “Your father commanded before he died, saying,

‘You shall tell Joseph, “Now please forgive the disobedience of your brothers, and their sin, because they did evil to you.”’ Now, please forgive the disobedience of the servants of the God of your father.” Joseph wept when they spoke to him.
His brothers also went and fell down before his face; and they said, “Behold, we are your servants.”
Joseph said to them, “Don’t be afraid, for am I in the place of God?
As for you, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good, to save many people alive, as is happening today.
Now therefore don’t be afraid. I will provide for you and your little ones.” He comforted them, and spoke kindly to them.

lessons.still: Put today’s biggest worry into one sentence in your mind. Then say to the Lord: “Lord, I cannot see through what people intend, but I believe you mean it for good.”
teach: After Jacob died, Joseph’s brothers were afraid: “It may be that Joseph will hate us.” They fell down before him and said, “Behold, we are your servants.” Joseph held all the authority of Egypt; revenge would have been easy. Instead he wept and said, “Don’t be afraid, for am I in the place of God? As for you, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good, to save many people alive.” Joseph did not deny his brothers’ evil; he said plainly, “you meant evil against me.” But he placed that evil beneath God’s greater purpose.

It is like a piece of embroidery. From the back you see knots and loose threads and clashing colours, with no visible pattern; turn it over and a complete picture appears. Redundancy, betrayal and unwanted transfers at work are the knots on the back. In prison Joseph could not see the front, but God wasted not a single stitch. The knot you cannot understand today may be the very stitch that one day helps “to save many people alive”.

“Am I in the place of God?” This question is the watershed between the self-centred life and the self-emptied life. The self-centred life wants to take God’s place: keeping the accounts, taking revenge, deciding who should be punished. The self-emptied life lets God be God and lets people be people: it calls evil evil, yet hands judgement to God, and then chooses to comfort and speak kindly. This week we have watched Joseph go from slave to prisoner to prime minister. But his greatest victory was not reaching high office; it was forgiving from high office. The goal of being used by God in adversity is to become a blessing to others.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The self-centred life wants to take God’s place; the self-emptied life lets God be God. Humility draws out humility: Joseph’s forgiveness restored a broken family. Building God’s order: through one forgiving man God saved many lives.
lessons.scene: Ruth runs a small accounting practice in Christchurch. Three years ago her business partner left to set up on her own, taking half the clients. Now that former partner’s firm is facing a tax audit and running out of cash. She phones Ruth: “I know I have no right to ask, but could you look over my books?” Ruth holds the phone, silent for several seconds…
q: Who is God? — “God meant it for good.” How can you see God’s good purpose in your own story?
Who am I? — Is there someone you want to judge, as if you stood “in the place of God”?
How shall I respond? — How should Ruth respond? How can forgiveness and sensible boundaries go together?
lessons.jesus: The cross is the ultimate case of people meaning evil and God meaning it for good. Betrayal, false accusation, crucifixion: human evil reached its peak there, yet God used it to bring salvation and save countless lives. The risen Jesus stood among his disciples and said, “Peace be to you,” just as Joseph told his brothers, “Don’t be afraid.”
lessons.pray: God who rules over all things, some hurts still make no sense to me. Thank you that you mean it for good. Take away my desire to stand in your place, and help me leave judgement to you. Give me Joseph’s tenderness to speak comfort to those who hurt me, and wisdom to set healthy boundaries. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Write down an old hurt, and beside it: God meant it for good
Speak one word without a barb to someone who wronged you
Memorise Genesis 50:20 and recite it at lunch
lessons.noon: “you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good” — Lord, right now I hand you what I cannot understand.

mem.t: Two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their labour.

lessons.title: A Threefold Cord
lessons.theme: God designed us to overcome together, not as lone heroes

v: Two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their labour.
For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow; but woe to him who is alone when he falls, and doesn’t have another to lift him up.
Again, if two lie together, then they have warmth; but how can one keep warm alone?
If a man prevails against one who is alone, two shall withstand him; and a threefold cord is not quickly broken.

lessons.still: Interlace your fingers and feel your two hands holding each other up. Pray: “Lord, today keep me from pushing on alone and proud; make me willing to work alongside others.”
teach: The Teacher in Ecclesiastes surveys labour under the sun and sees “one who is alone, and he has neither son nor brother. There is no end to all of his labour” (Ecclesiastes 4:8). Then he says: “Two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their labour.” He paints three pictures: when one falls, the other lifts him up; on a cold night two keep each other warm; under attack, two can withstand the enemy. The last line is the best: “a threefold cord is not quickly broken.” Many believers see the third strand as God in the middle. That is not the literal meaning, but it is a fine application.

Work culture worships the hero who “handles it all”: rewriting the slides alone at midnight, carrying the whole project single-handed. But every scaffolder on a building site knows the strongest scaffold does not depend on the thickest pole. It depends on the diagonal braces clamped across one another. A single pole, however thick, will sway; poles locked together can hold up a whole building. Teams are the same. Your strengths brace a colleague’s weaknesses, and their strengths cover your blind spots. “Woe to him who is alone when he falls, and doesn’t have another to lift him up.”

The self-centred life would rather burn out than ask for help, because asking feels like admitting you are not good enough. Or it wants to be the thickest pole so everyone notices. The self-emptied life admits it needs others and gladly becomes a support to them. In 235, the “2” is a spiritual companion: at work you need at least one person who prays with you and holds you up. This week we learn to live out “two are better than one” in our teams.
lessons.light: 321 Light: 235 begins with the “2”: find one spiritual companion, then build a team. Relationships matter more than things: a partnership of one heart lasts longer than a glittering individual performance. Let Jesus be the third strand in the middle of your team.
lessons.scene: Shuyu is a freelance illustrator in Taipei who has run a one-woman studio for five years, often working through the night to meet deadlines. Recently a sister from church who works in animation invited her to set up a studio together and take on major brand projects. Shuyu worries about arguments over roles and unclear profit-sharing. Used to calling all the shots, she stares at the partnership proposal email and still hasn’t pressed reply…
q: Who is God? — “They have a good reward for their labour.” What does this reveal about God’s intention in creating us?
Who am I? — Do you tend to go it alone, or do you gladly work alongside others? Why?
How shall I respond? — How could Shuyu reply to the proposal with prayer and clear agreements?
lessons.jesus: When Jesus sent out his followers, he “sent them two by two” (Luke 10:1). In his deepest anguish in Gethsemane he took three disciples with him and said, “Stay here and watch with me” (Matthew 26:38). If the Son of God valued companions, so should we. And he himself has become the companion who will never leave us.
lessons.pray: Triune God, you yourself are the eternal fellowship of Father, Son and Holy Spirit. Tear down the pride in me that says “I have to do everything myself”. Make me willing to ask for help and glad to support others. In my team today, let me be one of those braces locked together with the rest. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Ask a colleague to help you with one thing today
Spend ten minutes helping a stuck colleague think it through
Message a spiritual companion at work to check in
lessons.noon: “a threefold cord is not quickly broken” — Lord, right now be the third strand in the middle of our team.

lessons.title: The Eye Can’t Tell the Hand
lessons.theme: A team is like a body: every member is necessary

v: But now God has set the members, each one of them, in the body, just as he desired.
If they were all one member, where would the body be?
But now they are many members, but one body.
The eye can’t tell the hand, “I have no need for you,” or again the head to the feet, “I have no need for you.”
No, much rather, those members of the body which seem to be weaker are necessary.
When one member suffers, all the members suffer with it. When one member is honoured, all the members rejoice with it.

lessons.still: Wiggle your fingers and roll your shoulders, thanking God for every part of your body. Pray: “Lord, today help me notice the least noticed person on my team.”
teach: The Corinthian church was richly gifted but loved comparison. Some thought themselves the most spiritual; others thought themselves useless. Paul uses the picture of a body: “God has set the members, each one of them, in the body, just as he desired.” Position is God’s placement, not something we grab. He says, “The eye can’t tell the hand, ‘I have no need for you’”; and more surprisingly, “those members of the body which seem to be weaker are necessary.” You might barely use your elbow for a month, but your heart cannot stop for a second. The least visible parts are often the most vital.

Picture a restaurant. The head chef gives television interviews; the front-of-house manager is all smiles. But if the dishwasher calls in sick, by eight o’clock there is not a clean plate in the place. Even the finest steak has to be served on something. Workplaces have visible roles, such as sales, presenters and those who collect the awards, and invisible ones, such as systems support, warehousing, accounts and cleaning. A godly team deliberately sees and honours the invisible people, because God gives “more abundant honour to the inferior part”.

“When one member suffers, all the members suffer with it. When one member is honoured, all the members rejoice with it.” This is a team’s thermometer. The self-centred life sees someone suffer and thinks, “Glad it’s not me”; sees someone honoured and feels a twinge of envy. The self-emptied life can weep with them and rejoice with them, knowing we belong to one body whose head is Christ. People matter more than tasks: the most precious thing in a team is not its processes but members who care for one another.
lessons.light: 321 Light: People matter more than tasks: every person is a member placed by God’s own hand. Humility means returning to my proper place: not grabbing someone else’s role, and not despising my own. With our focus on Christ the head, we stop ranking the members.
lessons.scene: Ben has worked night shifts in systems support for a bank’s IT department in Singapore for three years. Every time an upgrade succeeds, the thank-you email goes to the daytime project team; no one mentions the crew watching screens at three in the morning. Today his manager asks him to fill in a form: “Will you continue on night shift next year?” He stops at the box marked “Reason”, the cursor blinking…
q: Who is God? — “God has set the members… just as he desired.” How does this God view the role you hold now?
Who am I? — Are you more prone to think “I don’t need others” or “others don’t need me”?
How shall I respond? — How should Ben fill in that box? And how could he honour the other invisible people on his team?
lessons.jesus: Jesus is the head of the church, yet he chose the least honoured places: born in a manger, raised in despised Nazareth, crucified outside the city wall. He has given “more abundant honour” to people like us who are lacking. In him, no member is surplus to requirements.
lessons.pray: Lord, thank you for placing me in this team and this role. Heal the comparison in my heart, so that I despise neither others nor myself. Help me see the colleagues who serve quietly, and give them the honour they deserve. May we weep together and rejoice together, because we all belong to you. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Thank one behind-the-scenes colleague specifically
Mention a backroom colleague’s contribution in a meeting
When a colleague is knocked back, send a caring message
lessons.noon: “When one member is honoured, all the members rejoice with it” — Lord, right now help me truly rejoice in my colleague’s success.

lessons.title: Holding Up Moses’ Hands
lessons.theme: Those on the front line need people holding them up

v: So Joshua did as Moses had told him, and fought with Amalek; and Moses, Aaron, and Hur went up to the top of the hill.
When Moses held up his hand, Israel prevailed. When he let down his hand, Amalek prevailed.

But Moses’ hands were heavy; so they took a stone, and put it under him, and he sat on it. Aaron and Hur held up his hands, the one on the one side, and the other on the other side. His hands were steady until sunset.
Joshua defeated Amalek and his people with the edge of the sword.

lessons.still: Raise both arms for ten seconds and feel them start to grow heavy. As you lower them, pray: “Lord, today let me hold up someone’s heavy hands, and let me allow others to hold up mine.”
teach: Israel’s first battle after leaving Egypt was fought in an unusual way: Joshua fought in the valley while Moses raised his hands on the hilltop. “When Moses held up his hand, Israel prevailed. When he let down his hand, Amalek prevailed.” The problem is that even the most spiritual hands get tired: “Moses’ hands were heavy.” So Aaron and Hur brought a stone for him to sit on, and held up his hands, “the one on the one side, and the other on the other side. His hands were steady until sunset.” The victory was God’s, yet it was won through a team.

It is like a resuscitation in an emergency department. One doctor does chest compressions while a nurse prepares drugs, someone keeps time, someone manages the airway. After two minutes even the strongest arms tire, so someone calls “Swap!” and another person takes over at once. Nobody thinks swapping is shameful, because the goal is that the patient lives. Work is the same: Joshua on the front line, Moses on the hill, and Aaron and Hur, the rarely remembered support. A team stays “steady until sunset” because someone is willing to carry a stone and hold up an arm.

Moses was humble enough to sit down and be helped; Aaron and Hur were humble enough to serve unseen. A self-centred leader hides their exhaustion; a self-centred colleague only wants to be Joshua. A self-emptied team covers for one another, with eyes fixed on God alone. Moses later built an altar and called it “The LORD our Banner”. Pushing on endlessly is not the same as being spiritual. If you are already burnt out, let your team share the load, and if needed seek help from someone you trust or a professional.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The “5” in 235 is a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades, each in their place and covering for one another. Humility draws out humility: when the leader admits weakness, the team is willing to help. Let Jesus receive all the glory: the banner is the LORD’s, not Moses’.
lessons.scene: Meifeng is the ward manager of a medical ward at a hospital in Kaohsiung. Three nurses resigned this month, and she has now worked twelve days in a row; yesterday she nearly fainted at the nurses’ station. A senior colleague takes her aside: “Give the rota to me and the team leaders. Go home early today.” Meifeng says, “I’m fine,” but her hand is still gripping the rota…
q: Who is God? — The victory came from God, yet he worked through Aaron and Hur holding up Moses’ hands. What does this show about how God likes to work?
Who am I? — In your team, are you more often a Moses who won’t be helped, or a Hur who will carry the stone?
How shall I respond? — Should Meifeng let go of the rota? How could she let her team hold her up?
lessons.jesus: On the road to Golgotha, the soldiers “grabbed one Simon of Cyrene… and laid the cross on him to carry it after Jesus” (Luke 23:26). The Lord who upholds all things allowed a stranger to share his load. He was not afraid to be seen in weakness, because he came precisely to carry the burden of sin we could never carry.
lessons.pray: The LORD our Banner, I confess that I often push on alone and won’t let anyone see that my hands are heavy. Give me humility to sit down and be helped, and eyes to see whose hands on my team are growing heavy, so that I will carry a stone for them. Let us hold steady together until sunset. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Hand one task to a colleague today instead of doing it all
Ask your manager or a colleague: “What can I take on for you?”
Pray specifically for the most exhausted person on your team
lessons.noon: “His hands were steady until sunset” — Lord, right now hold up my heavy hands, and let me hold up others’.

lessons.title: I Planted, Apollos Watered
lessons.theme: Don’t hoard information or grab credit, for God gives the growth

v: doing nothing through rivalry or through conceit, but in humility, each counting others better than himself;
each of you not just looking to his own things, but each of you also to the things of others.
I planted. Apollos watered. But God gave the increase.
So then neither he who plants is anything, nor he who waters, but God who gives the increase.

lessons.still: Before you switch on your computer, think of one colleague by name. Pray: “Lord, today help me share what is good, give the credit to you, and give it to whoever deserves it.”
teach: The Corinthian church split into factions: some said, “I follow Paul,” others, “I follow Apollos.” Paul refused to compete for credit. He said, “I planted. Apollos watered. But God gave the increase.” Both planting and watering are needed, but “neither he who plants is anything, nor he who waters”; the real fruit comes from God. To the Philippians he is even more direct: “doing nothing through rivalry or through conceit, but in humility, each counting others better than himself; each of you not just looking to his own things, but each of you also to the things of others.”

There are two kinds of people at work. One locks information on their own hard drive, because “only I know this” feels safe. The other puts files on the shared drive so the whole team can pick up the work. The first is like keeping your hand on the only tap; the second is like switching on drip irrigation so the whole field drinks. Credit works the same way. When the boss asks, “Whose idea was this?”, in that second do you say “Mine,” or “Chen raised it first; I just pulled it together”? Conceit often looks like quietly deleting someone else’s name from a slide.

The self-centred life hoards information and grabs credit because its worth rests on being seen. The self-emptied life shares gladly because its worth is already settled in Christ. Letting Jesus receive all the glory is very concrete at work: give the credit first to God, then fairly to everyone who planted and watered. Don’t ruin relationships for the sake of things: winning the credit and losing a colleague’s trust is a bad bargain. Humility draws out humility, and sharing draws out sharing.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Let Jesus receive all the glory: the one who plants and the one who waters are nothing. Relationships matter more than things: credit is a thing; colleagues are relationships. Self-denial means living for Jesus and for others, not for myself.
lessons.scene: Qihang is a product manager at an internet company in Shanghai. Last month’s redesign was a huge success, but the core idea came from Xiao Jiang, the new intern, who mentioned it in passing at a weekly meeting; Qihang turned it into a full proposal. Tomorrow he presents to the vice-president, and the last slide reads “Proposed by: Qihang”. His cursor rests on that line…
q: Who is God? — “God gave the increase.” How does this change the way you think about whose results they really are?
Who am I? — Is there information or credit you are clutching tightly and won’t let go of?
How shall I respond? — How should Qihang change that slide? What could he say in tomorrow’s presentation?
lessons.jesus: Jesus performed many miracles, yet often told people not to spread the news. He said, “I don’t seek my own glory. There is one who seeks and judges” (John 8:50). He gave the glory to the Father, kept the shame of the cross for himself, and left the crown for us. Those who follow him can loosen their grip on credit too.
lessons.pray: Lord of glory, I confess that I care a great deal about being seen. Sometimes I hold information back; sometimes I quietly draw credit to myself. Forgive me. Help me count others better than myself, share gladly, and honour every co-worker fairly. May all our team’s results bring glory to you in the end. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Move one file only you have into the team’s shared drive
Thank a colleague by name in an email or meeting
Check your slides list every contributor
lessons.noon: “I planted. Apollos watered. But God gave the increase.” — Lord, right now let me give the credit to you and to my team-mates.

lessons.title: Which Piece of the Puzzle Am I?
lessons.theme: Use the gift you have received to serve one another as good managers of God’s grace

v: For even as we have many members in one body, and all the members don’t have the same function,
so we, who are many, are one body in Christ, and individually members of one another,
As each has received a gift, employ it in serving one another, as good managers of the grace of God in its various forms.

If anyone speaks, let it be as it were the very words of God. If anyone serves, let it be as of the strength which God supplies, that in all things God may be glorified through Jesus Christ, to whom belong the glory and the dominion forever and ever. Amen.

lessons.still: Think back: who found last week a little easier because you helped? Thank God for that small thing. Then pray: “Lord, today show me the missing piece in my team.”
teach: Paul writes, “For even as we have many members in one body, and all the members don’t have the same function.” Peter shows us how to use our part: “As each has received a gift, employ it in serving one another, as good managers of the grace of God in its various forms.” Gifts are not private property but resources God has entrusted to us; a manager’s job is to make sure they flow to where they are needed. Peter adds that we should serve “as of the strength which God supplies, that in all things God may be glorified through Jesus Christ”: not by gritting our teeth, and not for our own reputation.

A team is like a thousand-piece jigsaw. Some people are corner pieces; you know at once where they go. Others are pieces of blue sky that look almost the same and are easily overlooked. But if a single piece is missing, the picture will always have a hole. To find your piece, ask three questions. What do people keep coming to me for? What work makes time fly for me? Where does the team keep getting stuck, and could I fill that gap? Where the three answers meet is often the piece God has put in your hand.

This week we have learned that two are better than one, that members care for each other, that we hold up one another’s hands, and that we share the credit. It all lands on one action: step in to fill a gap. The self-centred life asks, “What can this team give me?” The self-emptied life asks, “What is this team missing, and what can I supply?” Filling the gap is not grabbing everything; it is faithfully managing the part God has given you and respecting other people’s parts. When everyone serves in their proper place, the team becomes God’s instrument for building God’s order at work.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Build God’s order: everyone in their proper place, serving one another with their gifts. Change from the inside out: once my thinking shifts, I move from consuming my team to serving it. May God be glorified in all things through Jesus Christ.
lessons.scene: Priya is a research assistant in a biotech company’s lab in Singapore. She is no good at presenting and often feels she could disappear from the team without anyone noticing. Yet whenever the experimental data turns into chaos and nobody can find a file, people always end up asking her. Tomorrow the team meeting will discuss next year’s roles. The team leader asks, “Who wants to take something on?” Her hand goes halfway up, then comes down…
q: Who is God? — “As good managers of the grace of God.” How does God expect you to use the gifts he has entrusted to you?
Who am I? — Ask yourself today’s three questions: which piece of the team’s puzzle might you be?
How shall I respond? — Should Priya raise her hand again? What could she take on?
lessons.jesus: Luke records that at the Last Supper “a dispute also arose amongst them, which of them was considered to be greatest” (Luke 22:24). John records that Jesus “took a towel and wrapped a towel around his waist” and washed their feet himself (John 13:4). The King of kings gladly filled the lowest place. When we fill a gap, we are following in his footsteps.
lessons.pray: God of many gifts, thank you for placing me in this team and putting a gift in my hands. Open my eyes to see the missing piece. Give me courage to raise my hand and take it on, and humility not to take someone else’s place. Let me serve in the strength you supply, so that you are glorified in all things. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Use the three questions to write down your puzzle piece
Fill one small gap in your team that nobody covers
Tell a colleague which gift you see in them
lessons.noon: “As each has received a gift, employ it in serving one another” — Lord, right now show me the piece I can supply.

mem.t: If your brother sins against you, go, show him his fault between you and him alone. If he listens to you, you have gained back your brother.

lessons.title: Between You and Him Alone
lessons.theme: The first step in conflict: go yourself, go privately, go to win your brother

v: “If your brother sins against you, go, show him his fault between you and him alone. If he listens to you, you have gained back your brother.
But if he doesn’t listen, take one or two more with you, that at the mouth of two or three witnesses every word may be established.
If he refuses to listen to them, tell it to the assembly. If he refuses to hear the assembly also, let him be to you as a Gentile or a tax collector.

lessons.still: Think of someone you have grumbled about in your heart recently. Before listing their faults, pray one sentence for them: “Lord, I want to win them back, not beat them.”
teach: Jesus gives clear steps for handling conflict: “If your brother sins against you, go, show him his fault between you and him alone.” Notice three things. It is “go”: you take the initiative rather than waiting for an apology. It is “between you and him alone”: privately, not publicly. And the goal is “you have gained back your brother”: not winning the argument, but regaining the relationship. If he will not listen, “take one or two more with you”, and only then “tell it to the assembly”. It is a path that escalates step by step, and every step leaves room for the other person to turn back.

At work we often do it backwards. First we complain to three people by the coffee machine, then we drop a sarcastic line in the group chat, and only at the end, or never, do we talk to the person concerned. It is like an engineer who finds a bug and, instead of raising a ticket with the person responsible, posts a mocking screenshot to the whole company channel. The bug stays unfixed, and trust breaks first. Jesus’ order is like a proper fault-reporting process: report it one-to-one to the person responsible; if that fails, ask a manager to look at it together; only then go through formal procedures. At work the formal route might be HR or a more senior manager.

This principle takes courage and humility. The self-centred life makes two common mistakes: staying silent while keeping score, or telling everyone except the person concerned. The self-emptied life goes directly, longing to win the other person back, because people matter more than tasks. Before you go, ask the Holy Spirit to search you: “Do I want to restore, or to vent?” Deal with your own heart first, then with the problem. Where harassment or illegality is involved, go straight to the formal channels and seek help from someone you trust or a professional.
lessons.light: 321 Light: People matter more than tasks: the goal is to have “gained back your brother”, not to win the point. Humility draws out humility: a private, gentle conversation gives the other person a way back and keeps the relationship open. Let Jesus be King in every conversation.
lessons.scene: Zhenbang is a site manager for a construction company in Ipoh. Ah Cheng, one of the supervisors, has twice failed to build to the drawings, and Zhenbang got shouted at by the client. At lunch several foremen gather in the site cabin running Ah Cheng down, waiting for Zhenbang to join in. Ah Cheng is squatting outside on his own, eating his packed lunch. Zhenbang, mug of tea in hand, stands at the cabin door…
q: Who is God? — Jesus designed these steps. What do they show about how much he values winning back a brother?
Who am I? — When a colleague gets it wrong, do you usually stay silent, tell everyone, or go and talk to them?
How shall I respond? — Should Zhenbang step into the cabin or walk over to Ah Cheng? How should he begin?
lessons.jesus: Jesus did not wait for us to apologise first. We had sinned against God, yet he came: he went to us himself, from heaven into our midst, showing us our fault and opening the way back. He made that journey to gain us back. The few steps we take towards a colleague today follow in his footsteps.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, you came looking for me and did not count my wrongs behind my back. Forgive me for the times I have talked about colleagues behind theirs. Give me courage to speak privately and gently to the one who has wronged me, and a heart that longs to win them back rather than defeat them. May our relationship be restored. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Join no conversation behind anyone’s back today
Book a one-to-one with that colleague; ask their view first
Before you talk, write down what you hope the relationship becomes
lessons.noon: “If he listens to you, you have gained back your brother” — Lord, right now let me want to win them back, not beat them.

lessons.title: Leave Your Gift at the Altar
lessons.theme: Reconciliation with others comes before our offerings to God

v: “If therefore you are offering your gift at the altar, and there remember that your brother has anything against you,
leave your gift there before the altar, and go your way. First be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift.
If it is possible, as much as it is up to you, be at peace with all men.

lessons.still: Close your eyes and ask the Lord, “Is there anyone who has something against me right now?” Be still for ten seconds. Let the first name that comes to mind rest in your heart, and pray one sentence for them.
teach: This time Jesus speaks from the other direction. It is not that someone has wronged you, but that you “remember that your brother has anything against you”. Offering a sacrifice at the temple was holy and solemn, yet Jesus says, “leave your gift there before the altar, and go your way. First be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift.” Imagine someone who has queued for a long time leading a lamb, finally reaching the altar, and then having to leave the gift and go back to make peace. Jesus’ point is clear: when our relationships with others are blocked, our worship of God is blocked too.

It is like a quarterly report ready to submit, when the final check shows one cell that doesn’t reconcile. You could submit it anyway and pretend not to notice. But any experienced accountant knows that if that cell isn’t sorted out, next quarter’s error will be bigger. Workplace relationships are the same: the colleague hurt by something you said, the department whose resources you took, are the cells that don’t reconcile. Paul says, “If it is possible, as much as it is up to you, be at peace with all men.” “If it is possible” admits the other person may not be willing; “as much as it is up to you” means I must do all I can on my side.

This lesson challenges us to deal not only with what others owe us, but with what we owe others. The self-centred life remembers how others wronged it and rarely recalls how it hurt them. The self-emptied life is sensitive to others’ grievances and willing to bow first. The order of relationships is God, self, others, tasks: our relationship with God moves us to repair our relationships with people. Sunday’s worship and Monday’s apology belong together. First be reconciled, then come and offer your gift.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Life first, then relationships, then ministry: reconciled relationships come before service. Humility is the key to revival: the one who bows first often breaks the deadlock for a whole team. Focus on Jesus, not on who was wrong first.
lessons.scene: Bohong teaches science at a primary school in Taipei. At last week’s department meeting he publicly shot down his colleague Jiarong’s lesson plan, and his tone was harsh. Since then she has lowered her eyes whenever they pass in the corridor. It is Friday after school. Bohong has packed up and is hurrying off to lead a Bible study at church. He passes Jiarong’s desk; she is still marking, head down…
q: Who is God? — Jesus says, “First be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift.” What kind of worship does this God care about?
Who am I? — Right now, is there anyone who might be holding something against you?
How shall I respond? — Should Bohong stop at Jiarong’s desk before going to church? What could he say?
lessons.jesus: We were once estranged from God, even his enemies, and it was Jesus who made peace on the cross. He did not wait at the altar for us to come; he became the offering himself, so that we could be reconciled to God. Those who have been reconciled like this can become reconcilers too.
lessons.pray: Lord, on the cross you reconciled me to God. Show me who has been hurt by my words or actions. Give me humility to apologise first, without excuses or blame-shifting. If the other person isn’t ready to make peace yet, help me do all I can on my side and leave the outcome with you. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Write down the name of someone who may hold a grievance
Send one sincere apology today, with no “but” attached
If you can’t meet now, pray for them and book a time
lessons.noon: “First be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift.” — Lord, right now let me bow first, then come before you.

lessons.title: When Paul and Barnabas Parted
lessons.theme: Godly people can clash, but God can mend what is broken

v: After some days Paul said to Barnabas, “Let’s return now and visit our brothers in every city in which we proclaimed the word of the Lord, to see how they are doing.”
Barnabas planned to take John, who was called Mark, with them also.
But Paul didn’t think that it was a good idea to take with them someone who had withdrawn from them in Pamphylia, and didn’t go with them to do the work.
Then the contention grew so sharp that they separated from each other. Barnabas took Mark with him and sailed away to Cyprus,
but Paul chose Silas and went out, being commended by the brothers to the grace of God.
He went through Syria and Cilicia, strengthening the assemblies.
Only Luke is with me. Take Mark and bring him with you, for he is useful to me for service.

lessons.still: Take a deep breath and recall a working relationship that once went sour. Say to the Lord: “Lord, I hand that relationship to you. Mend it in your own time.”
teach: Paul and Barnabas were a golden partnership. When everyone doubted Paul, it was Barnabas who “took him and brought him to the apostles” (Acts 9:27), and together they completed the first missionary journey. But before the second, they argued over whether to take Mark, and “the contention grew so sharp that they separated from each other.” Paul prioritised the mission, because Mark had once withdrawn from them; Barnabas prioritised the person, and wanted to give Mark a second chance. Scripture does not declare who was right. Both had a point, both loved the Lord, and still they could not agree.

It is like two chefs who open a restaurant together. One insists on standardisation, every dish weighed to the gram; the other cares about developing new cooks and lets apprentices learn by trial and error. Both philosophies are sound, but one kitchen cannot hold them both. Sometimes the most mature response is not to hang on until both are hurt, but to part well, open two branches, and each serve different customers. As a result the mission team became two: Barnabas sailed to Cyprus, and Paul “went through Syria and Cilicia, strengthening the assemblies.”

The most beautiful part is the ending. Years later, writing from prison, Paul said: “Take Mark and bring him with you, for he is useful to me for service.” The young man he once refused became a help to him in his final years. Parting is not always failure, and disagreement does not have to mean a broken friendship. Self-centredness turns an argument into a permanent feud; the self-emptied life leaves God room to mend. At work you may disagree with colleagues, even go separate ways, but never close the door to reconciliation.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Humility draws out humility: Paul later admitted that Mark was “useful to me”. People matter more than tasks: opinions may differ, but keep the door of the relationship open. Review and correction, two of the eight steps: Paul’s own life grew through correction.
lessons.scene: Hemi has run a café in Wellington with a university friend for five years. His friend wants to expand and franchise; Hemi wants to keep the small shop and look after the regulars in the neighbourhood. They have argued for three months, and last night the friend said, “Maybe we should just split.” This morning Hemi stands by the coffee machine. A long message is typed on his phone, listing everything his friend has done wrong over the years, and his thumb is resting on send…
q: Who is God? — From Mark’s story, what do you see of how God uses rupture and parting?
Who am I? — In a disagreement, are you more like Paul, who prioritises the mission, or Barnabas, who prioritises the person?
How shall I respond? — How could Hemi rewrite that message so they can part without becoming enemies, leaving a door open for the future?
lessons.jesus: Peter denied Jesus three times, yet Jesus did not cut him off. On resurrection morning the angel told the women: “go, tell his disciples and Peter” (Mark 16:7). Jesus is the Lord who always keeps the door open. He opened the door of reconciliation for us, and he teaches us to keep the door open for others.
lessons.pray: Lord of reconciliation, you know the disagreements and wounds between me and some colleagues. Help me keep reverence for you even in an argument, and never say the words that slam the door. If we must part, help us part well, each strengthening your work. And in your time, mend our relationship as you mended things between Paul and Mark. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Pray specifically once for a relationship that has gone sour
In a disagreement, name the other person’s strengths first
Delete the door-slamming sentence before you press send
lessons.noon: “Take Mark and bring him with you” — Lord, right now mend the broken relationship I carry in my heart.

lessons.title: Swift to Hear
lessons.theme: Understand the person before tackling the problem; human anger does not produce God’s righteousness

v: So, then, my beloved brothers, let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger;
for the anger of man doesn’t produce the righteousness of God.
He who answers before he hears, that is folly and shame to him.

lessons.still: Place your hands by your ears for three seconds, then in front of your mouth for three seconds. Pray: “Lord, today let my ears clock in before my mouth does.”
teach: James gives a formula that is simple to say and hard to do: “let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger.” The reason: “the anger of man doesn’t produce the righteousness of God.” Anger may silence the other person and win you the moment, but it cannot produce the justice and reconciliation God wants. Proverbs agrees: “He who answers before he hears, that is folly and shame to him.” Many workplace conflicts happen not because positions are far apart, but because we start firing back before we have heard the other person out.

Good listening is like the “read-back” used in a customer service centre. When a customer has poured out a long complaint, an experienced agent doesn’t rush to explain but says, “Let me check I’ve understood: your order arrived three days late and nobody told you, is that right?” That one sentence often halves the customer’s volume, because a person’s deepest need is often not to be agreed with but to be understood. Next time there is conflict, try it: read back what the other person said until they say, “Yes, exactly,” and only then give your view.

When the self-centred life listens, its mind is busy preparing a rebuttal and its ears are just for show. The self-emptied life sets itself aside and genuinely wants to understand the other person’s world. This is what it means to rely on the Spirit with your heart rather than on yourself with your head: listening with the head hunts for flaws, listening with the heart looks for the person. Swift to hear is humility; slow to speak is self-control; slow to anger is the fruit of the Spirit ripening in you. One person who listens first can create a team that listens.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Rely on the Spirit with your heart, not on yourself with your head: the heart brings joy, the head brings worry. 920: every colleague you clash with is one of your “2”; in listening you practise the self-emptied “0” and bear the “9”, fruit such as patience, gentleness and self-control.
lessons.scene: Yawen is a customer service supervisor at an e-commerce company in Hsinchu. The warehouse team leader storms into her office: “What on earth are your people telling customers? Thanks to you we’ve had a complaint go all the way to the general manager!” Yawen has proof in hand that the warehouse made the mistake first. She takes a deep breath, her rebuttal already on the tip of her tongue…
q: Who is God? — “The anger of man doesn’t produce the righteousness of God.” How is God’s righteousness different from our anger?
Who am I? — When others speak, are you mostly trying to understand them, or preparing your rebuttal?
How shall I respond? — What could Yawen’s first sentence be, if she is to be swift to hear and slow to speak?
lessons.jesus: Jesus often asked before he answered. He asked blind Bartimaeus, “What do you want me to do for you?” (Mark 10:51). He let Thomas voice his doubts before responding to him in person. The Lord of all things stooped to listen; we who so often speak too quickly need to learn from his ears.
lessons.pray: Lord, I confess I often start defending myself before I have heard half of what is said, and sometimes I speak in anger. Give me ears that are swift to hear, a mouth that is slow to speak, and a heart that is slow to anger. In today’s conflicts, help me understand the person before I tackle the problem, so that your righteousness is worked out among us. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: In conversation today, read back what the other person said at least once
When criticised, ask one question before defending yourself
In meetings, wait three seconds after others finish before speaking
lessons.noon: “let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger” — Lord, right now let my ears go before my mouth.

lessons.title: The Night Before a Hard Conversation
lessons.theme: Speak truth in love: prepare your heart, then your words

v: but speaking truth in love, we may grow up in all things into him who is the head, Christ,
A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger.

lessons.still: Write the name of the person you need to talk to tomorrow on a piece of paper, and rest both hands on it. Pray: “Lord, I want to speak the truth, and to speak it in love. Prepare my heart first, then my words.”
teach: Paul writes, “speaking truth in love, we may grow up in all things into him who is the head, Christ.” Truth without love is like surgery without anaesthetic: it hurts so much the patient just wants to escape. Love without truth is like prescribing painkillers without operating: the illness never heals. Proverbs adds wisdom about tone: “A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger.” The same truth spoken at a different temperature can lead to a completely different outcome. Paul also reminds us to speak “only what is good for building others up as the need may be, that it may give grace to those who hear” (Ephesians 4:29).

Preparing for a hard conversation is like a pilot’s pre-flight checklist. First, check your heart: is my aim to win this person back, or to let off steam? Second, check the facts: are these facts, or my assumptions? Third, check your opening: use “I noticed… I felt… I hope…”, not “You always… You never…”. Fourth, check your landing: think through how they might react, and prepare for the part where you may need to apologise. Only when the checklist is complete do you take off.

This week we have learned to speak privately, to be reconciled first, to keep the door open when we disagree, and to be swift to hear. Finally, we bring it all into one real conversation. The self-centred life either avoids the conversation or turns it into a trial. The self-emptied life walks in with prayer and leaves the outcome with God. The conversation may not succeed the first time, but each time you can become more like Christ. If the other person is bullying you or acting unlawfully, please don’t face it alone; ask someone you trust or a professional to go with you. Let Jesus be King from your very first sentence.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The eight steps of changing our thinking: after information, revelation and conviction comes practice. This conversation is your practice ground; afterwards comes review and correction. Let Jesus be King in every word.
lessons.scene: Xiulan is a senior associate at an accounting firm in Kunming. For six months her colleague Lao Zheng has been taking the reports she prepares, changing the cover page and handing them to the manager, so that all the credit goes to him. She has prayed for two weeks and decided to ask him for a chat at lunch tomorrow. Tonight she sits at the dining table, opens her notebook, writes her first opening line, then crosses it out…
q: Who is God? — “Into him who is the head, Christ.” How is Christ your head in a difficult conversation?
Who am I? — When a hard conversation looms, are you more likely to avoid it, or to turn it into a trial?
How shall I respond? — Using today’s four-point checklist, help Xiulan write tomorrow’s opening line.
lessons.jesus: At the well, Jesus told the Samaritan woman the most painful truth about her life: “you have had five husbands” (John 4:18). But he said it only after first offering her living water. He never spoke truth in order to win, but in order to save. With him, grace and truth always arrive together.
lessons.pray: Lord, tomorrow I face a difficult conversation. Search my heart first, and remove every wish to vent or get even. Give me clear facts, a gentle tone, and ears ready to listen. If I am in the wrong too, make me willing to admit it. I leave the outcome of this conversation with you; please be King between us. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Use the four-point checklist to draft an opening line
Rewrite “You always” as “I noticed”
Pray for the other person five minutes before you talk
lessons.noon: “speaking truth in love” — Lord, right now let my truth carry your love.

mem.t: bearing with one another, and forgiving each other, if any man has a complaint against any; even as Christ forgave you, so you also do.

lessons.title: Seventy Times Seven
lessons.theme: Those forgiven a fortune learn to release the small change others owe

v: Then Peter came and said to him, “Lord, how often shall my brother sin against me, and I forgive him? Until seven times?”
Jesus said to him, “I don’t tell you until seven times, but, until seventy times seven.
Then his lord called him in and said to him, ‘You wicked servant! I forgave you all that debt because you begged me.
Shouldn’t you also have had mercy on your fellow servant, even as I had mercy on you?’
His lord was angry, and delivered him to the tormentors until he should pay all that was due to him.
So my heavenly Father will also do to you, if you don’t each forgive your brother from your hearts for his misdeeds.”

lessons.still: Before work, lay your open hands on your knees, as if setting down a stack of receipts. Say to the Lord, “Lord, you cancelled a debt I could never repay. Today I am willing to release what others owe me.” Stay quiet for thirty seconds, let a face come to mind, and hand that person to him.
teach: Peter thought he was being generous: “Until seven times?” Some rabbis of the day are said to have taught that forgiving three times was enough, so Peter doubled it and added one. Jesus replied, “I don’t tell you until seven times, but, until seventy times seven.” He did not mean we should count to four hundred and ninety; he meant we should stop counting. Then he told a story. A servant owed his master a sum he could not repay in a lifetime, and the master, moved with compassion, cancelled it all. The same man walked out, seized a fellow servant who owed him a little, and demanded every penny.

At work, most of us keep a private ledger of accounts receivable: the colleague who took credit for your idea, the manager who embarrassed you in a meeting, the supplier who pinned the mistake on you. Every entry is dated, totalled, with interest added. The longer the ledger grows, the more we become the servant with his hands around a colleague’s throat. The other person may have forgotten long ago; the one being choked is us. Jesus’ story is a year-end audit. First open your own books before God: the fortune you owed has been written off. Then look again at the small sum someone owes you, and you will know what to do with it.

Forgiveness is not pretending nothing happened, nor is it a feeling that arrives once and for all. Often it is a repeated decision: when the memory returns today, you hand it to the Lord again. That, too, is part of “seventy times seven.” Jesus asks us to forgive “from your hearts”, and that comes not from gritted teeth but from being melted by grace. Behind unforgiveness there is often self-centredness: I want to be the judge; I want them to pay. Humility returns us to our proper place. God is God, and vengeance is his. I am simply someone who has been forgiven, and who now forgives.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Change your thinking and you change your life. Moving from “they owe me” to “I owe the Lord far more” is moving from a human view to God’s view. People matter more than things: a small debt is not worth losing a working relationship, still less your own heart.
lessons.scene: Yawen is a planner at an advertising agency. Last month the pitch she stayed up all night to write was presented by her teammate Chenghan to the boss as “something we came up with together”. This morning Chenghan messages her: “My child has a fever. Could you present to the client for me this afternoon?” Yawen stares at the screen, fingers frozen over the keyboard.
q: Who is God? — From the master who was moved with compassion and cancelled the whole debt, what do you see about how God treats you?
Who am I? — In your private ledger, which entry is hardest to write off right now?
How shall I respond? — If you were Yawen, how would you reply to Chenghan? Is forgiving him the same as presenting for him?
lessons.jesus: Jesus did not only teach forgiveness seventy times seven; he is the one who paid our unpayable debt. As the nails went through his hands he said, “Father, forgive them, for they don’t know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34). We can forgive because we have first been forgiven like this.
lessons.pray: Merciful Lord, thank you for cancelling a debt I could never pay. I confess I am still keeping score on a colleague; every time I see him in a meeting, I remember. Today I hand this account to you once more. Help me to forgive from my heart and to stop quietly waiting for him to pay. Let your grace melt me, so that I can walk lightly in my workplace. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Write down the hardest debt to release, and pray over it once
When that person comes to mind today, pray: “Lord, I hand it to you again”
Greet that colleague normally, without bringing up the past
lessons.noon: “I don’t tell you until seven times, but, until seventy times seven” — Lord, right now the memory has come back, and I hand it to you once more.

lessons.title: As Christ Forgave You
lessons.theme: Put on the Lord’s forgiveness each morning, and you will have forgiveness to give

v: Put on therefore, as God’s chosen ones, holy and beloved, a heart of compassion, kindness, lowliness, humility, and perseverance;
bearing with one another, and forgiving each other, if any man has a complaint against any; even as Christ forgave you, so you also do.
Above all these things, walk in love, which is the bond of perfection.

lessons.still: Imagine putting on a coat and slowly doing up each button. Say to the Lord, “Lord, today I put on compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness and patience, not my moods.” The last button is called love.
teach: Paul uses the language of getting dressed: “Put on therefore, as God’s chosen ones, holy and beloved, a heart of compassion, kindness, lowliness, humility, and perseverance.” Then he becomes very practical: “if any man has a complaint against any.” Paul does not assume believers will never rub each other up the wrong way; he expects that they will. His standard is not “once they apologise, we’ll see,” but “even as Christ forgave you, so you also do.” And above everything else we are to walk in love, which binds all the virtues together.

Many workplaces have a uniform: the doctor’s white coat, the high-visibility vest on a building site, the chef’s apron. Once it is on, you know who you are today and what you are responsible for, and you don’t take your apron off just because you are in a bad mood. Paul is saying that Christians at work wear a uniform too. A cold remark from a colleague or a sharp message from a parent is like a gust of wind trying to blow your coat open. The answer is not to argue with the wind but to fasten the buttons a little tighter. Bearing with others is not weakness; it is a kind of spiritual professionalism.

“Even as Christ forgave you” is the engine of the whole passage. We do not first become loving and then forgive; we first remember how the Lord forgave us — before we apologised, before we had changed, he had already forgiven. That moves the starting line of forgiveness: it begins not with the other person’s behaviour but at the cross. When you put on the Lord’s forgiveness each morning, you have something in your hands to give away. Change from the inside out begins with this garment.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Jesus is my example — as he treats me, so I treat others. Five-fold change from the inside out: first put on Christ in my life, then forgiveness can show in my relationships. Lean on the Spirit with my heart, rather than calculating with my head who owes whom.
lessons.scene: Shuhui is a senior teacher at a primary school. A new young colleague replied in the parents’ group chat, “This is something the previous teacher didn’t handle well,” and several parents have since messaged Shuhui with pointed questions. At the two o’clock year-group meeting, the two of them will sit at the same table to divide up jobs for sports day.
q: Who is God? — “Even as Christ forgave you”: how did he forgive you? Did he wait for you to apologise first?
Who am I? — Compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness, patience: which one do you most often “forget to put on”?
How shall I respond? — If you were Shuhui, which garment would you put on before walking into that meeting?
lessons.jesus: Jesus first put on our likeness: he “emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Philippians 2:7). He wore compassion and gentleness into the crowds, and in the end even his clothes were divided by soldiers casting lots, so that we might be clothed in his righteousness. Every virtue we can wear today he bought by stripping himself first.
lessons.pray: Lord, thank you for forgiving me before I had even admitted I was wrong. As I walk into the office today, I want to wear my hurt and my defensiveness. Please change me into compassion, kindness and patience instead. I place the colleague who embarrassed me in your hands. Help me to speak gently in the meeting, and let love bind us together. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Before leaving home, recite the five garments of Colossians 3:12
Before the meeting, breathe for three seconds and pick one to put on
Thank a colleague who has upset you, for something specific
lessons.noon: “even as Christ forgave you, so you also do” — Lord, right now I remember how you forgave me, and I let go of this complaint.

lessons.title: Am I in the Place of God?
lessons.theme: Joseph told the truth, and placed his wound inside God’s sovereignty

v: Joseph said to his brothers, “I am Joseph! Does my father still live?” His brothers couldn’t answer him; for they were terrified at his presence.
Joseph said to his brothers, “Come near to me, please.” They came near. He said, “I am Joseph, your brother, whom you sold into Egypt.
Now don’t be grieved, nor angry with yourselves, that you sold me here, for God sent me before you to preserve life.
For these two years the famine has been in the land, and there are yet five years, in which there will be no ploughing and no harvest.
God sent me before you to preserve for you a remnant in the earth, and to save you alive by a great deliverance.
So now it wasn’t you who sent me here, but God, and he has made me a father to Pharaoh, lord of all his house, and ruler over all the land of Egypt.
Joseph said to them, “Don’t be afraid, for am I in the place of God?
As for you, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good, to save many people alive, as is happening today.
Now therefore don’t be afraid. I will provide for you and your little ones.” He comforted them, and spoke kindly to them.

lessons.still: Place a hand on your chest and recall a workplace memory that still hurts. Say to the Lord, “Lord, perhaps they meant it for evil, but I trust that you meant it for good.” Don’t rush to explain; simply lay it before him quietly.
teach: At seventeen, Joseph was sold to Egypt by his own brothers. He became a slave, was falsely accused, and sat in prison; thirteen years passed before he stood as ruler of Egypt. When the brothers who sold him came to buy grain, he held all the power, and a single word could have taken revenge. Instead he wept aloud and said, “I am Joseph, your brother, whom you sold into Egypt.” He did not pretend it had not happened; he named it plainly. But then he said, “it wasn’t you who sent me here, but God.” Years later, after their father died and the brothers were afraid again, Joseph still said, “am I in the place of God?”

Joseph looked at his life the way an engineer looks at a construction cross-section. When the foundations go in, the ground is dug deep, steel is cut and bent, and there is dust and noise everywhere. Passers-by see only a mess; only the one holding the plans knows that the deep pit will carry the whole tower. At work, being made redundant, sidelined, or passed over for a role can feel like that pit. Joseph never said his brothers were right. He said, “you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good.” Both sentences are true at once.

Joseph’s forgiveness has three layers. He tells the truth (“whom you sold”). He places the harm within God’s sovereignty (“but God”). And he acts generously (“I will provide for you”). The hinge is the question, “am I in the place of God?” Revenge means climbing into God’s judgement seat, which is self-centredness itself. Joseph humbly returned to his proper place and let God be God. So he did not have to carry hatred through life; instead he became the one who saved many people alive. Forgiveness releases not only the other person, but also you, to fulfil what God has entrusted to you.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Humility means laying down power and returning to my proper place. Joseph held great power yet said, “am I in the place of God?” The shift of perspective: from human intentions to God’s intentions, from temporary hurt to an eternal plan. Humility breeds humility, and a broken family was saved.
lessons.scene: Zhengxiong has worked at a machinery factory for twenty years. Years ago, the apprentice he personally promoted went over his head with complaints, and Zhengxiong was moved out of management. Now, after a restructure, he has been named manager of a new department, and on the staff list is that apprentice’s name. The HR manager asks, “Do you want to keep him?”
q: Who is God? — From Joseph’s story, how do you see God remaining in control even through people’s malice?
Who am I? — Is there a past hurt at work that you have not yet placed within the frame of “but God”?
How shall I respond? — If you were Zhengxiong, how would you answer the HR manager? How would forgiveness shape your decision?
lessons.jesus: Joseph was sold by his brothers for twenty pieces of silver; Jesus was betrayed by a disciple for thirty. Joseph came up out of the pit and saved his family; Jesus rose from the grave and saved the nations. The risen Lord stood among the disciples who had deserted him, and his first words were, “Peace be to you” (John 20:19). He is the greater Joseph.
lessons.pray: Lord of history, thank you that you did not leave me in the pits of my working life. When I remember the season of betrayal and being frozen out, it still hurts. But I choose to believe that you meant it for good. Take away my desire to sit in your place and judge. Like Joseph, help me to speak the truth and also to comfort others with kind words. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Write one line: “They meant… but God meant…”
Pray one sentence of blessing for a former boss who hurt you
Speak a word of comfort to an anxious team member today
lessons.noon: “Don’t be afraid, for am I in the place of God?” — Lord, right now I lay down my wish to judge, and let you be God.

lessons.title: Forgiveness Is Not Trust
lessons.theme: Forgiveness cancels the past debt; trust is rebuilt step by step

v: Repay no one evil for evil. Respect what is honourable in the sight of all men.
If it is possible, as much as it is up to you, be at peace with all men.
Don’t seek revenge yourselves, beloved, but give place to God’s wrath. For it is written, “Vengeance belongs to me; I will repay, says the Lord.”
“Behold, I send you out as sheep amongst wolves. Therefore be wise as serpents and harmless as doves.

lessons.still: Clench your fists, then slowly open them. Say to the Lord, “Lord, I let go of the hand that wants revenge, but please give me wise eyes.” Wait another ten seconds and ask the Spirit to guide every judgement you make today.
teach: Before Joseph revealed himself to his brothers, he tested them. He held them in custody “that your words may be tested, whether there is truth in you” (Genesis 42:16), kept Simeon back, and had a silver cup hidden in Benjamin’s sack. Only when Judah offered himself as a slave in Benjamin’s place did Joseph know they had truly changed. That was not revenge; it was wisdom. Paul says, “If it is possible, as much as it is up to you, be at peace with all men.” Those words admit that peace is not always in your hands. And Jesus told his disciples to be “wise as serpents and harmless as doves.”

Forgiveness and trust are like an IT department handling a security breach. You can choose not to pursue the colleague who clicked a phishing link, and not to shame him in front of the whole company. But his system access is restored only gradually, after retraining and passing a test. Forgiveness is a decision that writes off the debt; trust is a security pass that is reactivated floor by floor as behaviour proves reliable. Confuse the two, and you may think you cannot forgive because you are not ready to restore access; or, having forgiven, you may hand over the keys to the whole building.

Forgiveness looks backwards and deals with a past debt; trust looks forwards and weighs future risk. You can sincerely forgive a business partner who misused funds, yet not let him run the accounts again. You can forgive a manager who repeatedly bullies you, while keeping records and seeking help from HR, a trusted person or a professional. Obedience has limits: if asked to do something illegal, “We must obey God rather than men” (Acts 5:29). Boundaries are not self-centredness; they are love — caring for the life God has entrusted to you, and not letting the other person keep stumbling in the same place.
lessons.light: 321 Light: People matter more than things, but loving people is not indulging them. Scripture is my standard: forgiveness follows the cross, trust follows wisdom. The Spirit is my guide, showing me when to open the door and when to wait — wise as serpents, harmless as doves.
lessons.scene: Andrew runs a small design studio in Singapore. Last year his freelance partner Sam took two clients with him and set up on his own. Now Sam has phoned to apologise; money is tight, he wants to work together again, and he asks Andrew to pay half the fee up front. Andrew has already forgiven him, but he has not yet pressed “transfer”.
q: Who is God? — God is the God of grace and the God of wisdom. How are both at work in you?
Who am I? — Have you ever confused forgiving with trusting again, and got stuck as a result?
How shall I respond? — If you were Andrew, how would you forgive Sam and still set sensible boundaries for working together?
lessons.jesus: Jesus forgave freely, yet “Jesus didn’t entrust himself to them, because he knew everyone” (John 2:24). He loved Judas to the end and washed his feet, but was never controlled by him. After the resurrection he asked Peter three times, “do you love me more than these?” and step by step entrusted him again. Jesus’ love is full of grace and full of truth.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, thank you for forgiving me and patiently trusting me again. I have decided not to pursue what that person owes me, but I don’t know whether to trust him with things again. Give me a heart wise as a serpent and harmless as a dove, neither repaying evil for evil nor acting naively. If I face demands at work that cross the line, give me courage to say no, and lead me to people who can help. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Make two columns: what I have forgiven / what I still need to see
Set one clear checkpoint on a partnership you are unsure of
If you are being harmed repeatedly, talk to someone you trust today
lessons.noon: “If it is possible, as much as it is up to you, be at peace with all men” — Lord, right now I do what I can, and leave the rest with you.

lessons.title: A Letter of Reconciliation
lessons.theme: Write the truth before God first, and let the Spirit decide when to send it

v: “If therefore you are offering your gift at the altar, and there remember that your brother has anything against you,
leave your gift there before the altar, and go your way. First be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift.
For perhaps he was therefore separated from you for a while that you would have him forever,
no longer as a slave, but more than a slave, a beloved brother—especially to me, but how much rather to you, both in the flesh and in the Lord.
If then you count me a partner, receive him as you would receive me.
But if he has wronged you at all or owes you anything, put that to my account.

lessons.still: Take out your phone or a sheet of paper, but don’t write yet. Say to the Lord, “Lord, you reconciled me to yourself in Christ. Today, put words of reconciliation into my hands.” In the silence, let a face come to mind.
teach: Jesus said that if, while offering your gift at the altar, you “remember that your brother has anything against you” — notice, it is the other person who holds the grievance — you should first go and be reconciled, then come back and offer your gift. God values relationships even above our offerings. Paul’s letter to Philemon is a letter of reconciliation. Onesimus, a slave, had left his master and came to faith alongside Paul. Paul writes to Philemon, “receive him as you would receive me,” and adds, “if he has wronged you at all or owes you anything, put that to my account.” In one short chapter there is truth, a request, a guarantee, and hope.

At work, many conflicts are not unspoken; they turn into arguments the moment someone speaks. Writing a letter you may never send is like setting out on a building site before the concrete is poured: chalk lines mark where the walls and doors will go, and only when everything checks out does the pouring begin. In the letter, write down the hurt (the truth), your own share of responsibility (the confession), what you hope for (the request), and finally a blessing. When you have finished, you may find your anger has cooled. You may even discover that you are the one who needs to apologise first.

Whether to send it, leave to the Spirit’s leading. Sometimes the time is right: you send it, or invite the person for a coffee. Sometimes they have left the company, or the relationship is not safe, and the letter becomes your prayer before God. The point is not how the other person responds but that your heart is first reconciled to God. God “gave to us the ministry of reconciliation” (2 Corinthians 5:18); in the office we are ambassadors of reconciliation. Life first, then relationships: first let the Lord heal me, then let him mend relationships through me.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The order of relationships is God, then myself, then others, then tasks. First be reconciled to God, then face myself honestly, and only then make peace with others and deal with the work. The 920 practice starts here: the colleague I am at odds with is the “2” God has placed beside me, so that I can learn the self-emptied “0” and bear the Spirit’s “9” fruits.
