lessons.scene: At an accounting firm in Kuala Lumpur, Xiao Yu and her colleague Jiaming had a blazing row over a delayed audit report. For three months they have not spoken in the pantry. Tonight, after working late, Xiao Yu opens her laptop and starts a blank email. She types Jiaming’s name in the “To” field, and the cursor blinks in the subject line.
q: Who is God? — The God who says “First be reconciled to your brother”: how much does he value your relationships with colleagues?
Who am I? — In this conflict, what is the part you need to own?
How shall I respond? — If you were Xiao Yu, what would your first sentence be? Would you send it?
lessons.jesus: Paul says, “put that to my account.” That is exactly what Jesus did for us. All we owed God, he took upon himself; he brings us before the Father as if to say, “Receive them as you would receive me.” “God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself” (2 Corinthians 5:19). Every letter of reconciliation we write is a copy of that greatest letter.
lessons.pray: Lord who reconciles, thank you that in Christ you do not count my trespasses against me. Today I think of the colleague who has gone cold on me, and my pride does not want to speak first. Give me humility to write the truth, and to write what I did wrong. If the time has come, give me courage to send it; if not yet, heal my heart first. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Write a reconciliation letter to a colleague and save it as a draft
Include at least one line: “Where I was wrong was…”
Pray for the recipient, then ask the Spirit whether to send it
lessons.noon: “First be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift” — Lord, right now I bring this broken relationship before you.

mem.t: Let no corrupt speech proceed out of your mouth, but only what is good for building others up as the need may be, that it may give grace to those who hear.

lessons.title: Inspect Before It Leaves
lessons.theme: No corrupt word out of our mouths, only words that build up as the need may be

v: Let no corrupt speech proceed out of your mouth, but only what is good for building others up as the need may be, that it may give grace to those who hear.
Don’t grieve the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you were sealed for the day of redemption.
Let all bitterness, wrath, anger, outcry, and slander be put away from you, with all malice.
And be kind to one another, tender hearted, forgiving each other, just as God also in Christ forgave you.

lessons.still: Before work, touch your lips lightly with a finger and say to the Lord, “Lord, my mouth is yours today. Guard it, so that every word I speak gives grace to those who hear.”
teach: The word translated “corrupt” carries the sense of something rotten, like fruit left out too long: open your mouth and the smell escapes. Paul does not simply tell us to swear less; he gives a positive standard: “only what is good for building others up as the need may be, that it may give grace to those who hear.” “Building up” is the language of constructing a house. Then he adds, “Don’t grieve the Holy Spirit of God.” When we speak, the Spirit is listening, and a cutting remark can grieve him. Finally Paul lists what must go — bitterness, wrath, anger, outcry, slander — and calls us to be kind, tender-hearted and forgiving.

In a restaurant kitchen, every delivery is inspected: are the fish’s eyes clear, are the leaves wilting? Anything spoiled goes straight back, because one rotten tomato can ruin a whole pot of soup. Paul’s phrase “as the need may be” is that inspection, carried out on every sentence before it leaves the mouth. Is it the right moment? Who will it help? A shout on the production line, a sneer in a meeting, an eye-roll emoji in the group chat can seem small, yet they can turn the whole team sour.

But the tongue’s problem is rooted in the heart. Jesus said, “out of the abundance of the heart, the mouth speaks” (Matthew 12:34). So this is not a lesson in communication technique; it is a renewal of the heart. When bitterness is removed, good words flow out naturally. When we remember that “God also in Christ forgave you,” we are less likely to use words as knives. Change your thinking and you change your life; change your life and you change how you live — even your tone of voice.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Five-fold change from the inside out — thinking, life, living, relationships, ministry — and our words are the thermometer of our life. Letting Jesus be King includes letting him be King of my tongue. The Spirit is my guide; I do not want to grieve him.
lessons.scene: Guohua is a team leader on an electronics production line. Today another batch has been returned by the customer because a new worker inserted the wrong component. He walks over to her, the words already rising in his throat: “Are you even using your brain?” The whole line stops working and watches him.
q: Who is God? — The Holy Spirit can be grieved by our words. What does that tell you about him?
Who am I? — Which recent sentence of yours would never have been spoken if you had inspected it first?
How shall I respond? — If you were Guohua, what could you say that points out the error and still builds up the new worker?
lessons.jesus: Jesus’ words never rotted. To the woman brought before him he said, “Neither do I condemn you. Go your way. From now on, sin no more” (John 8:11). In one sentence there is grace and there is truth. When insulted he did not insult in return, yet with his words he opened blind eyes, comforted a widow, and called the dead out of the tomb. His mouth was a spring of life.
lessons.pray: Lord, I confess that my mouth often runs ahead of my heart. Forgive me for that barbed comment in yesterday’s meeting. Today guard my lips, so that when I correct my team, reply to clients and post in group chats, I speak words that build up. I do not want to grieve your Spirit. May my words give grace to those who hear. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Before sending any message, ask: will this build someone up?
When correcting someone, first name one thing they did well
Apologise to the person you spoke harshly to yesterday
lessons.noon: “only what is good for building others up as the need may be, that it may give grace to those who hear” — Lord, right now I am about to speak; guard my mouth.

lessons.title: Gossip Tastes Good
lessons.theme: Rumours are delicious; let them stop with me

v: The words of a gossip are like dainty morsels: they go down into a person’s innermost parts.
For lack of wood a fire goes out. Without gossip, a quarrel dies down.
As coals are to hot embers, and wood to fire, so is a contentious man to kindling strife.
The words of a whisperer are as dainty morsels, they go down into the innermost parts.

lessons.still: Imagine holding a stick of firewood, about to toss it onto a fire. Say to the Lord, “Lord, today I will not be that stick. When other people’s stories reach me, let them stop here.” Then gently put the stick down.
teach: Solomon uses a disarmingly honest image: “The words of a gossip are like dainty morsels: they go down into a person’s innermost parts.” The saying appears twice in Proverbs, as if he feared we would miss it. Gossip attracts us because it tastes good: the listener feels trusted, the teller feels important. But it goes down into the innermost parts. Once swallowed it cannot be undigested, and from then on you see that person differently. Another proverb is just as blunt: “For lack of wood a fire goes out. Without gossip, a quarrel dies down.”

Office gossip is like late-night fried chicken from a street stall: it smells wonderful, one piece leads to another, and afterwards you feel greasy, thirsty and unable to sleep. At handover someone lowers her voice — “Did you hear? Apparently she…” — and everyone’s hands go still. You do not have to start the story. Just ask, “And then what?” and you have already added a log. By the time a rumour has gone round a team and come back, it is often unrecognisable.

Behind gossip there is often self-centredness: using others’ faults to raise ourselves, using inside information to prove we are in the know. But God calls us to be the people who let the fire go out. We need not denounce anyone loudly; we simply stop adding wood. We can gently change the subject, say “We don’t really know, so let’s not guess,” or suggest asking the person directly. When a team has someone with whom the news stops, everyone is safer. That is how a godly order is built at work.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Relationships matter more than things; no piece of news is worth a colleague’s reputation. Pride provokes pride, and gossip spreads the blaze; humility breeds humility, and when one person stops, the fire dies. Keep the focus on Jesus, not on other people’s business.
lessons.scene: Manting is a nurse at a hospital. At the night-shift handover, her colleague Lydia whispers, “Did you know the ward sister has had a complaint against her? Something to do with her family, apparently.” A few others gather round, and every eye turns to Manting, who knows the ward sister best. They are waiting for her to fill in the details.
q: Who is God? — The God who says “Without gossip, a quarrel dies down”: how does he view office rumours?
Who am I? — In gossip, are you more often the one who starts it, the one who adds wood, or the one who puts it out?
How shall I respond? — If you were Manting, how would you respond in that moment, neither cold nor adding fuel?
lessons.jesus: Jesus was slandered more than anyone: called a glutton and a drunkard, accused of casting out demons by the prince of demons, and at his trial surrounded by false witnesses. He did not spread rumours in return or fight gossip with gossip. He entrusted himself to the Father who judges justly. Our reputation is in his hands, so we need not build ourselves up on other people’s.
lessons.pray: Lord, I confess I enjoy gossip, and sometimes I pass it on. Forgive me for the words I have swallowed and then served to others. Today in the pantry, in the group chats and around the lunch table, make me someone who lets the fire go out. When people start talking about someone, give me wisdom to steer gently away, and remind me to pray for the person being discussed. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: When you hear gossip, don’t ask “And then what?”
Prepare one sentence to change the subject, and use it today
Pray quietly for a colleague who is being talked about
lessons.noon: “For lack of wood a fire goes out. Without gossip, a quarrel dies down” — Lord, right now let those words stop with me.

lessons.title: Apples of Gold
lessons.theme: The right word, at the right time, in the right way

v: A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in settings of silver.
As an earring of gold, and an ornament of fine gold, so is a wise reprover to an obedient ear.
A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger.
The tongue of the wise commends knowledge, but the mouths of fools gush out folly.

lessons.still: Run through today’s meetings and messages in your mind. Say to the Lord, “Lord, help me say the right thing, at the right time, in the right way.” Take three deep breaths, then begin work.
teach: “A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in settings of silver.” Picture a fine piece of craftsmanship: golden fruit resting in a basket of woven silver, precious inside and beautifully presented. “Fitly” means spoken truly, skilfully and at the right moment. The next proverb says a wise reprover to an obedient ear is like a gold earring — good feedback is itself an ornament. Elsewhere Proverbs is even more direct: “A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger.” The same message, in a different tone, produces a completely different result.

Think of a barista making a pour-over. With the same beans, water that is too hot tastes bitter, too cool tastes sour, and a few seconds’ difference in extraction changes the flavour entirely. Words at work are the same. The right content at the wrong time — in front of the whole team, or just after someone has been told off — turns bitter. The same content, in a gentle tone and in a one-to-one conversation, can be received. Annual reviews, replying to complaints, telling your boss “we can’t do this” — all require this kind of careful extraction.

But fitting words are not smooth words or empty diplomacy. Apples of gold are precious because they are real gold; speaking fitly begins with honesty. We do not need more techniques; we need wisdom from the Spirit — leaning on him with our hearts, not scheming with our heads. Asking God for a word before you speak is a small habit that slowly changes your life, until colleagues say, “Talking things through with her is easy, and you can trust what she says.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Lean on the Spirit with your heart, not on yourself with your head — the heart brings joy, the head brings worry. A fitting word is often received in a three-second prayer before speaking. The Spirit is my guide; he knows when to speak and when to be still.
lessons.scene: Caijie is a project manager at a logistics company. Her boss wants a timeline by Monday that simply cannot be met. She has worked late for two weeks straight, and her team is close to breaking point. Now she stands at her boss’s door, revised plan in hand, about to say, “We can’t do it.”
q: Who is God? — The God who gives wisdom like apples of gold: how does he want to help you speak?
Who am I? — When you speak, is the content usually right but the tone wrong, or the tone kind but the truth left unsaid?
How shall I respond? — If you were Caijie, how would you turn “we can’t do it” into a fitting word?
lessons.jesus: Jesus spoke more fitly than anyone. When tested over taxes, he said, “Give therefore to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s” (Matthew 22:21). At the well with the Samaritan woman, he began with a drink of water and led her to living water. His words carried the weight of truth and the warmth of grace.
lessons.pray: Lord of wisdom, today I have a difficult conversation ahead. I am afraid of being too hard and angering my boss, and of being too soft and leaving my team to suffer. Give me a fitting word, like apples of gold in settings of silver. Make me honest and gentle; let me stand up for my team while respecting my manager’s authority. If my team truly cannot cope, show me whom to ask for help. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Before an important conversation, pray ten seconds for one word
Rephrase one criticism more gently before you say it
If overwork is ongoing, talk with someone you trust or with HR
lessons.noon: “A gentle answer turns away wrath” — Lord, right now I want to argue back; soften my words.

lessons.title: The Tongue in the Group Chat
lessons.theme: One mouth should not bless God and curse people

v: So the tongue is also a little member, and boasts great things. See how a small fire can spread to a large forest!
And the tongue is a fire. The world of iniquity amongst our members is the tongue, which defiles the whole body, and sets on fire the course of nature, and is set on fire by Gehenna.
For every kind of animal, bird, creeping thing, and sea creature is tamed, and has been tamed by mankind;
but nobody can tame the tongue. It is a restless evil, full of deadly poison.
With it we bless our God and Father, and with it we curse men who are made in the image of God.
Out of the same mouth comes blessing and cursing. My brothers, these things ought not to be so.
Do all things without complaining and arguing,

lessons.still: Before you open your phone, turn it face down on the desk. Say to the Lord, “Lord, in every group chat today I am your witness. Before I press send, I will ask you first.”
teach: James says the tongue is a little member that can set a whole forest ablaze. More painfully, “With it we bless our God and Father, and with it we curse men who are made in the image of God.” Singing hymns on Sunday, slating the boss in the group chat on Monday — James says, “these things ought not to be so.” Paul adds, “Do all things without complaining and arguing.” This is not a ban on naming difficulties; it is a warning against grumbling that ferments, spreads from person to person, and never intends to solve anything.

A complaints chat is like a smoking room with the doors and windows shut. One person lights up and the whole room fills with smoke; stay long enough and even the non-smokers go home smelling of it. A line like “How did someone like that ever become section chief?” attracts a dozen laughing emojis, and everyone feels relieved. But the next morning in the office, they look at the section chief differently. Today our tongue is not only in our mouth but at our fingertips; screenshots travel, and messages leave a record.

So what about real unfairness? Scripture never asks us to pretend all is well. We can pour out our hearts to God as honestly as the psalmists; we can speak directly and respectfully with the person concerned; we can raise the issue through proper channels. Where there is bullying or illegal conduct, keep records, and seek a trusted person or professional help where needed. But talking behind backs and venting in chats only feeds the fire. When our focus turns from others back to Jesus, we find strength to use the same mouth to bless God and to bless people.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Keep the focus on Jesus, not on myself, others or circumstances. People matter more than things: don’t wound a person with words over a matter that frustrates you. Shift perspective — from worldly venting to godly building, turning complaints into prayers and proposals.
lessons.scene: Bohong is a civil servant in city government. His department has a group chat without the managers in it, where everyone mocks the new section chief daily. Today the chief rejected the team’s proposal in a meeting, and dozens of messages pour in at once. Someone tags Bohong: “You’re the best writer here — give us a classic!”
q: Who is God? — People are “made in the image of God”. How does that change the way you see the manager you want to mock?
Who am I? — In which group chat have your fingertips recently said what ought not to be said?
How shall I respond? — If you were Bohong, how would you reply to that message?
lessons.jesus: Jesus had plenty to complain about: slow disciples, hostile religious leaders, friends who fell asleep when he needed them most. Yet he carried his burden to Gethsemane and poured it out to the Father, not to the crowd. On the cross his mouth spoke forgiveness, promise and trust. From beginning to end, he used the same mouth to bless.
lessons.pray: Lord, I confess I often type in group chats what I would never dare say before you. Cleanse my mouth and my fingertips. Today, when I am frustrated with my manager or company, help me to tell you first, and then to communicate with respect. When someone leads the criticism, give me wisdom not to add fuel or pass judgement, but to bring peace. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Delete one complaint you haven’t sent yet
Rewrite one complaint as a concrete proposal
Post one word of appreciation for someone in a group chat
lessons.noon: “Do all things without complaining and arguing” — Lord, right now I want to complain; let me speak to you first.

lessons.title: Three Good Words Today
lessons.theme: Words that build up work like drip irrigation: a little each day

v: Therefore exhort one another, and build each other up, even as you also do.
Let your speech always be with grace, seasoned with salt, that you may know how you ought to answer each one.

lessons.still: Hold up three fingers and say to the Lord, “Lord, today I will speak three words that build people up. Show me the three people who need to be blessed.” Close your eyes and ask the Spirit to bring the first face to mind.
teach: Paul tells the Thessalonians, “exhort one another, and build each other up, even as you also do.” “As you also do” means this is not an occasional performance but a daily habit. To the Colossians he writes, “Let your speech always be with grace, seasoned with salt.” In the ancient world salt flavoured and preserved food; too little and it is bland, too much and it is inedible. Words that build up are seasoned just right: sincere, specific and well judged.

In a greenhouse, growers use drip irrigation, sending water a little at a time to the roots of every seedling, rather than flooding the beds once a week. Words that build up work the same way. Don’t save them all for the year-end dinner; give them drop by drop each day. “Thanks for fixing that report yesterday.” “You were really patient with that customer.” “That’s a great idea — tell me more.” Specific, sincere and timely: that is drip irrigation at work.

Why three a day? Because good words take practice, like any new habit. This is the “practice” and “repetition” of the eight steps: three today, three tomorrow, and slowly your eyes learn to look for God’s grace in other people. This is not flattery or popularity-seeking; it is letting Jesus love every “2” around you through your mouth. The whole atmosphere of your workplace might begin to change with your three sentences.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The 920 practice — every colleague is my “2”; I practise the self-emptied “0”, so that the Spirit’s “9” fruits grow out of my mouth. The practice and repetition of the eight steps: three words a day, shaping a mouth for life.
lessons.scene: Jinhui manages a Chinese supermarket in Auckland, where most of the staff are students working part-time. Tonight the stocktake has run late and everyone is too tired to talk. Jinhui notices a student quietly rearranging a shelf someone else had left in a mess. Jinhui is still holding the stock sheet, about to move on to the next aisle.
q: Who is God? — How has the God who builds us up used someone’s words to build you up? Recall one such sentence.
Who am I? — Do you more easily notice people’s mistakes, or their good?
How shall I respond? — If you were Jinhui, what would you stop and say to that student? Who will receive your three words today?
lessons.jesus: Jesus always saw the good others missed. The crowd saw Zacchaeus the tax collector; Jesus called him by name and said he would stay at his house that day. The crowd saw a widow drop in two small coins; Jesus said she had given more than all the rest. His words built up one overlooked person after another, and today they build me up too.
lessons.pray: Lord, thank you for building me up with your words, reminding me when I am discouraged that I am loved by you. Today open my eyes to see what is good in my colleagues, and give me courage to say it. I will speak three words that build up: to someone who works quietly, to someone often criticised, and to someone I don’t much like. Let my speech always be with grace, seasoned with salt. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Before ten o’clock, give your first specific word of affirmation
Before lunch, give the second to someone often overlooked
Before you leave, give the third to someone you find difficult
lessons.noon: “exhort one another, and build each other up” — Lord, right now show me someone who needs building up.

mem.t: Lets not become conceited, provoking one another, and envying one another.

lessons.title: Thousands and Ten Thousands
lessons.theme: Envy made a king see his finest commander as his enemy

v: As they came, when David returned from the slaughter of the Philistine, the women came out of all the cities of Israel, singing and dancing, to meet King Saul with tambourines, with joy, and with instruments of music.
The women sang to one another as they played, and said, “Saul has slain his thousands, and David his ten thousands.”
Saul was very angry, and this saying displeased him. He said, “They have credited David with ten thousands, and they have only credited me with thousands. What can he have more but the kingdom?”
Saul watched David from that day and forward.
Saul was afraid of David, because the LORD was with him, and had departed from Saul.
Therefore Saul removed him from his presence, and made him his captain over a thousand; and he went out and came in before the people.
David behaved himself wisely in all his ways; and the LORD was with him.
When Saul saw that he behaved himself very wisely, he stood in awe of him.

lessons.still: Lay out in your mind the comparisons you may meet today — the sales board, the promotion list, the good news on social media. Say to the Lord, “Lord, my worth is not on a leaderboard. My place is in your hands.”
teach: Saul was the winner. He was king, fresh from victory. But the women sang a song: “Saul has slain his thousands, and David his ten thousands.” Because of one number, “Saul was very angry,” and “Saul watched David from that day and forward.” He grew afraid, because he could see that the LORD was with David. We can imagine Saul lying awake that night, the song replaying in his head. The most frightening thing about envy is this: it made a king see his finest commander as his greatest enemy.

Many offices display a live sales dashboard, the numbers ticking over every hour. It is meant to motivate, but it can become the song Saul heard. You closed eight deals this month and were delighted, until you saw that the new colleague closed twenty. In that moment your eight lost their shine. That is how envy works: it does not care how much you have, only that someone else has more. So you begin to pick holes in his work in meetings and to play down his contribution in front of the boss.

Saul’s problem was not that David was too strong, but that Saul wanted to be king on his own terms for ever, terrified of losing his place: “What can he have more but the kingdom?” That is self-centredness — treating the position God gave as private property. Humility lays down power and returns to its proper place: my position is God’s gift, and whom he gives greater gifts to is his business. When I confess, “God is King, and I am not,” I can move from Saul’s suspicious glare to Jonathan’s blessing. Jonathan was also a prince, yet he “loved him as his own soul.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Self-centredness is the root of the fall, and it shows itself as pride; pride is leaving my place and grasping power. Saul clutched his throne and lost everything. When I let Jesus be King, I need not fear anyone being better than me.
lessons.scene: Yanting is a sales supervisor at an insurance company. Kavitha, a new member of his team, has seen her figures soar, and this month she has overtaken him. At the morning briefing the general manager praises Kavitha in front of everyone, then turns to Yanting: “Your new recruit is impressive. Why not have her share her approach with everyone next week?”
q: Who is God? — “The LORD was with him.” God has the right to give gifts to whom he chooses. How do you regard his sovereignty?
Who am I? — What kind of “thousands and ten thousands” most easily makes you eye someone with suspicion?
How shall I respond? — If you were Yanting, how would you answer the general manager?
lessons.jesus: Jesus was envied by the religious leaders all the way to the cross; Pilate “knew that because of envy they had delivered him up” (Matthew 27:18). Yet Jesus himself never envied, because he knew the Father loved him. He even promised that those who believe in him “will do greater works than these” (John 14:12). He delighted to see others lifted up, because his place in the Father was secure.
lessons.pray: Lord, I confess that when others are praised, something sours in my heart. Forgive me for quietly glaring, like Saul, at a colleague who is better than me. My place is your gift; my worth is not on a leaderboard. Make me like Jonathan, able to rejoice sincerely in others’ gifts, and faithful in my own post. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Write down the name of someone you envy, and give it to God
Say three times in your heart: “God is King, and I am not”
Today, affirm one of that colleague’s strengths to their face
lessons.noon: “Saul watched David from that day and forward” — Lord, right now I will not glare at others; I will look to you.

lessons.title: Is Your Eye Evil Because I Am Good?
lessons.theme: The master’s generosity never reduces your share

v: When the first came, they supposed that they would receive more; and they likewise each received a denarius.
When they received it, they murmured against the master of the household,
saying, ‘These last have spent one hour, and you have made them equal to us who have borne the burden of the day and the scorching heat!’
“But he answered one of them, ‘Friend, I am doing you no wrong. Didn’t you agree with me for a denarius?
Take that which is yours, and go your way. It is my desire to give to this last just as much as to you.
Isn’t it lawful for me to do what I want to with what I own? Or is your eye evil, because I am good?’
So the last will be first, and the first last. For many are called, but few are chosen.”

lessons.still: Cup your hands together and imagine the Lord placing today’s grace in them. Say to him, “Lord, what you give me is enough. Today I will not look at other people’s hands, only at your grace.”
teach: Early in the morning a landowner hired workers for a denarius a day. Through the morning, at midday, in the afternoon and even as the day was ending, he went out and hired more. At pay time, starting with the last, everyone received a denarius. The first workers “supposed that they would receive more,” but they too received a denarius, and they murmured against the master. He replied, “Friend, I am doing you no wrong… is your eye evil, because I am good?” They had not been cheated; they had been defeated by comparison. Had they never seen the others’ pay, they would have gone home content with their denarius.

The most painful moment at work is often not receiving your bonus but overhearing in the pantry what someone else received. A figure that seemed fair becomes a grievance the moment you compare it. You are counting hours and years of service; God is counting grace. The junior who joined after you but was promoted before you, the colleague who seems to coast yet lands the big client — this parable reminds us that the master’s generosity to others has never reduced your share.

The point of this parable is not pay policy but grace. We are all the workers hired at the end of the day, brought into God’s kingdom by grace. When we forget that we were hired by grace, we start measuring others by merit. The opposite of an envious eye is not pretending not to care; it is a heart full of gratitude. Shift the perspective from earth to heaven, from the temporary to the eternal: in God’s kingdom “the last will be first, and the first last”, and the rankings are turned upside down.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Shift perspective — from human arithmetic to God’s grace, from earthly rankings to a heavenly view. Keep the focus on Jesus, not on other people’s payslips. A grateful heart is the cure for an envious eye.
lessons.scene: Huiru has worked as a firmware engineer at a tech company in Taichung for six years. Today the promotion list came out: Liqun, a junior who joined only two years ago, has been made senior engineer, while she stays where she is. In the afternoon Liqun comes over: “Could you look at some code for me? You know this area better than anyone on the team.”
q: Who is God? — The master who says “I am good”: what does he show you about God’s heart?
Who am I? — Where has comparison recently made your eye envious?
How shall I respond? — If you were Huiru, how would you respond to Liqun’s request?
lessons.jesus: Jesus said to the criminal beside him, “today you will be with me in Paradise” (Luke 23:43). Here was someone “hired” in the very last hour of his life, yet he received grace in full. Jesus is the generous master, who paid every worker’s wage with his own life, so that we need no longer compare ourselves by merit.
lessons.pray: Generous Lord, thank you for hiring me when I did not deserve it. I confess that when others are promoted or given a rise, my eye turns envious and I grumble. Help me remember that I came in by grace, and let me congratulate my colleagues sincerely. If one of them asks me for help today, let me share what I know without holding back. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: List three “denarii” God has already given you this year
Don’t ask about or compare others’ pay or bonuses
Offer help to a colleague who joined after you
lessons.noon: “is your eye evil, because I am good?” — Lord, right now I lay down comparison and count your grace to me.

lessons.title: Keep in Step with the Spirit
lessons.theme: Envy is not suppressed by willpower but crowded out by the Spirit’s fruit

v: But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith,
gentleness, and self-control. Against such things there is no law.
Those who belong to Christ have crucified the flesh with its passions and lusts.
If we live by the Spirit, let’s also walk by the Spirit.
Let’s not become conceited, provoking one another, and envying one another.

lessons.still: Sit quietly and say softly, “Holy Spirit, today I live by you, and I will walk by you.” Then for thirty seconds, name the fruit of the Spirit one word at a time: love, joy, peace, patience…
teach: Paul first lists the fruit of the Spirit, from love to self-control. Then he says that those who belong to Christ have crucified the flesh with its passions. Then: “If we live by the Spirit, let’s also walk by the Spirit.” Only then comes this week’s verse: “Let’s not become conceited, provoking one another, and envying one another.” The order matters. Envy is not pushed down by willpower; it is crowded out by a life that is bearing fruit. The word for “walk” here carries the sense of falling into line, keeping in step behind a leader.

In a marathon there are pacers, runners with balloons tied to their backs who hold a steady time; follow them and you will finish. Many runners fail because they keep glancing sideways, lose their rhythm whenever someone overtakes them, and never finish. At work, the “conceit” Paul mentions is fed by those overtaking us: whose work was shortlisted, whose presentation the boss liked, who was invited to the senior meeting. Walking by the Spirit means keeping your eyes on the pacer ahead and matching his stride, not anyone else’s.

Paul names two diseases. “Provoking one another” often comes from feeling superior and needling others. “Envying one another” often comes from feeling inferior and resenting others. Both are rooted in comparison, and both are self-centredness. The cure is not to feel better or worse about ourselves, but to stop putting ourselves at the centre — the self-emptied life, where it is no longer I but Christ who lives in me. When our focus is on Jesus, we can step off the track of comparison and bear the fruit of joy and peace.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The self-emptied life is not emptiness; it is entering the infinite. When Christ lives in me, I no longer need to measure myself against others. The Spirit is my guide — keep in step with him, and you step off the track of comparison.
lessons.scene: Hemi is a video editor at a production company in Wellington. His work has been shortlisted for an industry award; his teammate Ruohan’s has not. At lunch he is about to post the shortlist notice in the team chat, his finger hovering over “send” — when he sees that Ruohan has just written: “Congrats.”
q: Who is God? — How does the Spirit bear fruit in your life, rather than asking you to grit your teeth?
Who am I? — Are you more prone to “provoking one another” (feeling superior) or “envying one another” (feeling inferior)?
How shall I respond? — If you were Hemi, how would you share this good news without provoking?
lessons.jesus: Jesus needed status less than anyone. “Jesus therefore, perceiving that they were about to come and take him by force to make him king, withdrew again to the mountain by himself” (John 6:15). After his miracles he often told people not to spread the news. His stride matched only the Father’s: “I always do the things that are pleasing to him” (John 8:29). His joy did not rest on applause but on the Father’s presence.
lessons.pray: Holy Spirit, I confess I keep glancing at other people’s lanes: who is more popular, who is faster. Sometimes I compare in secret; sometimes I want to show off. Grow in me the fruit of love, joy and peace, and crowd envy and pride out of my heart. Today help me keep in step with you, not chasing status, but longing only for the Lord Jesus to be glorified. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: When you catch yourself comparing, pray: “Keep in step”
When sharing good news, name the team’s specific contribution
Skip one scroll through peers’ social media today
lessons.noon: “If we live by the Spirit, let’s also walk by the Spirit” — Lord, right now I won’t watch the other lanes; I will keep in step with you.

lessons.title: He Must Increase
lessons.theme: Rejoicing with those who rejoice is the freedom of a heart filled with God’s love

v: They came to John and said to him, “Rabbi, he who was with you beyond the Jordan, to whom you have testified, behold, he baptises, and everyone is coming to him.”
John answered, “A man can receive nothing unless it has been given him from heaven.
You yourselves testify that I said, ‘I am not the Christ,’ but, ‘I have been sent before him.’
He who has the bride is the bridegroom; but the friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices greatly because of the bridegroom’s voice. Therefore my joy is made full.
He must increase, but I must decrease.
Rejoice with those who rejoice. Weep with those who weep.

lessons.still: Think of a colleague or friend who has had good news recently, and hold their face in your heart. Say to the Lord, “Lord, give me a heart that can rejoice for them.” Then, in your heart, really say to them: “Congratulations.”
teach: John the Baptist’s disciples were unsettled: “everyone is coming to him.” The crowds were flowing away from John’s riverbank towards Jesus, like an old shop watching its customers walk into the new one across the road. John’s reply is one of the finest workplace attitudes in Scripture: “A man can receive nothing unless it has been given him from heaven.” He called himself the friend of the bridegroom, who “rejoices greatly because of the bridegroom’s voice,” and concluded, “He must increase, but I must decrease.” Paul likewise teaches, “Rejoice with those who rejoice. Weep with those who weep.”

In an orchestra, the second violins are rarely remembered by the audience, yet without them the leader’s solo has no harmony. Good musicians know that when the whole piece sounds beautiful, that is their success too. At work, rejoicing with those who rejoice is not a forced smile. It is seeing a colleague win an award, gain a promotion or land a major project, and knowing that we are playing the same piece in the same orchestra, and the conductor is God.

It is often said that weeping with those who weep is easier than rejoicing with those who rejoice. When others cry, we feel no threat; when others celebrate, we feel outshone. To rejoice sincerely we need a heart filled with God’s love. When I know I am fully accepted by God, another person’s good news cannot reduce my worth. This is the freedom of the self-emptied life: it is no longer about my being seen, but about letting Jesus receive all the glory.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Let Jesus receive all the glory — “He must increase, but I must decrease” is the best commentary on it. Humility breeds humility: when I sincerely rejoice for a colleague, the team moves from comparison to a win for everyone.
lessons.scene: Grace works at an architecture practice in Singapore. She joined at the same time as her university classmate Peishan. Today the firm announced that Peishan’s design for a community library has won first prize in a competition, and there is a celebration tonight. Grace’s entry was not shortlisted. On her phone she types, “Sorry, I can’t make it tonight,” deletes it, then types it again.
q: Who is God? — “A man can receive nothing unless it has been given him from heaven.” How does this shape the way you see God giving gifts?
Who am I? — Weeping with those who weep, or rejoicing with those who rejoice: which is harder for you, and why?
How shall I respond? — If you were Grace, how would you approach tonight’s celebration?
lessons.jesus: John was glad to decrease because he had seen who Jesus is. And Jesus himself, when his disciples returned from their mission, “rejoiced in the Holy Spirit” (Luke 10:21), thanking the Father for revealing these things to little children. He rejoiced in his disciples’ growth, and today he rejoices over every small step we take.
lessons.pray: Lord, I confess that other people’s good news sometimes leaves a sour taste in me. Help me, like John the Baptist, to know that everything is given from heaven. Today I want to bless the colleague who has been honoured — not just to say congratulations, but to thank you for them in my heart. Let my joy depend not on being seen, but on your increase. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Congratulate a colleague with good news in person today
Thank God for one specific part of their achievement
Go to a colleague’s celebration without making excuses
lessons.noon: “Rejoice with those who rejoice” — Lord, right now I think of that colleague; help me rejoice for them sincerely.

lessons.title: Praying for the One Ahead of Me
lessons.theme: Prayer swaps envy’s plug for heaven’s standard

v: For where jealousy and selfish ambition are, there is confusion and every evil deed.
But the wisdom that is from above is first pure, then peaceful, gentle, reasonable, full of mercy and good fruits, without partiality, and without hypocrisy.
doing nothing through rivalry or through conceit, but in humility, each counting others better than himself;
each of you not just looking to his own things, but each of you also to the things of others.

lessons.still: Write in your heart the name of the colleague who is more successful than you. Say to the Lord, “Lord, I give them to you, and I give myself to you. Today I will pray for them rather than compete with them.”
teach: James is blunt: “where jealousy and selfish ambition are, there is confusion and every evil deed.” Envy does not stay in the heart; it throws a whole team into disorder. But he goes on to describe another wisdom, the wisdom from above, which is “first pure, then peaceful, gentle, reasonable, full of mercy.” Paul gives the practical direction: “in humility, each counting others better than himself; each of you not just looking to his own things, but each of you also to the things of others.” The most thorough way to deal with envy is to look to that person’s interests — by praying for them.

On a business trip abroad, if your plug does not match the socket, it will not go in, and forcing it can cause sparks; you need an adapter. An envious heart and another person’s success are like two incompatible standards. Prayer is the adapter. When you bring their name before God, the connection between you is switched to heaven’s standard. It is very hard to pray for someone’s health, family and work to be blessed while quietly cursing them in your heart.

At first such prayers may feel forced — perhaps no more than a gritted “Lord, bless them.” That is fine. This is the “practice” and the “repetition” of the eight steps. Prayer often changes the one praying first. After a few weeks you may find you genuinely want them to do well, and even want to learn from them. This is how 235 begins: someone you once envied may become your “2”, a spiritual companion, or a comrade alongside you at work.
lessons.light: 321 Light: 235 — becoming a “2”, a spiritual companion, with someone living the self-emptied life. Through prayer, the colleague I envy may become someone who walks with me. Humility breeds humility: the one who prays first is the first to be set free.
lessons.scene: Wenbin is a financial analyst at a foreign company in Shanghai. His university classmate and colleague Ethan has just been posted to the London head office, an opportunity the whole department envies. Today is Ethan’s last day; there is a team photo, and everyone is signing a farewell card. When the card reaches Wenbin, he holds the pen and cannot write a word.
q: Who is God? — The God who gives “the wisdom that is from above”: how does he see you and that colleague?
Who am I? — “Counting others better than himself”: in your team, for whom is this hardest?
How shall I respond? — If you were Wenbin, what would you write on the card? Afterwards, how would you pray for Ethan?
lessons.jesus: On the night he was betrayed, Jesus prayed for Peter, who was about to deny him: “I prayed for you, that your faith wouldn’t fail” (Luke 22:32). Today he still “lives forever to make intercession for them” (Hebrews 7:25). When we pray for others, we are learning his ways and joining in the work he is doing right now.
lessons.pray: Lord, today I want to pray for the colleague who is more successful than me. Bless their work, their family and their health; give them wisdom in their new role, and let them know your love more deeply. I confess this prayer is not easy for me. Cleanse the envy in my heart, and help me count them better than myself. Be glorified in both of us. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Pray for that colleague today about three specific things
Write them a sincere card or message of blessing
Ask them to teach you something you genuinely want to learn
lessons.noon: “in humility, each counting others better than himself” — Lord, right now I bring their name before you.

mem.t: If I then, the Lord and the Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one anothers feet.

lessons.title: A Basin and a Towel
lessons.theme: The one with all authority did the lowliest task

v: Jesus, knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands, and that he came from God and was going to God,
arose from supper, and laid aside his outer garments. He took a towel and wrapped a towel around his waist.
Then he poured water into the basin, and began to wash the disciples’ feet and to wipe them with the towel that was wrapped around him.
So when he had washed their feet, put his outer garment back on, and sat down again, he said to them, “Do you know what I have done to you?
You call me, ‘Teacher’ and ‘Lord.’ You say so correctly, for so I am.
If I then, the Lord and the Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet.
For I have given you an example, that you should also do as I have done to you.

lessons.still: Look down at your feet and imagine the Lord Jesus kneeling in front of you, a towel in his hands. Say to him, “Lord, you washed me first. Today I am willing to bend down and serve the people around me.”
teach: It was the evening before the Passover, and Jesus knew his hour had come. “Having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end.” John records carefully that Jesus, “knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands,” then “arose from supper,” wrapped a towel around his waist, poured water into a basin, and washed the disciples’ feet. In that culture, washing feet was usually a servant’s job; we can imagine each disciple waiting for someone else to do it. The one with all authority did the lowliest task. Afterwards he said, “If I then, the Lord and the Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet.”

Picture an area manager for a restaurant chain arriving an hour before opening. The toilets are blocked and the staff are in a panic, so without a word he rolls up his sleeves and picks up the plunger. Years later, the staff remember not his sales presentations but that moment. The final leadership lesson Jesus left his disciples was not a strategy deck but a basin of water and a towel. Washing feet at work means doing the things nobody wants to do, the things that leave others cleaner and lighter.

The key is that word “knowing”. Jesus knew where he had come from, where he was going and what was in his hands, so he did not need a position to prove himself. Insecure leaders have to cling to their titles; those who are secure in God are free to bend down. This is the humility at the heart of 321: laying down power and returning to my proper place. When I know who I am — God’s child, washed by the Lord — I can pick up a towel for colleagues, team members and clients.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Jesus is my example — “For I have given you an example.” Life first, then relationships, then ministry: washing feet is not a management technique but the overflow of a life. Letting Jesus be King means letting his towel become my sceptre.
lessons.scene: Zixuan is CEO of a start-up in Taipei. The company has just closed a funding round, and tonight everyone is working late to launch the product. At one in the morning the kitchen bin is overflowing, coffee cups are piled high, and several engineers are still staring at their screens. Zixuan’s investor presentation is not finished. He stands at the kitchen door, looking at the rubbish.
q: Who is God? — Jesus knew “the Father had given all things into his hands”. Why did he choose to pick up a towel?
Who am I? — Does your security come from your title, or from knowing who you are?
How shall I respond? — If you were Zixuan, what would you do right now, and why?
lessons.jesus: The foot-washing was only a preview. Within hours, Jesus would lay aside not just his outer garments but his life, and wash away not just the dust on our feet but the sin of our whole selves. On the cross he “loved them to the end.” We can wash one another’s feet because we have first been washed by his blood.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, who loves me to the end, thank you for bending down to wash me. I confess I often want to sit in my seat and wait to be served, avoiding the tasks nobody sees. Today help me pick up a towel at work: to plug a gap for a colleague, clear up a mess, shield my team from a storm. Let my authority become a tool for serving. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Do one small task today that nobody wants to do
Don’t pull rank; ask first, “Can I help?”
Publicly give credit to someone on your team
lessons.noon: “For I have given you an example, that you should also do as I have done to you” — Lord, right now let me bend down as you did.

lessons.title: Authority and the Towel
lessons.theme: Authority is not a remote control but a toolbox for serving

v: Jesus, knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands, and that he came from God and was going to God,
arose from supper, and laid aside his outer garments. He took a towel and wrapped a towel around his waist.
Jesus summoned them and said to them, “You know that they who are recognised as rulers over the nations lord it over them, and their great ones exercise authority over them.
But it shall not be so amongst you, but whoever wants to become great amongst you shall be your servant.
Whoever of you wants to become first amongst you shall be bondservant of all.
For the Son of Man also came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.”

lessons.still: Lay both hands flat on your desk: one stands for your position, the other for your service. Say to the Lord, “Lord, the authority you have given me is meant to pick up a towel. Today let these two hands work together.”
teach: John’s Gospel has a detail worth pausing over: Jesus, “knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands,” then picked up a towel. All things and a towel were in his hands at the same moment. Mark records that James and John asked to sit at Jesus’ right and left, and the other ten were indignant. Jesus said that rulers over the nations “lord it over them,” and their great ones “exercise authority over them. But it shall not be so amongst you.” “Whoever of you wants to become first amongst you shall be bondservant of all,” for “the Son of Man also came not to be served but to serve.”

The world sees authority as a remote control: sit on the sofa, press a button, and others must move. Jesus sees authority as a toolbox: the greater the authority, the more tools you hold and the more you can repair. A manager who sets the rota can use it to care for a colleague whose family is going through a hard time. One who approves budgets can secure the equipment front-line staff need. One who has a voice in meetings can speak up for those who stay silent. Authority itself is not sin; the question is whether I use it to serve myself or others.

Self-centred leadership treats power as a personal crown: I want people to obey me, fear me, flatter me. Humble leadership recognises authority as a trust from God, and myself as a steward. Jesus did not abandon his identity — “You call me, ‘Teacher’ and ‘Lord.’ You say so correctly, for so I am” — but he used it to serve. This is not weak leadership but stronger leadership: a team led with a towel goes further than a team driven with a whip.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Pride is leaving my place and grasping power; humility is laying down power and returning to my place. Authority and a towel can rest in the same hands, because those who let Jesus be King know who the true King is. This is how to build God’s order at work.
lessons.scene: Meiling is an area manager for a pharmacy chain in Kuala Lumpur, just three months into the role. Today she is drawing up next month’s rota. Daniel, a senior pharmacist, says quietly, “You used to be on the front line — you know nobody wants weekend shifts. Just give them all to the new staff, like we’ve always done. Saves trouble.” Meiling looks at the new staff column, and her mouse stops.
q: Who is God? — Jesus held all things and picked up a towel. What kind of authority does that show you?
Who am I? — Whatever authority you hold, large or small, have you recently used it to serve yourself or others?
How shall I respond? — If you were Meiling, how would you draw up the rota?
lessons.jesus: Jesus is the only one who truly holds all authority: “All authority has been given to me in heaven and on earth” (Matthew 28:18). Yet he used that authority to give his life as a ransom for many. His crown was woven of thorns; his throne was a cross. He shows us that where authority is highest, service is deepest.
lessons.pray: King of kings, thank you for using your authority to serve and redeem me. The position, budget and decisions you have placed in my hands are all your trust. Let me not use them to protect my own convenience, but to protect those with the least voice. Today, as I plan rotas, assign work and make decisions, remind me of your towel. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Write down one authority you hold, and who it could serve
Before one decision today, consider the most vulnerable person
In a meeting, make space for a quiet colleague to speak
lessons.noon: “the Son of Man also came not to be served but to serve” — Lord, right now let me use the authority in my hands to serve.

lessons.title: What Do You Want Me to Do for You?
lessons.theme: Leaders serve first, and begin by asking what others need

v: A dispute also arose amongst them, which of them was considered to be greatest.
He said to them, “The kings of the nations lord it over them, and those who have authority over them are called ‘benefactors.’
But not so with you. Rather, the one who is greater amongst you, let him become as the younger, and one who is governing, as one who serves.
For who is greater, one who sits at the table, or one who serves? Isn’t it he who sits at the table? But I am amongst you as one who serves.
Jesus asked him, “What do you want me to do for you?” The blind man said to him, “Rabboni, that I may see again.”

lessons.still: Think of the first person you will meet today — a team member, colleague or client. Say in your heart, “Lord, when I see them, help me ask first, ‘How can I help you?’”
teach: At the Last Supper the disciples were still arguing about “which of them was considered to be greatest.” Jesus did not scold them; he redefined greatness: “the one who is greater amongst you, let him become as the younger, and one who is governing, as one who serves.” Then he asked: who is greater, the one at the table or the one who serves? “But I am amongst you as one who serves.” Jesus often served by beginning with a question. To the blind man by the road near Jericho he said, “What do you want me to do for you?” Of course he knew the answer, but he let the man name his own need, and so gave him back his dignity.

Many managers greet their team with “How’s progress?”, like a monitoring system that only reads data. Switch to “How can I help you?” and it is like moving the system from monitoring mode to support mode. What has someone stuck may be a phone call only you can make, a decision only you can sign off, or simply a sentence that says, “I’m behind you.” That single question often moves a team more than ten reports.

But “How can I help you?” is not a slogan. If you ask, you must listen; if you listen, you must act; if you cannot act, you must say so honestly. This means laying aside the mindset of “I’m here to direct you” and admitting that others face difficulties I cannot see. It puts into practice the truth that people matter more than tasks: care first for the person doing the work, and the work itself goes better. When leaders serve first, teams learn to serve one another. Humility breeds humility, and a department begins to build God’s order.
lessons.light: 321 Light: People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things. Ask about the person before the task; serve before you demand. Humility breeds humility — when the leader bends first, the team learns to support one another.
lessons.scene: Wanting is head of curriculum at a secondary school, overseeing more than a dozen teachers. With the end of term approaching, a young teacher has missed three weeks of lesson-plan deadlines, and Wanting has drafted a sharply worded reminder. Just before she presses send, she remembers that this teacher has often been alone in the staffroom late into the evening.
q: Who is God? — “What do you want me to do for you?” What does this question show you of Jesus’ heart?
Who am I? — Is your first sentence to colleagues usually about progress, or about their needs?
How shall I respond? — If you were Wanting, would you send the email, or go and ask a question first?
lessons.jesus: Jesus is almighty God, yet he stopped by the roadside near Jericho to ask a blind man what he wanted. He did not force his answer on people; he listened first. Today he asks you the same: “What do you want me to do for you?” Before we ask others that question, let the Lord serve us in this way.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, thank you for stopping beside me and asking what I need. I confess I am often in a hurry for results and forget to care for the people doing the work. Today slow me down, so that I first ask my team, my colleagues and my clients, “How can I help you?” Give me patience to hear their answer, and wisdom and strength to respond. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: When you see a team member today, ask first what they need
After hearing a request, give a concrete reply the same day
Add an item to your weekly meeting: “How can I help you?”
lessons.noon: “But I am amongst you as one who serves” — Lord, right now let me serve first and ask later.

lessons.title: You Will Never Wash My Feet
lessons.theme: Accepting service is also humility

v: Then he came to Simon Peter. He said to him, “Lord, do you wash my feet?”
Jesus answered him, “You don’t know what I am doing now, but you will understand later.”
Peter said to him, “You will never wash my feet!” Jesus answered him, “If I don’t wash you, you have no part with me.”
Simon Peter said to him, “Lord, not my feet only, but also my hands and my head!”
Jesus said to him, “Someone who has bathed only needs to have his feet washed, but is completely clean. You are clean, but not all of you.”

lessons.still: Hold out both hands, palms up. Say to the Lord, “Lord, I am used to giving, not to receiving. Today I am willing to let you serve me, and to let others help me.” Let those words settle quietly into your heart.
teach: When Jesus reached Peter, Peter was startled: “Lord, do you wash my feet?” Then, flatly: “You will never wash my feet!” It sounds humble, but pride is hidden in it. Peter wanted to honour Jesus his own way, not to be loved Jesus’ way. Jesus said, “If I don’t wash you, you have no part with me.” At once Peter swung to the other extreme: “Lord, not my feet only, but also my hands and my head!” Jesus gently explained that someone who has bathed only needs their feet washed. Peter’s problem was that he wanted to control how he was loved.

There is a kind of colleague who, whenever you offer help, says, “No, no, I’m fine,” and ends up alone at the office past midnight. He is like an old computer that keeps clicking “remind me later” on every system update, running slower and slower until it crashes. At work, receiving help is often harder than giving it: admitting you don’t know, letting a younger colleague teach you new software, letting a co-worker share your load, letting a client see your limits. All of this takes humility.

Self-centredness shows itself not only in looking down on others but in refusing to owe anyone. “I don’t need anyone” sounds like independence, but often it is reluctance to be in the place of the one served, because there I lose control. Yet the first step of the gospel is receiving: let Jesus wash me, and I have a part with him. A leader who accepts help shows the team that here weakness can be named and help can be received. That is humility in which everyone wins.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Humility means laying down power and returning to my place — including laying down the role of the one who always gives. Let God be God: let the Lord serve me first, and I will have something to give. Humility breeds humility, and the team dares to ask one another for help.
lessons.scene: Xiulan has run a small noodle shop in Tainan for twenty years. She recently injured her wrist, and the doctor has told her to rest for two weeks. Her daughter-in-law has offered to mind the shop, and regular customers have offered to help with the prep. Yet Xiulan still gets up at four in the morning, stands over a pot of broth, and thinks, “Better to put up with it myself than trouble anyone.”
q: Who is God? — “If I don’t wash you, you have no part with me.” Why did Jesus insist on serving Peter?
Who am I? — Do you find it easier to give help or to receive it? When did you last turn help away?
How shall I respond? — If you were Xiulan, what would you do this morning?
lessons.jesus: Jesus also received service. Mary anointed him with perfume; women supported him from their own means; on the cross he said, “I am thirsty!” (John 19:28). The perfect Son of God was willing to be served. This tells us that receiving help is not failure; it is living in love.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, like Peter I often say, “You will never wash my feet.” I don’t want to owe anyone or look weak; I always want to hold it together myself. Forgive my pride. Teach me to receive your service, and the help of colleagues, family and friends. Today, if someone holds out a hand, let me say “Thank you” rather than “I’m fine.” In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Accept someone’s help today and simply say “Thank you”
Ask a junior or younger colleague to teach you something
Tell your manager honestly about a task you can’t manage
lessons.noon: “If I don’t wash you, you have no part with me” — Lord, right now I stop pretending to be strong, and let you serve me.

lessons.title: One Act of Foot-Washing This Week
lessons.theme: The blessing is not in knowing but in doing

v: For I have given you an example, that you should also do as I have done to you.
Most certainly I tell you, a servant is not greater than his lord, neither is one who is sent greater than he who sent him.
If you know these things, blessed are you if you do them.
Bear one another’s burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ.

lessons.still: Go through the names of everyone on your team, like taking a register. With each name, say, “Lord, let me serve them.” Finally ask him, “This week, whose feet can I wash?”
teach: After washing their feet, Jesus said three things. “For I have given you an example” — this was not a performance but a pattern to follow. “A servant is not greater than his lord” — if the master has bent down, we have no excuse not to. “If you know these things, blessed are you if you do them” — the blessing is not in knowing but in doing. Paul turns this into everyday team life: “Bear one another’s burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ.” Foot-washing is not a feeling; it is an action.

Foot-washing at work is often small, as small as a bolt properly tightened in a car workshop: nobody takes a photo of it, yet the car runs safely because of it. Taking a difficult complaint call for a colleague, tidying a new starter’s spreadsheet, covering a shift when someone has a family emergency, sorting out the shared folder everyone avoids, ordering dinner for a team working late — none of these appear in performance targets, but God sees every one.

Why one act this week? Because in the eight steps, information and revelation must be followed by practice; truth that is not practised is soon forgotten. Don’t let it become a chance to show off, either; Jesus taught that when we do good, our left hand should not know what our right hand is doing (Matthew 6:3). Afterwards, review it with God: what was my motive? The other person’s reaction is not the point; the point is whether I have become more like Jesus. This week’s towel will begin to change your leadership, and your team.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The eight steps’ practice, review and correction — once you know, go and do it. Life first, then relationships, then ministry: one small act of foot-washing is where life flows into relationships, and on into the whole team.
lessons.scene: Jianbang is a site manager. The schedule is tight this week, and the crew have been racing the clock under a blazing sun every day. On Friday afternoon a young worker’s motorbike breaks down at the site gate. He lives a long way off, and his face is full of worry. Jianbang checks his watch: he still has a safety report due by five.
q: Who is God? — The Lord who says “blessed are you if you do them”: which action of yours does he want to bless this week?
Who am I? — What act of service do you most often know about but not do?
How shall I respond? — If you were Jianbang, what would you do? Whose feet will you wash on your team this week?
lessons.jesus: Among those whose feet Jesus washed was Judas, who was about to betray him. Jesus did not pick out the people who deserved to be served; he served everyone in front of him. He did not just perform one act of foot-washing; his whole life was a towel wrapped around his waist for us, and on the cross he bore all our burdens.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, thank you for wrapping a towel around your waist for me, and for bearing my burdens. This week show me who on my team needs a helping hand. Let me act not to be seen but out of love for you; even with the colleague I find difficult, make me willing to bend down. Move me from knowing to doing, and let me taste the blessing you promise in serving. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Pray once through the name of everyone on your team
Choose one person this week and wash their feet in a concrete way
At the weekend, ask God: was my motive like Jesus’?
lessons.noon: “If you know these things, blessed are you if you do them” — Lord, right now move me from knowing to doing.

mem.t: Masters, give to your servants that which is just and equal, knowing that you also have a Master in heaven.

lessons.title: Who Holds the Scales?
lessons.theme: Those who hold authority have a Master above them too

v: Masters, give to your servants that which is just and equal, knowing that you also have a Master in heaven.
You masters, do the same things to them, and give up threatening, knowing that he who is both their Master and yours is in heaven, and there is no partiality with him.

lessons.still: Sit down and rest your open hands on your knees, like a pair of scales. Say to the Lord: “Lord, today I hold rotas, reviews and decisions in my hands, but you are my Master in heaven. Weigh my heart first.” Take three quiet breaths.
teach: When Paul wrote to the Colossians, masters held almost total power over their servants. The law protected the master, not the servant. Yet Paul gave masters a command: “give to your servants that which is just and equal”. His reason was a single line: “knowing that you also have a Master in heaven.” To the Ephesians he was even blunter: “give up threatening”, because master and servant share one Master in heaven, “and there is no partiality with him.” In that world these were astonishing words. Master and slave, it turns out, stand before the same Lord.

Today’s workplace has no slaves, but it has rotas, pay-rise lists, year-end bonuses and promotion shortlists. Who gets the good shifts, who is always stuck with weekends, whose mistakes are magnified and whose are quietly forgotten: authority hides in these little boxes. Think of the scales on a market stall. You hold the beam; your team cannot see the weights, only the result. Fairness means never sticking a hidden magnet under the pan, never quietly adding or subtracting because someone is charming, comes from your hometown, or makes you look good.

The deepest thing in these verses is that they put the master back in the servant’s place. You manage others, and you are managed by a Master in heaven. 321 teaches that pride is leaving our proper place to grab power, and humility is laying power down to return to our place. When a manager remembers, “I have a Master too,” authority stops being a throne and becomes a trust. He no longer drives people by threat but wins their hearts by fairness. Change that view, and your team will meet not just a system, but a leader who lets Jesus be King.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Humility is laying down power and returning to our proper place. A manager’s place is not “the greatest” but “the one entrusted”. To let Jesus be King is to admit that the beam of the scales is finally in his hand. Fairness breeds fairness, and a win-win can begin with a single rota.
lessons.scene: Zhihao runs six bubble-tea shops in Taichung. Next week he announces year-end bonuses. His cousin Akai manages one shop: average figures, but a smooth talker. At another shop, deputy manager Yaling has quietly brought staff turnover to the lowest in the company and never asks for credit. The accountant messages: “Boss, do we follow last year’s list, or the numbers?” Zhihao stares at the screen and does not reply.
q: Who is God? — “There is no partiality with him.” What does this line show you about your Master in heaven?
Who am I? — Under the scales in your hands, is there a magnet you would rather not admit to?
How shall I respond? — If you were Zhihao, how would you answer the accountant? Where can you be fairer in one decision today?
lessons.jesus: Jesus is the only Lord truly worthy of the throne, yet he said, “I am amongst you as one who serves” (Luke 22:27). He never judged by appearances: tax collectors and Pharisees, fishermen and officials were all called and loved alike. With his own blood he bought us, who deserved nothing. That is the fairness and grace of our Master in heaven.
lessons.pray: Master in heaven, thank you that you never show favouritism to me. Today I hold lists, rotas and ratings in my hands. Weigh my heart, remove the magnet of favouritism, and take away any wish to trade threats for efficiency. Help me remember that I too will give account to you, and let my team taste your justice and kindness in my fairness. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Check one list you are responsible for: is any of it biased?
Find a quiet, overlooked colleague and thank them specifically
Give today’s instructions without any threatening tone
lessons.noon: “knowing that you also have a Master in heaven” — Lord, right now I hand the authority in my hands back to you.

lessons.title: Wages Don’t Stay Overnight
lessons.theme: Paying people what they are owed, on time, is the fear of God

v: “‘You shall not oppress your neighbour, nor rob him. “‘The wages of a hired servant shall not remain with you all night until the morning.
You shall not oppress a hired servant who is poor and needy, whether he is one of your brothers or one of the foreigners who are in your land within your gates.
In his day you shall give him his wages, neither shall the sun go down on it, for he is poor and sets his heart on it, lest he cry against you to the LORD, and it be sin to you.

lessons.still: Open your calendar or accounts list and glance at today’s payments, expense claims or approvals. Say to the Lord: “Lord, there are people behind these numbers. Let me withhold from no one today what is theirs.”
teach: Hired labourers in the ancient world were mostly paid by the day: work today, get paid today, and only then is there food on the table tonight. So the law says, “The wages of a hired servant shall not remain with you all night until the morning.” Deuteronomy reveals God’s heart even more clearly: “In his day you shall give him his wages, neither shall the sun go down on it, for he is poor and sets his heart on it.” God notices something employers often miss. For you it is a day’s delay; for him it may be his family’s dinner. If he cries to the Lord, God says, “it be sin to you.” Heaven hears the sigh of the poor.

Today, “overnight” might look like this: the contractor’s invoice pushed to next month, overtime pay “noted for later”, expense claims sitting in a drawer for three weeks, an intern’s allowance delayed again and again, a supplier’s final payment stretched as long as possible. Finance calls it “optimising cash flow”, but God’s ledger has another column. Think of it like this: money in your account that belongs to someone else is like a colleague’s lunch left in your fridge. However long it stays, it never becomes yours; it only goes off. Paying on time is not just a finance skill. It is character.

The heart of this law is not accounting but seeing people. 321 teaches that people matter more than tasks and relationships more than things; never damage a relationship for the sake of things. When we treat other people’s wages as our working capital, we put ourselves at the centre and make the weakest carry our risk. That is the self-centred life. Change your thinking and your life changes: from “delay as long as possible” to “in his day you shall give him his wages”. Your company may not instantly earn more, but your staff and suppliers will see in you a God who does not oppress.
lessons.light: 321 Light: People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things. Paying people what they are owed, on time, writes the order “God, self, others, tasks” into your ledger. Let Jesus be King of your payment process.
lessons.scene: Meizhu runs a small renovation company in Johor Bahru with eight craftsmen on day rates. A major client’s payment is a month late, and the account holds barely enough for wages. Her business partner suggests, “Hold the workers’ pay for two weeks; they won’t leave anyway.” Just then the senior craftsman, Ah Cai, messages: “Boss, my child’s school fees are due next week. Can wages be paid this week?”
q: Who is God? — God notices that the poor “set their heart” on their wages. What does that show you about his heart?
Who am I? — In your work, is there something owed to someone else that you are holding back?
How shall I respond? — If you were Meizhu, how would you reply to Ah Cai? Besides praying, what practical options are there?
lessons.jesus: Jesus never defaults. What he promised, he fulfilled. He said he would give his life as a ransom for many, and on the cross he paid in full, crying, “It is finished!” (John 19:30). He did not leave our debt to God overnight, and the grace we receive from him never waits until sundown. This generous, punctual Lord is our model whenever we pay.
lessons.pray: Righteous and loving Lord, thank you for hearing the sigh of the poor. Search my accounts, my expense claims, and the promises I have made but not yet kept. If there is anything I owe and have delayed, give me courage to deal with it today. If I am facing a cash-flow crisis, give me wisdom and honesty, so that I do not push the burden onto the weakest. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Find one payment or claim you can process early
Sign off a team member’s claim today, not tomorrow
Update a waiting supplier on their payment, unasked
lessons.noon: “In his day you shall give him his wages, neither shall the sun go down on it” — Lord, right now keep me from withholding what is owed to anyone.

lessons.title: Ears of Grain Left Behind
lessons.theme: A good employer’s grace often lives in the margin beyond the rules

v: Behold, Boaz came from Bethlehem, and said to the reapers, “May The LORD be with you.” They answered him, “May The LORD bless you.”
Then Boaz said to his servant who was set over the reapers, “Whose young lady is this?”
The servant who was set over the reapers answered, “It is the Moabite lady who came back with Naomi out of the country of Moab.
She said, ‘Please let me glean and gather after the reapers amongst the sheaves.’ So she came, and has continued even from the morning until now, except that she rested a little in the house.”
Then Boaz said to Ruth, “Listen, my daughter. Don’t go to glean in another field, and don’t go from here, but stay here close to my maidens.

Let your eyes be on the field that they reap, and go after them. Haven’t I commanded the young men not to touch you? When you are thirsty, go to the vessels, and drink from that which the young men have drawn.”
When she had risen up to glean, Boaz commanded his young men, saying, “Let her glean even amongst the sheaves, and don’t reproach her.
Also pull out some for her from the bundles, and leave it. Let her glean, and don’t rebuke her.”

lessons.still: Picture yourself walking into a field of barley and greeting each person there. Say to the Lord: “Lord, may my first words at work today be a blessing. Help me notice the one standing at the edge.”
teach: When Boaz walks into his field, his first words are not “How’s progress?” but “May The LORD be with you.” The workers answer, “May The LORD bless you.” Employer and workers greet each other with blessing. Then he notices a stranger gleaning, asks who she is, and does three things. He gives her safety: “Haven’t I commanded the young men not to touch you?” He gives her provision: when thirsty, she may drink what the young men have drawn. And he gives her dignity: “don’t reproach her”, and even, “pull out some for her from the bundles, and leave it.”

The law already required farmers to leave the edges of the field for the poor (Leviticus 19:9–10). Boaz goes one step further, and does it in a way that spares her embarrassment.
