It is like a bakery that leaves the day’s bread on a shelf by the door so that anyone in need can simply take some without having to ask. Good managers leave a few “ears of grain” at the edge of the KPIs: an extra week for a new hire to settle in, flexible hours for someone doing the school run, another chance for someone whose performance has wobbled. That is not spoiling people. It is giving the system some warmth.

Boaz’s generosity is not a performance; it flows from knowing God. He blesses Ruth as one who has come to take refuge under the wings of “the LORD, the God of Israel”. He knows that his field and his harvest also sit under those wings. People who know they have received grace naturally leave grain behind. 321 teaches that self-denial means living for Jesus and for others, not for ourselves. When you leave a margin of grace at work, you are building God’s order: a place where the weak can stand too.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Self-denial means living for Jesus and for others, not for self. Boaz blesses first, then notices, then provides: life first, then relationships, then ministry. The grain left at the edge of the system is where Jesus receives the glory.
lessons.scene: Fulai runs a kiwifruit packhouse in Tauranga, New Zealand. This picking season a middle-aged woman, Mere, has joined; her husband died last year, and she works more slowly than the young ones. The quality supervisor suggests not rostering her next week. Fulai stands by the conveyor belt, watching her sort each fruit with great care, and the pen over his roster stops moving.
q: Who is God? — From Boaz’s field, what do you see about how God cares for people on the margins?
Who am I? — When you walk into work, are your first words usually about progress, or a blessing?
How shall I respond? — If you were Fulai, how would you “leave grain” for Mere while still caring for the team’s efficiency?
lessons.jesus: Boaz is a picture of something greater: the close relative who at his own cost redeemed Ruth. Jesus is our true kinsman-redeemer. He sees us standing at the edge of the field with nothing, and he does not shame or scold us; he invites us to sit and eat with him. He does more than leave grain for us. He gives himself as the bread of life.
lessons.pray: Lord who blesses, thank you that when I had nothing you let me glean grace in your field. Today give me Boaz’s eyes to see the one on my team who is a little slower, a little shyer, standing at the edge. Let my first words be blessing, and let my systems leave some grain behind, so that the weak find safety and dignity under my care. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Make your first words at work a blessing to someone
Ask someone on the edge of the team what they need
Review one rule: can it leave more room for grace?
lessons.noon: “May The LORD be with you” — Lord, right now let me treat everyone around me with blessing.

lessons.title: The Manager with a Scalpel
lessons.theme: Necessary decisions can be made, but make them with grace

v: So when they had eaten their breakfast, Jesus said to Simon Peter, “Simon, son of Jonah, do you love me more than these?” He said to him, “Yes, Lord; you know that I have affection for you.” He said to him, “Feed my lambs.”
He said to him again a second time, “Simon, son of Jonah, do you love me?” He said to him, “Yes, Lord; you know that I have affection for you.” He said to him, “Tend my sheep.”

He said to him the third time, “Simon, son of Jonah, do you have affection for me?” Peter was grieved because he asked him the third time, “Do you have affection for me?” He said to him, “Lord, you know everything. You know that I have affection for you.” Jesus said to him, “Feed my sheep.
but speaking truth in love, we may grow up in all things into him who is the head, Christ,

lessons.still: Write today’s hardest conversation on a sticky note and press it under your palm. Say to the Lord: “Lord, I must speak the truth. Let me speak it in love. Let my words cut into the problem, not the person.”
teach: Peter’s three denials were the worst failure among the disciples. After the resurrection Jesus did not pretend nothing had happened, nor did he strike Peter off in public. After breakfast he asked him three times, “Do you love me?” Three denials met with three questions, and each question came with a fresh commission: “Feed my lambs,” “Tend my sheep.” Scripture says Peter “was grieved”. Truth hurts. But this pain was not meant to humiliate; it was meant to restore. Jesus meets failure by opening the wound honestly and then lifting the person up with a new trust.

In the workplace, reviews, discipline and even dismissals are sometimes unavoidable responsibilities. The question is not whether, but how. A butcher and a surgeon both hold a blade. The difference is that the surgeon diagnoses before cutting, avoids vital organs while cutting, and stitches and cares afterwards. A manager who leads with grace does the same: sets clear expectations and offers real chances to improve beforehand; deals with the issue, not the person, and in private rather than in public; and still cares where they go afterwards. Paul says we grow by “speaking truth in love”. Truth without love is cruelty; love without truth is indulgence.

321 says never hurt people for the sake of tasks, but that does not mean never dealing with problems. Sometimes the most loving thing is to tell someone honestly: this role is not right for you. When you make hard decisions believing that people matter more than tasks, you are not wielding power; you are carrying a trust. And remember: if your company asks you to carry out something illegal or clearly unjust, obedience has limits (Acts 5:29). Where needed, seek help from someone you trust or from a professional.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Rely on the Holy Spirit with your heart, not on yourself with your head. Pray before the hard conversation; keep your focus on Jesus, not on your own reputation or their reaction. Humility breeds humility: a manager who speaks truth with grace often receives honesty in return.
lessons.scene: Eunice is head of HR at a logistics firm in Singapore. The company has decided to close a department. The list of twelve names is final, and tomorrow from nine she will meet each of them. Legal has given her a “standard script”: ten minutes, signature, collect the access card. She looks at the name of the warehouse team leader who has served nineteen years, and closes the script file.
q: Who is God? — Jesus asked Peter three times, “Do you love me?” What does this show you about how he treats those who fail?
Who am I? — When a hard truth must be spoken, do you tend to cut like a butcher, or avoid saying it at all?
How shall I respond? — If you were Eunice, how would you “speak truth in love” in tomorrow’s meetings?
lessons.jesus: Jesus knew Peter’s failure before it happened and told him, “I prayed for you, that your faith wouldn’t fail” (Luke 22:32). He reviews us not to condemn but to restore. The Lord who has authority to judge all the earth took the severest penalty himself on the cross, so that before him we hear a commission, not a verdict.
lessons.pray: Lord, you know the decision I have to make today and how hard that conversation will be. Help me speak the truth in love: neither running away nor being cruel. Let me be clear as I explain, gentle as I listen, and faithful in praying for them afterwards. If an unjust demand comes to me, give me the courage to say no. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Before a hard talk, pray for the person by name
Affirm their contribution first, then name the issue
Afterwards send a caring message, not about work
lessons.noon: “speaking truth in love” — Lord, right now let my words heal, not harm.

lessons.title: More Than “Recalculating”
lessons.theme: Feedback names not only mistakes but God’s grace in a person

v: We always give thanks to God for all of you, mentioning you in our prayers,
remembering without ceasing your work of faith and labour of love and perseverance of hope in our Lord Jesus Christ, before our God and Father.
Greet Prisca and Aquila, my fellow workers in Christ Jesus,
who risked their own necks for my life, to whom not only I give thanks, but also all the assemblies of the Gentiles.

lessons.still: Think of someone you lead or work alongside, and quietly say their name in your heart. Say to the Lord: “Lord, thank you for placing them beside me. Open my eyes today to see what you are doing in them.”
teach: Paul was a demanding leader, yet his letters overflow with specific affirmation. He tells the Thessalonians he keeps “remembering without ceasing your work of faith and labour of love and perseverance of hope”. He does not just say, “You’re great.” He names their work, their labour, their perseverance. In the last chapter of Romans he greets more than twenty co-workers by name, and says Prisca and Aquila “risked their own necks for my life”, adding that not only he but all the churches give thanks for them.

Many managers are like a satnav. As long as you drive the right way, it says nothing; take one wrong turn and it immediately announces, “Recalculating.” Over time your team remembers only where they went wrong, not where they went right. Blessing-shaped feedback turns the satnav round: “Your patience with complaints these past three weeks kept two long-standing clients with us.” Specific, true, and pointing to character, not just results. Words like that are a map, showing someone where to keep going.

321’s 920 says that everyone connected to me is my “2”; I practise the self-emptied “0” so that the nine (“9”) fruits of the Spirit grow in my relationships. Genuine praise requires taking the spotlight off ourselves. Self-centred people find it hard to praise others, because someone else’s strength feels like a threat. A self-emptied manager can say, “This is a gift God has placed in you.” Then feedback becomes blessing: Jesus receives the glory, and the people on the team become more like who they were made to be.
lessons.light: 321 Light: 920 — every team member is my “2”. Blessing-shaped feedback lets the self-emptied “0” bear the fruit of kindness and goodness. Crediting God’s grace in a person is how we let Jesus receive all the glory.
lessons.scene: Shaoen is a technical team lead at a software company in Shanghai, writing year-end reviews. The system has only three fields: “Targets met”, “Areas to improve”, “Overall rating”. Xiao Zhou had no headline product this year, but quietly brought two new hires up to speed and spent a whole week on call when the system went down. Shaoen’s cursor rests on “Areas to improve”. He wants to write something else first.
q: Who is God? — Paul remembered his co-workers’ “work, labour and perseverance”. What does this show you about how God remembers what we offer?
Who am I? — Is your feedback to others more like a satnav saying “Recalculating”, or like a map?
How shall I respond? — If you were Shaoen, what specific, blessing-filled sentence would you write for Xiao Zhou?
lessons.jesus: The first time Jesus met Peter, he looked at him and said, “You shall be called Cephas” (John 1:42). Before Peter had grown into it, Jesus spoke his future. He does the same with us: he sees our mistakes, but he also declares the work he will complete in us. His word is the deepest blessing-shaped feedback in the world.
lessons.pray: Lord, thank you for calling me with words of hope before I had grown into them. Open my eyes today to see your work in my colleagues and team. Let my reviews name grace as well as problems, and let my lips speak what builds others up, giving grace to those who hear. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Send one specific word of affirmation to a colleague
At your next meeting, publicly thank someone behind the scenes
Reread a review you wrote and add what they did well
lessons.noon: “labour of love” — Lord, right now I remember my co-workers’ labour and give you thanks for them.

mem.t: Iron sharpens iron; so a man sharpens his friends countenance.

lessons.title: The Apprentice in the Passenger Seat
lessons.theme: Developing people begins by letting them watch you walk with God

v: The LORD spoke to Moses face to face, as a man speaks to his friend. He turned again into the camp, but his servant Joshua, the son of Nun, a young man, didn’t depart from the Tent.
Joshua the son of Nun was full of the spirit of wisdom, for Moses had laid his hands on him. The children of Israel listened to him, and did as the LORD commanded Moses.

lessons.still: Close your eyes and think of someone senior who once invested in you, and thank God for them. Then think of someone who works beside you now. Say to the Lord: “Lord, today may they see you in me.”
teach: Exodus tells us “The LORD spoke to Moses face to face, as a man speaks to his friend.” Then comes a line that is easy to skip: when Moses returned to the camp, “his servant Joshua, the son of Nun, a young man, didn’t depart from the Tent.” Joshua’s training did not begin in a classroom; it began at Moses’ side. When Moses went up the mountain of God, Joshua went with him (Exodus 24:13). When Israel fought Amalek, Joshua led in the valley while Moses raised his hands on the hilltop (Exodus 17:9–12). Years later, Scripture says Joshua “was full of the spirit of wisdom, for Moses had laid his hands on him.”

Old apprenticeships often said, “Watch for three years first.” Developing someone is not handing them a manual and walking away. Nobody learns to drive from the Highway Code alone. First you sit in the passenger seat and watch how the instructor checks the mirrors and judges when to brake; then you take the wheel while they sit beside you. Take a junior colleague to meet clients, let them sit in on your meetings, let them hear how you handle a difficult phone call, even how you face failure. The final step is the “laying on of hands”: public authorisation, your endorsement, so the team knows that from today they can follow this person.

What Joshua learned from Moses was first not tactics but a life lived in God’s presence; that is why he “didn’t depart from the Tent”. 321 says: life first, then relationships, then ministry. The aim of mentoring is not to clone myself, but to see the other person filled with the Spirit, meeting God face to face. Moses could not enter Canaan; Joshua could. Good mentors are glad when their students go further than they did. That is the self-emptied life: not my legacy remembered, but God’s work carried on.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The “3” in 235 means building spiritual parent-and-child relationships. With Moses and Joshua, walking together came before handing over: life first, then relationships, then ministry. A leader who lets Jesus be King prepares a stage for a successor, rather than keeping it for himself.
lessons.scene: Guangming is a senior machinist at a precision engineering plant in Hsinchu, a year from retirement. The plant manager has paired him with Azhe, a twenty-six-year-old engineer. Guangming has always felt, “It’s quicker to do it myself than to teach him.” Today a key machine is making a strange noise, and a client’s order ships tomorrow morning. Azhe, standing beside him, asks quietly: “Master, could I try this one?”
q: Who is God? — God spoke with Moses “face to face” and appointed Joshua through the laying on of hands. What does this show you about how God values passing faith on?
Who am I? — In your work, is there someone sitting in the “passenger seat”, waiting for you to let go of the wheel?
How shall I respond? — If you were Guangming, how would you answer Azhe? Who could see a little more of your work today?
lessons.jesus: Jesus “appointed twelve, that they might be with him, and that he might send them out to preach” (Mark 3:14). First with him, then sent. For three years the disciples watched him rise before dawn to pray, heal the sick, face his accusers, and stoop to wash their feet. Before he ascended he entrusted his mission to them and poured out the Spirit. He is the best mentor, because he gave his own life to his students.
lessons.pray: Lord, thank you for the mentors you have sent to walk with me. Today give me the heart of Moses: not only to do the job well, but to raise people up. Help me not to fear slowness or being surpassed, and let those beside me see how I depend on you. May my work keep bearing fruit in others long after I have gone. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Invite a junior colleague to sit in on a meeting or call
While you work, explain why you do it that way
Send a thank-you message to someone who mentored you
lessons.noon: “The LORD spoke to Moses face to face, as a man speaks to his friend” — Lord, right now I draw near to you first, and then lead others to you.

lessons.title: The Bottleneck on the Line
lessons.theme: Delegating is not laziness; it lets more people share the load

v: Moses’ father-in-law said to him, “The thing that you do is not good.
You will surely wear away, both you, and this people that is with you; for the thing is too heavy for you. You are not able to perform it yourself alone.
Listen now to my voice. I will give you counsel, and God be with you. You represent the people before God, and bring the causes to God.
You shall teach them the statutes and the laws, and shall show them the way in which they must walk, and the work that they must do.

Moreover you shall provide out of all the people able men which fear God: men of truth, hating unjust gain; and place such over them, to be rulers of thousands, rulers of hundreds, rulers of fifties, and rulers of tens.

Let them judge the people at all times. It shall be that every great matter they shall bring to you, but every small matter they shall judge themselves. So shall it be easier for you, and they shall share the load with you.
If you will do this thing, and God commands you so, then you will be able to endure, and all these people also will go to their place in peace.”

lessons.still: Lay out today’s to-do list and circle three things that truly only you can do. Then look at the rest. Say to the Lord: “Lord, I am not the saviour. Help me let go of what I should, and hand it to the people you have prepared.”
teach: Moses sat judging the people from morning to evening, and the people stood queuing from morning to evening. His father-in-law Jethro watched for a day and said bluntly, “The thing that you do is not good. You will surely wear away, both you, and this people that is with you; for the thing is too heavy for you.” Then he offered a plan. Moses should “represent the people before God” and teach them; then choose “able men which fear God: men of truth, hating unjust gain” to lead at different levels. “Every great matter they shall bring to you, but every small matter they shall judge themselves.” The outcome was a win-win: “So shall it be easier for you, and they shall share the load with you.”

Many founders and managers live in Exodus 18. Every email gets a personal reply, every quote a personal check; even a paper jam in the printer gets brought to them. It is like a factory where only one station on the whole line can release goods for shipping. However hard-working that person is, they become the bottleneck for the entire plant. Jethro’s plan has three keys. First return to your own role (prayer and teaching). Choose people for character first (fearing God, truthful, not greedy). Then define clearly the scope of their authority (great matters and small ones). Delegating is not dumping tasks on people; it is growing people.

Why is letting go so hard? Sometimes we fear others will do it badly; sometimes we secretly enjoy the feeling that “nothing works without me”. 321 says the self-centred life wants to be lord and king, to take God’s place. If Moses had kept carrying everything alone, it might have looked like responsibility, but it could have been pride: leaving his place to grab power. Humility is returning to our place: I am not the saviour, only God’s servant. When you let go, colleagues get the chance to grow, you find rest, and everyone can go home in peace.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Pride is leaving our proper place to grab power; humility is laying power down and returning to our place. Delegating lets people be people and lets God be God. Humility breeds humility: when a manager lets go, the team learns to take responsibility, and God’s order is built.
lessons.scene: Weiting founded an online skincare business in Kuala Lumpur and grew it to fifteen staff in three years. She still answers every customer message and approves every social media post herself, going to bed at one each night. Today her marketing lead, Daniel, hands her a campaign proposal: “Boss, could I take full charge of this one?” Her finger hovers over the reply “Let me take a look first”.
q: Who is God? — God spoke through a father-in-law’s honest advice. What does this show you about how God cares for weary leaders?
Who am I? — Which of your tasks are not really “only I can do this” but “I don’t want to let go”?
How shall I respond? — If you were Weiting, how would you reply to Daniel, and how would you define his authority?
lessons.jesus: Jesus had only a few short years on earth, yet he did not keep everything to himself. He sent out the twelve, and later appointed seventy others and “sent them two by two ahead of him” (Luke 10:1). After he ascended he poured out the Spirit so that the whole church would share his mission. The Lord who can do all things is glad to work alongside weak people like us.
lessons.pray: Lord, I confess I often carry everything alone, until I am exhausted and those around me are too. Break down the pride in me that says, “Nothing works without me.” Give me eyes to see colleagues who fear you and can be trusted, courage to hand things over, and patience to walk with them as they learn. Bring me back to the place you have given me. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Choose one task to hand to a colleague today, and hand it over
Tell them clearly what they may decide for themselves
Use five minutes of the time saved to pray for your team
lessons.noon: “So shall it be easier for you, and they shall share the load with you” — Lord, right now I put down the burden and place my people in your hands.

lessons.title: Signing as Guarantor
lessons.theme: Developing people often starts with believing in someone others gave up on

v: When Saul had come to Jerusalem, he tried to join himself to the disciples; but they were all afraid of him, not believing that he was a disciple.

But Barnabas took him and brought him to the apostles, and declared to them how he had seen the Lord on the way, and that he had spoken to him, and how at Damascus he had preached boldly in the name of Jesus.
Barnabas planned to take John, who was called Mark, with them also.
But Paul didn’t think that it was a good idea to take with them someone who had withdrawn from them in Pamphylia, and didn’t go with them to do the work.
Then the contention grew so sharp that they separated from each other. Barnabas took Mark with him and sailed away to Cyprus,

lessons.still: Think of a colleague or team member you have privately “given up on”, and say their name. Say to the Lord: “Lord, you did not give up on me. Let me look at them once more through your eyes.”
teach: When Saul came to Jerusalem after his conversion, the disciples “were all afraid of him, not believing that he was a disciple”. After all, he had persecuted the church. “But Barnabas took him and brought him to the apostles,” and told them how Saul had seen the Lord and preached boldly. Barnabas staked his own reputation on Saul. Years later it was Mark’s turn. Mark had left the team partway through a mission, and Paul refused to take him again; “the contention grew so sharp that they separated from each other.” Once again Barnabas chose the person others thought unreliable. Later, near the end of his life, Paul asked Timothy to bring Mark, “for he is useful to me for service” (2 Timothy 4:11).

Loans need a guarantor; job applications need a referee. Barnabas is the person who signs in the guarantor box when nobody else dares. Workplaces have their own Sauls and Marks: the new hire who made a big mistake, the colleague who left and wants to come back, the team member with a label stuck on them. Good mentors see not only the gap in the CV, but what God might do in a life. Of course, Paul’s concern was not unreasonable; endorsement needs wisdom, not naivety. But many turning points begin when someone says, “I’ll walk with them and let them try again.”

Barnabas’s name means “Son of Encouragement” (Acts 4:36). He not only encouraged people; he was willing to step back. At first Scripture speaks of “Barnabas and Saul”; later it is usually “Paul and Barnabas”. He was not afraid to be overtaken by the one he had raised up. That is the self-emptied life. In 321’s 235, the “3” is building spiritual parent-and-child relationships. A spiritual parent does not only pick the easiest children to raise, but reaches out once more to the one who has fallen.
lessons.light: 321 Light: People matter more than tasks. Barnabas would rather take a risk than give up on a person. A self-emptied leader is not afraid of being surpassed, and wants only God’s work fulfilled. This kind of endorsement lets Jesus receive the glory, rather than building our own network.
lessons.scene: Timothy is a project manager at an engineering consultancy in Singapore. Last year an intern, Ajie, walked out in the middle of a project without notice, leaving the team working late for weeks to fill the gap. Now Ajie has written to say his family was in crisis at the time; he deeply regrets it and wants to apply again. In the team chat, the department head writes: “We can’t use someone like that again.” Timothy opens Ajie’s letter, then looks back at the chat.
q: Who is God? — God gave Saul and Mark a second chance through Barnabas. What does this show you about his grace?
Who am I? — Are you more like the disciples who were “all afraid of him”, or like Barnabas, willing to sign?
How shall I respond? — If you were Timothy, how would you reply in the chat, holding both wisdom and grace together?
lessons.jesus: Jesus is the one who vouches for us to the end. When, like Saul, we have a dark past, or like Mark, we have given up halfway, he speaks for us before the Father: “he is also able to save to the uttermost those who draw near to God through him, seeing that he lives forever to make intercession for them” (Hebrews 7:25). He did not only sign as our guarantor; he paid our debt with his life.
lessons.pray: Lord, thank you that when I was least reliable, you still accepted me and stood surety for me. Forgive me for labelling people so quickly. Today give me the eyes and courage of Barnabas, and the wisdom to discern. Let the person others have given up on see your grace again through my companionship. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Say a word of belief to a colleague who is often criticised
Revisit a request you once refused, and pray about it again
Pray for someone you mentored who later stumbled
lessons.noon: “But Barnabas took him and brought him to the apostles” — Lord, right now make me someone who welcomes others.

lessons.title: From Vending Machine to Well
lessons.theme: Good questions help people find answers God has already placed in them

v: Counsel in the heart of man is like deep water, but a man of understanding will draw it out.
Jesus went out, with his disciples, into the villages of Caesarea Philippi. On the way he asked his disciples, “Who do men say that I am?”
They told him, “John the Baptiser, and others say Elijah, but others, one of the prophets.”
He said to them, “But who do you say that I am?” Peter answered, “You are the Christ.”

lessons.still: When the first person comes to you with a question today, don’t rush to answer. Right now, say to the Lord: “Lord, give me listening ears and a heart that doesn’t need to prove itself. Help me ask good questions.”
teach: Proverbs says, “Counsel in the heart of man is like deep water, but a man of understanding will draw it out.” Wisdom is not only giving answers but knowing how to draw out what lies in someone’s heart. Jesus was the master of questions. On the road to Caesarea Philippi he first asked, “Who do men say that I am?” A safe question; anyone could answer. Then he asked, “But who do you say that I am?” That question turns spectators into participants. Peter said, “You are the Christ.” Jesus said this was revealed to him by the Father (Matthew 16:17).

Managers often behave like vending machines: a team member inserts a question, and out drops a can of answer. It’s fast, but the team never learns to think, and the manager never gets to go home. Coaching conversations replace the vending machine with a well: “What do you think the core issue is?” “What have you tried?” “If there were no constraints, what would you do?” “What do you need from me?” Jesus asked the blind man, “What do you want me to do for you?” (Mark 10:51). He knew already, but he let the man voice his own longing.

321’s eight steps move from information to revelation and conviction. Lecturing can only give information; good questions make room for revelation, so people see for themselves, are convinced for themselves, and then truly practise. This requires relying on the Holy Spirit with your heart, not on yourself with your head. As you listen, rather than planning your next sentence, ask the Spirit quietly, “What does this person really need?” Admitting that I am not the source of every answer is humility.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Rely on the Holy Spirit with your heart, not on yourself with your head. Coaching questions walk people through the “revelation, conviction” part of the eight steps. A humble manager need not be the hero of every answer, but walks with people until they see God.
lessons.scene: Yutong is a product manager at a tech company in Shenzhen. Her new assistant, Xiao Lin, comes to her for the fifth time with the same kind of question: “How should I prioritise this request?” Yutong has three more meetings today, and the quickest thing would be to just tell him. She glances at the clock, takes a deep breath, and half-closes her laptop.
q: Who is God? — Jesus asked, “Who do you say that I am?” What does this show you about how he respects and leads people?
Who am I? — At work, are you more of an answer vending machine, or someone who draws water from the well?
How shall I respond? — If you were Yutong, which two questions would you ask Xiao Lin?
lessons.jesus: On the road to Emmaus the risen Jesus walked with two discouraged disciples and first asked, “What are you talking about as you walk, and are sad?” (Luke 24:17). He let them pour out their disappointment before explaining the Scriptures from Moses and the prophets. He knew everything, yet chose to ask first and listen first. This Lord, who never needs to prove himself, is our model for every conversation.
lessons.pray: Lord, you know all things, yet you ask me questions and listen to me. Heal my urge to rush to answers and to look capable. In every conversation today, help me listen first and then ask. Let my questions help colleagues find direction, and find you. May your Spirit remind me what each person truly needs. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: When asked a question today, first ask: “What do you think?”
Ask one open question in a meeting, then listen quietly
Note down the most helpful question you heard today
lessons.noon: “Counsel in the heart of man is like deep water” — Lord, right now help me listen patiently and draw out your wisdom.

lessons.title: Passing On the Starter
lessons.theme: Every disciple can become someone’s spiritual parent

v: You therefore, my child, be strengthened in the grace that is in Christ Jesus.
The things which you have heard from me amongst many witnesses, commit the same things to faithful men who will be able to teach others also.
But I hope in the Lord Jesus to send Timothy to you soon, that I also may be cheered up when I know how you are doing.
For I have no one else like-minded, who will truly care about you.
For they all seek their own, not the things of Jesus Christ.
But you know that he has proved himself. As a child serves a father, so he served with me in furtherance of the Good News.

lessons.still: Be still and ask the Holy Spirit one question: “Lord, who is the one you want me to invest in?” Don’t rush the answer. Let a name or a face come to mind, and place that person in the Lord’s hands.
teach: Paul tells Timothy, “The things which you have heard from me amongst many witnesses, commit the same things to faithful men who will be able to teach others also.” There are four generations in that one verse: Paul, Timothy, faithful people, and others. Developing people is not a one-off training course but a chain of inheritance. How does Paul describe Timothy? “I have no one else like-minded”; “As a child serves a father, so he served with me in furtherance of the Good News.” This is more than boss and subordinate; it is spiritual father and son. And it all begins with: “be strengthened in the grace that is in Christ Jesus.”

Every baker understands sourdough starter. A small portion of fermented dough is added to each new batch; the rest is fed and passed on. Some bakeries have kept the same starter going for decades, so that every loaf still carries the flavour of the very first one. Workplace mentoring is like that. The patience, honesty and skill you received from those before you are worked into the life of the next new colleague. You don’t need to be managing director before you start. A senior shop assistant, an experienced nurse, a site foreman can all have “that one person”.

321’s 235: become a “2” spiritual companion with the self-emptied, build “3” spiritual parent-and-child relationships, and become a “5” fivefold-ministry team of comrades. This week’s memory verse, “Iron sharpens iron”, reminds us that mentoring works both ways: while sharpening others, we are sharpened too. Today, ask the Spirit: who is the one I am to invest in? Pray for them first, then invite them for a coffee. Life first, then relationships, then ministry.
lessons.light: 321 Light: 235 — from “2” spiritual companions, to “3” spiritual parents and children, to a “5” team of spiritual comrades. The last of the eight steps is multiplication: what you have received, entrust to faithful people, so that God’s order is built generation after generation.
lessons.scene: Kai Wen is sous-chef at a restaurant in Auckland. Every evening after service, the dishwasher, Sione, quietly watches the chefs prep. Once he tasted a sauce Kai Wen had got wrong and could say exactly what it was missing. Next month the head chef will promote one kitchen assistant and asks Kai Wen for a recommendation: a skilled but indifferent veteran, or the dishwasher whose eyes light up.
q: Who is God? — Through Paul and Timothy, God passed faith from one generation to the next. What does this show you about how he values people?
Who am I? — What “starter” in your life did you receive from someone who went before you?
How shall I respond? — If you were Kai Wen, whom would you recommend, and how would you walk with them through the next step?
lessons.jesus: On the night he was betrayed, Jesus prayed for his disciples: “Not for these only do I pray, but for those also who will believe in me through their word” (John 17:20). His gaze went beyond the eleven in front of him to disciples in every age, including you today. We can develop others because he first worked his own life into ours.
lessons.pray: Lord, thank you for the mentors you placed in my life, and for working your own life into mine. Today show me the person you want me to invest in. Give me patience to walk with them and sincerity in how I treat them, and as I sharpen them, sharpen me to be more like Christ. May your grace be passed on through me, generation after generation. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Write down the name of the one you will invest in, and pray
Invite them for coffee this week and ask about their dreams
Teach them the most valuable work lesson you have learned
lessons.noon: “Iron sharpens iron” — Lord, right now, as I sharpen others, sharpen me as well.

mem.t: So then, as we have opportunity, lets do what is good towards all men, and especially towards those who are of the household of the faith.

lessons.title: Thirty Seconds at the Till
lessons.theme: Every customer is an opportunity God gives me to do good

v: Let’s not be weary in doing good, for we will reap in due season if we don’t give up.
So then, as we have opportunity, let’s do what is good towards all men, and especially towards those who are of the household of the faith.
having good behaviour amongst the nations, so in that of which they speak against you as evildoers, they may see your good works and glorify God in the day of visitation.

lessons.still: Before you leave home, pause with your hand on the door handle. Say to the Lord: “Lord, I will meet many people today, some only in passing. Don’t let me miss any opportunity you give me to do good.”
teach: At the end of Galatians Paul writes, “Let’s not be weary in doing good, for we will reap in due season if we don’t give up. So then, as we have opportunity, let’s do what is good towards all men, and especially towards those who are of the household of the faith.” Notice two phrases: “as we have opportunity” and “all men”. Doing good is not a charity event for when we have spare time; it happens in every moment of opportunity. And it is not only for brothers and sisters at church, but for everyone: customers, suppliers, passers-by, even competitors. Peter adds that those outside the faith may “see your good works and glorify God”.

A convenience-store cashier serves hundreds of customers a day, about thirty seconds each. Scan, change, bag: it can be just a process, or it can be a window for doing good. A sincere “Thanks, travel safely”, helping an elderly customer count their coins, heating up a rushed commuter’s lunch before they ask. Every workplace contact is like a window that opens for a few seconds: once it shuts, the moment is gone. A sales visit, a nurse changing a dressing, a call to customer service, a courier’s delivery: each one is a window.

Why “don’t give up”? Because doing good often goes unrewarded. Customers won’t add a star for your patience; sometimes they push their luck further. 321 calls us to shift perspective: from the temporary to the eternal, from earthly to heavenly. We don’t do good for our sales figures but because “we will reap in due season”, and the Lord of the harvest is God. Keep your focus on Jesus, not on the customer’s reaction, and your kindness won’t be snuffed out by other people’s coldness.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Shift perspective from the temporary to the eternal. Doing good to all people means seeing each customer as a “2” God has placed in front of me. Look to the Lord, not to the reward, and kindness won’t lose heart when people are cold.
lessons.scene: Siyu manages a convenience store in Kaohsiung. At ten at night, in the rush, a regular elderly man is slowly counting a handful of coins to buy a boxed meal and a bottle of milk. Five people are queuing behind him, and someone starts tutting loudly. Xiao Pan, a new staff member, looks at Siyu, asking with her eyes: should we ask him to step aside and count first?
q: Who is God? — “We will reap in due season.” What does this show you about how God remembers good deeds?
Who am I? — What kind of person today are you most likely to treat as a “process” rather than an “opportunity”?
How shall I respond? — If you were Siyu, how would you care for both the elderly man and the people queuing?
lessons.jesus: Scripture says Jesus “went about doing good” (Acts 10:38). He looked up and saw Zacchaeus in the tree, talked with a Samaritan woman at a well, and stopped in a pressing crowd for one person. The people he did good to were often those who could never repay him, even those who would later abandon him. This Lord who never gives up is doing good to us today.
lessons.pray: Lord who does good, thank you for showing me kindness first, when I had nothing to give back. Today open my eyes at the till, in the meeting room, on the other end of the phone, to see the opportunities you give me. When my kindness meets coldness, keep me from losing heart, and remind me that you are the Lord of the harvest. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Give each customer or colleague one sincere thank-you today
Help someone who looks like they need assistance, unasked
Before leaving work, ask: which opportunity did I miss?
lessons.noon: “as we have opportunity, let’s do what is good towards all men” — Lord, right now let me see the person you have put in front of me.

lessons.title: The Ticket Machine Can’t Call a Name
lessons.theme: Jesus stops in the crowd and turns a number back into a name

v: A certain woman who had a discharge of blood for twelve years,
and had suffered many things by many physicians, and had spent all that she had, and was no better, but rather grew worse,
having heard the things concerning Jesus, came up behind him in the crowd and touched his clothes.
For she said, “If I just touch his clothes, I will be made well.”
Immediately the flow of her blood was dried up, and she felt in her body that she was healed of her affliction.
Immediately Jesus, perceiving in himself that the power had gone out from him, turned around in the crowd and asked, “Who touched my clothes?”
His disciples said to him, “You see the multitude pressing against you, and you say, ‘Who touched me?’”
He looked around to see her who had done this thing.
But the woman, fearing and trembling, knowing what had been done to her, came and fell down before him, and told him all the truth.
He said to her, “Daughter, your faith has made you well. Go in peace, and be cured of your disease.”

lessons.still: The first time you speak with someone today, try looking them in the eye before you look at the screen. For now, say to the Lord: “Lord, you have seen me. Let me see people today, not just tickets.”
teach: This woman had been ill for twelve years. She “had suffered many things by many physicians, and had spent all that she had”. Under the law her condition made her unclean (Leviticus 15:25), so she could not freely touch others. She dared only to come “up behind him in the crowd” and touch his clothes. Healed, she could have slipped away. But Jesus stopped and asked, “Who touched my clothes?” The disciples thought the question absurd: look at the crowd! Yet Jesus “looked around to see her who had done this thing.” He listened as she “told him all the truth”, and then he called her “Daughter”.

Ticket machines in hospitals, banks and government offices are efficient, but they easily turn people into numbers: “Number thirty-seven to counter five.” Customers are the same; in the system they are a record ID, a ticket, a star rating. Jesus gives us three actions. See: look up at the person, not just at the screen. Listen: let them finish, and hear the struggle behind their words. Touch: respond in an appropriate way to what they really need. And remember, Jesus was on his way to an emergency at Jairus’s house, yet he still stopped for one person.

321 teaches that people matter more than tasks, and relationships more than things. In busy moments, the self-centred see only their own schedule; the self-emptied have room in their hearts to see people. Use your heart and you find joy; use only your head and you find worry. When we only use our heads to process “cases”, we soon burn out; when we use our hearts to see people, work gains warmth and meaning. 920 reminds us that everyone who comes to the counter may be the “2” God wants me to love.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Rely on the Holy Spirit with your heart, not on yourself with your head. Seeing, listening and touching are three ways of treating people from the heart. Turning a number back into a name is how people come before tasks at work.
lessons.scene: Mia works at the registration desk of a polyclinic in Singapore. At eleven in the morning the waiting area is full and the system has crashed again. An elderly woman comes to the counter for the third time, explaining in Hokkien that she can’t understand the numbers being announced and is afraid of missing hers. People behind her are growing impatient. Mia’s supervisor murmurs: “Ask her to sit down and wait for the announcement.”
q: Who is God? — Jesus stopped for one person while on the way to an emergency. What does this show you about how he values each individual?
Who am I? — When you are busy, what kind of person are you most likely to turn into a “number”?
How shall I respond? — If you were Mia, how could you truly see this woman without defying your supervisor?
lessons.jesus: Jesus healed not only the woman’s body but her years of shame. He called her “Daughter” in front of everyone, bringing someone who had been shut out back into the family of God. The Lord who stopped in that crowd stops in your busyness today: he sees you, hears you out, and touches your wounds with his nail-scarred hands.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, thank you that in a pressing crowd you noticed me hiding at the back. Slow my heart today. At the counter, on the phone and in meetings, help me look up and see people, listen patiently until they finish, and respond appropriately to what they really need. Let everyone I meet feel the warmth of being seen by you. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Call at least three customers or colleagues by name today
When someone speaks, put your phone down and hear them out
Follow up with a customer: has their problem been solved?
lessons.noon: “Go in peace” — Lord, right now let me carry your peace to the next person who comes to me.

lessons.title: The Mile Beyond the Warranty
lessons.theme: I am required to go one mile; love takes me the second

v: “You have heard that it was said, ‘An eye for an eye, and a tooth for a tooth.’
But I tell you, don’t resist him who is evil; but whoever strikes you on your right cheek, turn to him the other also.
If anyone sues you to take away your coat, let him have your cloak also.
Whoever compels you to go one mile, go with him two.
Give to him who asks you, and don’t turn away him who desires to borrow from you.
each of you not just looking to his own things, but each of you also to the things of others.

lessons.still: As you put on your shoes, say to the Lord: “Lord, today I will be asked to walk many ‘first miles’. Give me a free heart to walk the second mile gladly, wherever you lead.”
teach: Jesus said, “Whoever compels you to go one mile, go with him two.” In his day Roman soldiers could force local people to carry their gear for a distance, a humiliation of life under occupation. Ordinarily, you would carry the load your one mile, drop it and walk off, duty done and resentment intact. Jesus says: go with him another mile. The first mile is compelled; the second is chosen. The first is duty; the second is love. This is not weakness but a remarkable freedom: no one can take away my right to choose to love.

At work, contracts, job descriptions and warranty terms are the “first mile”. They are spelled out clearly; do them and you have done your job. The second mile is taking an old customer’s call after the warranty has expired, telling a homeowner their air-conditioner filter needs cleaning after the repair, adding a one-page explanation so the client’s colleagues can understand your work too. But discern carefully. The second mile is a free choice of love, not endless exploitation. If you are pushed into unpaid overtime every day, what you need is honest conversation and reasonable boundaries, and where necessary, help from someone you trust or a professional.

Paul says, “each of you not just looking to his own things, but each of you also to the things of others.” The second mile has power because it steps outside the calculation of “what I owe you and what you owe me”. 321 teaches that self-denial means living for Jesus and for others, not for ourselves. When you walk the second mile you are not flattering a customer; you are letting them meet a Lord who walked countless miles to find us. The shift in thinking is from “that’s not my job” to “this is my chance to love”.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Self-denial means living for Jesus and for others, not for self. The second mile is not forced; it is love flowing freely from the self-emptied life. Change your thinking and your life changes: from calculation to gladness.
lessons.scene: Jianxun repairs air-conditioners in Penang and covers six jobs a day. Today, at an elderly couple’s home, he has just fixed the unit and is packing up when the grandmother asks timidly, “Young man, the kitchen tap keeps dripping. Could you have a look?” It isn’t his line of work, and the next customer is already chasing him, but one glance tells him it probably just needs a new washer.
q: Who is God? — Jesus tells us to walk the second mile. What freedom and love in his heart does this reveal?
Who am I? — Do you usually stop at “I’ve done what the contract says”, or are you learning to take one more step gladly?
How shall I respond? — If you were Jianxun, how would you answer the grandmother, while still respecting the next customer?
lessons.jesus: Jesus walked far more than a second mile. He came from heaven to earth, from Bethlehem all the way to Golgotha; “though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor” (2 Corinthians 8:9). We have not even walked our first mile well, yet he carried the cross that was ours all the way to the end. We can go one more mile today because he first went the whole way for us.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, thank you for walking the road I could never finish. Today, when I am asked to do what is required, take away my resentment. When you give me the chance to go one step further, give me a glad and loving heart. Give me wisdom too, to tell the difference between love and the boundaries I need to set. May my second mile help someone see you. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Do one small thing for a customer beyond the contract today
When you hand in work, add one thoughtful note or tip
Check your boundaries: is there an honest conversation needed?
lessons.noon: “Whoever compels you to go one mile, go with him two” — Lord, right now give me glad love for the next step.

lessons.title: Earthing the Anger
lessons.theme: Don’t be dragged along by anger; answer curses with blessing

v: “But I tell you who hear: love your enemies, do good to those who hate you,
bless those who curse you, and pray for those who mistreat you.
To him who strikes you on the cheek, offer also the other; and from him who takes away your cloak, don’t withhold your coat also.
Give to everyone who asks you, and don’t ask him who takes away your goods to give them back again.
“As you would like people to do to you, do exactly so to them.
A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger.

lessons.still: Recall a customer or colleague who recently made you very angry. Breathe deeply and place their face in the Lord’s hands. Say: “Lord, I can’t love them, but you can. Let your gentleness flow out of me today.”
teach: Jesus’ words are hard: “love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, bless those who curse you, and pray for those who mistreat you.” Then he sums it up: “As you would like people to do to you, do exactly so to them.” Jesus does not say, “Wait until they become reasonable, then treat them well.” He hands the initiative back to us: how others treat me does not decide how I treat them. Proverbs adds a piece of practical wisdom: “A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger.”

When lightning strikes, a building with good earthing sends the current safely into the ground instead of letting it surge through the house and burn out the appliances. Facing a furious customer, our hearts need an earth wire too. Don’t rush to defend yourself; let them finish. Repeat back their need in a steady voice. Direct the anger at the problem itself rather than at each other’s character. Gentleness is not weakness but strength under control. But treating people well does not mean accepting abuse. If there is verbal abuse, harassment or a threat of violence, protecting yourself and your colleagues is right. Use your company’s procedures and, where necessary, seek help from someone you trust or a professional.

321 teaches that pride provokes pride and both sides lose, while humility breeds humility and both sides win. A customer’s cutting remark easily stirs the self-centred life in us: “Why should I have to put up with this?” In that moment our focus must turn from our own hurt and the other person’s unreasonableness back to Jesus. Praying for them is the best earth wire. When we hand our anger to the Lord who judges righteously, we can rely on the Spirit with our hearts and give a gentle answer.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Humility breeds humility; pride provokes pride. With unreasonable people, keep your focus on Jesus, not on your own grievance. Blessing them and praying for them is how Jesus is King in the hardest moments.
lessons.scene: Baoling is duty manager in the lobby of a hotel in Guangzhou. At eleven at night a business guest, angry that his room’s air-conditioning is noisy, is shouting insults at an intern on the front desk, demanding a full refund or he will post a one-star review. The intern’s eyes are filling with tears. As Baoling walks over, the guest turns and points at her: “So you’re the manager? This rubbish hotel of yours…”
q: Who is God? — Jesus tells us to bless those who curse us. What does this show you about how God treats his enemies?
Who am I? — When someone’s anger lands on you, is your first reaction to fight back, run away, or entrust it to God?
How shall I respond? — If you were Baoling, what would your first sentence be, and how would you protect the intern?
lessons.jesus: “When he was cursed, he didn’t curse back. When he suffered, he didn’t threaten, but committed himself to him who judges righteously” (1 Peter 2:23). On the cross he prayed for those who crucified him: “Father, forgive them, for they don’t know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34). He bore all our unreasonableness, so that we who were once God’s enemies might receive forgiveness and peace.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, you were cursed and did not curse back, crucified and still prayed for others. Today, when someone is unreasonable with me, be the earth wire in my heart, so I am not dragged along by anger. Give me a gentle tongue and a clear head, and courage to protect colleagues and set boundaries. I bless the person who hurt me; may they meet you too. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: When someone complains, let them finish before you respond
Pray one silent blessing over a customer who angered you
Ask your team: what is our procedure when someone is abusive?
lessons.noon: “A gentle answer turns away wrath” — Lord, right now let your gentleness guard my tongue.

lessons.title: Plane the Back of the Drawer
lessons.theme: Doing hidden work well lets people see the Father in heaven

v: You are the light of the world. A city located on a hill can’t be hidden.
Neither do you light a lamp and put it under a measuring basket, but on a stand; and it shines to all who are in the house.
Even so, let your light shine before men, that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven.
Do you see a man skilled in his work? He will serve kings. He won’t serve obscure men.

lessons.still: Open a piece of work you will hand in today and find a detail no one is likely to notice. Say to the Lord: “Lord, you can see this. Today I will do it well for you; may people see you.”
teach: Jesus says, “You are the light of the world. A city located on a hill can’t be hidden.” And then: “let your light shine before men, that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven.” Notice: people see our good works, but the glory goes to the Father in heaven. Our light is not our own; it reflects God’s glory. Proverbs adds, “Do you see a man skilled in his work? He will serve kings.” Diligent, careful work carries its own persuasive power.

Old carpenters say the back panel of a drawer and the underside of a cabinet, which customers will never see, reveal most clearly the craftsman’s heart. At work, the “back panel” might be code comments nobody will read, a restaurant’s cold store, steel reinforcement buried under concrete on a building site, the sources listed in a report’s appendix. Cutting corners in hidden places saves money in the short term but hollows out trust in the long run. For Christians, the quality of our products and services is not just a competitive edge; it is a letter to the world. The God I believe in is the one who “saw everything that he had made, and, behold, it was very good.”

But quality is not for showing off. 321’s two cores are: let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory. When a client praises your work, that is the moment to pass the glory to God, not to prove yourself. And when your care is overlooked, or business goes to someone who cuts corners, don’t lose heart: success is not proof, and failure is not condemnation. Letting Jesus be King of the hidden stages of your work is how God’s order is built.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The two cores — let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory. Good quality is light, but light exists to reveal the Father in heaven. Faithfulness in hidden places is how a godly system is built.
lessons.scene: Guodong runs a solid-wood furniture factory in Fujian. A major client has ordered two hundred desks at a rock-bottom price. His purchasing manager suggests: “Let’s use cheap plywood for the drawer backs and bottoms. Customers never pull the drawers out to check.” It would raise the margin by twenty per cent. Guodong turns a sample drawer over, stares at the panel, and says nothing for a long time.
q: Who is God? — God “saw everything that he had made, and, behold, it was very good.” What does this show you about how he views the quality of work?
Who am I? — In your work, which “back panel” are you most tempted to skimp on?
How shall I respond? — If you were Guodong, how would you answer the purchasing manager, and how would you talk to the client about price?
lessons.jesus: Before the cross Jesus prayed, “I glorified you on the earth. I have accomplished the work which you have given me to do” (John 17:4). There were no shortcuts in his work: from the manger to the cross, every step was perfect obedience. His salvation is not “good enough” but fully accomplished. Because he finished it, we can do each small thing well in him, for the Father’s glory.
lessons.pray: Father in heaven, thank you that all you made is very good, and that Jesus fully accomplished salvation. Today make me faithful in hidden places, without cutting corners or doing the bare minimum. When my work is praised, let me give the glory to you; when my care is overlooked, let me rest in your gaze. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Find one hidden detail and do it well today
Check one piece of work again and fix a small flaw
When praised, say silently: “Glory to God.”
lessons.noon: “You are the light of the world” — Lord, right now make me faithful in hidden places, reflecting your glory.

mem.t: doing nothing through rivalry or through conceit, but in humility, each counting others better than himself.

lessons.title: Focus Before You Shoot
lessons.theme: A leader’s first action is to kneel before God

v: When I heard these words, I sat down and wept, and mourned several days; and I fasted and prayed before the God of heaven,
and said, “I beg you, LORD, the God of heaven, the great and awesome God who keeps covenant and loving kindness with those who love him and keep his commandments,

let your ear now be attentive and your eyes open, that you may listen to the prayer of your servant which I pray before you at this time, day and night, for the children of Israel your servants, while I confess the sins of the children of Israel which we have sinned against you. Yes, I and my father’s house have sinned.
We have dealt very corruptly against you, and have not kept the commandments, nor the statutes, nor the ordinances, which you commanded your servant Moses.
“Remember, I beg you, the word that you commanded your servant Moses, saying, ‘If you trespass, I will scatter you amongst the peoples;

but if you return to me, and keep my commandments and do them, though your outcasts were in the uttermost part of the heavens, yet I will gather them from there, and will bring them to the place that I have chosen, to cause my name to dwell there.’
“Now these are your servants and your people, whom you have redeemed by your great power and by your strong hand.

Lord, I beg you, let your ear be attentive now to the prayer of your servant, and to the prayer of your servants who delight to fear your name; and please prosper your servant today, and grant him mercy in the sight of this man.” Now I was cup bearer to the king.

lessons.still: Before your first meeting or your first email today, stop and fold your hands over your chest. Say to the Lord: “Lord, before I act, let me see your will clearly.” Stay silent for ten seconds.
teach: Nehemiah was cupbearer to the king of Persia, a respected post in the palace. When he heard that Jerusalem’s wall was “broken down, and its gates are burnt with fire”, his first response was not to write a proposal. He “sat down and wept, and mourned several days” and “fasted and prayed before the God of heaven”. His prayer has clear layers. First worship: “the great and awesome God”. Then confession: “I and my father’s house have sinned”, not merely blaming others. Then he holds on to God’s promise. Only at the end does he make a specific request: “please prosper your servant today, and grant him mercy in the sight of this man.” Between the months of Chislev and Nisan (Nehemiah 1:1; 2:1), he prayed and waited for months before speaking to the king.

Every photographer knows: focus first, then press the shutter. If the focus is off, a thousand more clicks give you only blurred pictures. Many leaders, seeing a problem, rush to call meetings, draw up timelines and assign KPIs without first focusing on God. Nehemiah’s prayer was his focusing. Before God he saw the truth of the problem: not only the walls but the people’s sin. He saw his own position: “Now I was cup bearer to the king.” And he saw God’s heart. Prayer is not a delay to action; it is what gives action a clear focus.

One of 321’s three foundations is that the Holy Spirit is my guide. Rely on the Spirit with your heart, not on yourself with your head. Nehemiah’s prayer also carries humility: he counts himself among the guilty instead of criticising from above. Humility is the key to revival; a leader who first bows low before God is one God can use before people. Today, before your meetings, projects and hard decisions begin, take a few minutes to focus before God.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The Holy Spirit is my guide; humility is the key to revival. Nehemiah confessed and waited before God before he spoke before the king. Life first, then relationships, then ministry: leadership begins with prayer, not with a slide deck.
lessons.scene: Enlin is a senior civil servant in a government agency in Singapore. She has discovered that a meal-delivery scheme for seniors has stalled because departments keep passing the problem to one another, and in several districts elderly residents have had no meals for two weeks. She has drafted a strongly worded email to every department head, copying in the director. Her finger is on “Send” when she suddenly realises: she hasn’t prayed about this yet.
q: Who is God? — Nehemiah calls God “great and awesome” and the one “who keeps covenant and loving kindness”. How do these two sides shape your prayer?
Who am I? — When problems arise, is your first reaction to act, to complain, or to pray?
How shall I respond? — If you were Enlin, how would you pray before pressing “Send”? How might the email change?
lessons.jesus: Before choosing the twelve, Jesus “went out to the mountain to pray, and he continued all night in prayer to God” (Luke 6:12). He fasted before his public ministry and prayed in the garden before the cross. Though he is the Son of God, at every step he first focused before the Father. And today he “lives forever to make intercession” for us (Hebrews 7:25). We never pray alone.
lessons.pray: Great and awesome God, who keeps covenant and steadfast love, I confess that I often act first and pray later, or forget to pray at all. Before every decision today, focus my heart. Let me see the truth of the problem, and my own sin and position. Grant me favour before my managers, colleagues and clients, so that your purposes are fulfilled. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Pray for two minutes before today’s first meeting
Pray, then rewrite one emotionally charged email
Write a short prayer about one problem troubling you at work
lessons.noon: “please prosper your servant today, and grant him mercy in the sight of this man” — Lord, right now I come to you first, before I walk into the meeting room.

lessons.title: Inspecting the Walls by Night
lessons.theme: See the reality first, then invite people to build together

v: So I came to Jerusalem, and was there three days.
I arose in the night, I and a few men with me. I didn’t tell anyone what my God put into my heart to do for Jerusalem. There wasn’t any animal with me except the animal that I rode on.
I went out by night by the valley gate towards the jackal’s well, then to the dung gate; and I inspected the walls of Jerusalem, which were broken down, and its gates were consumed with fire.
Then I said to them, “You see the bad situation that we are in, how Jerusalem lies waste, and its gates are burnt with fire. Come, let’s build up the wall of Jerusalem, that we won’t be disgraced.”

I told them about the hand of my God which was good on me, and also about the king’s words that he had spoken to me. They said, “Let’s rise up and build.” So they strengthened their hands for the good work.

lessons.still: Think of a place you are responsible for but haven’t actually visited: a site, a warehouse, a classroom, a call centre. Say to the Lord: “Lord, give me your eyes, to see what is really there and what people really need.”
teach: When Nehemiah arrived in Jerusalem, he did not immediately call a public meeting. He stayed three days, then “arose in the night”, took a few men, and personally went round the city: “I inspected the walls of Jerusalem, which were broken down, and its gates were consumed with fire.” Only after seeing the reality did he say to the officials and people, “You see the bad situation that we are in, how Jerusalem lies waste, and its gates are burnt with fire. Come, let’s build up the wall of Jerusalem, that we won’t be disgraced.” Then he told them “about the hand of my God which was good on me”. The people answered, “Let’s rise up and build.”

Before quoting for a job, a good builder does a site survey: checks the pipes, takes measurements, feels the walls for damp. Contractors who quote from photographs alone often keep adding costs once work begins. Nehemiah was a leader who surveyed first and mobilised second. His mobilising had three features. First, he named the reality everyone could see, neither exaggerating nor glossing over it. Second, he said “we”, not “you”, placing himself inside the problem. Third, he testified to God’s hand: the foundation of vision is not the leader’s charisma but God’s work.

Nehemiah did not say, “Follow me and fulfil my dream.” He said, “let’s build.” The vision was not his empire but God’s city. 321 teaches that the self-centred treat their team as tools for their own ambitions, while self-emptied leaders know they are just one of the builders. When he gave the credit to “the hand of my God which was good on me”, he let Jesus receive all the glory. And a group of people gladly rising to build is the beginning of God’s order.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Let Jesus receive all the glory; build God’s order. Nehemiah grounded his vision in “the hand of my God” and replaced “I” with “we”. That is self-emptied leadership, and humility breeding humility.
lessons.scene: Bingqian has just been appointed head of academic affairs at an old junior high school in Pingtung. Enrolment has fallen for years, teachers’ morale is low, and the previous head’s reform plan was quietly ignored in meetings. Tomorrow he chairs his first staff meeting, armed with a polished slide deck. Tonight he walks alone through the empty campus, past peeling classrooms and an old honour board filled with the names of former students.
q: Who is God? — Nehemiah spoke of “the hand of my God which was good on me”. Have you seen God’s hand in your work?
Who am I? — When you lead, do you more often say “you need to” or “let’s do this together”?
How shall I respond? — If you were Bingqian, would you open tomorrow’s meeting with the slides, or with something else?
lessons.jesus: When Jesus “saw the multitudes, he was moved with compassion for them because they were harassed and scattered, like sheep without a shepherd” (Matthew 9:36). He saw first, felt compassion first, and only then said to his disciples, “The harvest indeed is plentiful, but the labourers are few” (Matthew 9:37). He also wept over Jerusalem (Luke 19:41). His vision always begins with seeing people and loving them.
lessons.pray: Lord, give me Nehemiah’s eyes, willing to look honestly at the broken places, and Nehemiah’s heart, willing to say “we”. Let me mobilise people not by my eloquence or my slides, but by testifying to your gracious hand. May my team run not for my dream, but rise together to build your city. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Walk round one place you are responsible for today
Ask a colleague: “What do you think is our biggest struggle?”
Next time you speak, change “you need to” into “let’s”
lessons.noon: “Let’s rise up and build” — Lord, right now let me build for you together with my companions.

lessons.title: Builders Carrying Weapons
lessons.theme: Under attack, pray and keep watch, and keep working

v: But we made our prayer to our God, and set a watch against them day and night because of them.

I looked, and rose up, and said to the nobles, to the rulers, and to the rest of the people, “Don’t be afraid of them! Remember the Lord, who is great and awesome, and fight for your brothers, your sons, your daughters, your wives, and your houses.”
When our enemies heard that it was known to us, and God had brought their counsel to nothing, all of us returned to the wall, everyone to his work.
From that time forth, half of my servants did the work, and half of them held the spears, the shields, the bows, and the coats of mail; and the rulers were behind all the house of Judah.
Those who built the wall, and those who bore burdens loaded themselves; everyone with one of his hands did the work, and with the other held his weapon.

lessons.still: Think of a remark that stung you recently. Write it down, then gently cross it out. Say to the Lord: “Lord, I give these words to you. Today help me remember that you are great and awesome, and not let mockery throw me off my stride.”
teach: As soon as work on the wall began, the mockery came. Sanballat sneered, “What are these feeble Jews doing?” Tobiah said that “if a fox climbed up it, he would break down their stone wall.” When mockery failed, a plot to attack followed. Nehemiah’s response was balanced: “we made our prayer to our God, and set a watch against them day and night.” Prayer and vigilance together. He encouraged the people: “Don’t be afraid of them! Remember the Lord, who is great and awesome.” The final picture: “everyone with one of his hands did the work, and with the other held his weapon.” The work did not stop, and neither did the watch.

Mockery and attacks at work are very real: a remark in a meeting like “How long will your project last?”, malicious online reviews, rumours spread by competitors, even someone quietly undermining you. Software engineers understand this. After a product launches, one hand keeps building new features while the other patches vulnerabilities and maintains the firewall. You can’t stop developing for fear of hackers, nor develop while ignoring security. Don’t let mockery break your rhythm, and don’t naively ignore real risks. Where necessary, keep records and seek legal or professional advice. That too is “setting a watch”.

The greatest damage mockery does is to turn our focus onto our enemies and our own weakness; even Judah said, “The strength of the bearers of burdens is fading.” 321 teaches us to keep our focus on Jesus, not on ourselves, others or circumstances. Nehemiah drew everyone’s eyes back to “the Lord, who is great and awesome”, and left justice in God’s hands rather than taking revenge. Relying on the Spirit with your heart, you can keep working with one hand and hold the weapon of prayer with the other.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Keep your focus on Jesus, not on yourself, others or circumstances. Under attack, don’t scheme a counter-attack with your head; rely on the Spirit with your heart. Work with one hand, pray with the other, leave justice to God, and let Jesus be King in the storm.
lessons.scene: Xiaolei founded a start-up in Chengdu that builds accessibility apps. Right after launch, an anonymous forum post accused her company of “plagiarism” and “deceiving investors”. Several staff are anxious, and some are privately asking whether they should look for other jobs. Investors have been calling too. Xiaolei looks at the post, now shared over a thousand times; her palms are sweating, and she badly wants to write a long rebuttal right now.
q: Who is God? — “Remember the Lord, who is great and awesome.” How does this change the way you see those who attack you?
Who am I? — When you are mocked, are you more likely to stop working, or to forget to pray and keep watch?
How shall I respond? — If you were Xiaolei, what would you do first today? Which matters need professional help?
lessons.jesus: On the cross Jesus heard people mock him: “He saved others, but he can’t save himself” (Matthew 27:42). He had the power to come down and prove himself, but he did not, because he was completing the work of salvation. When he was cursed he did not curse back, but committed himself to him who judges righteously. Because he did not stop, we have been saved.
lessons.pray: Great and awesome Lord, you know the words that have stung me and the fear in my heart. Guard my heart today, so that mockery does not throw me off course and I do not naively ignore real danger. Give me wisdom to know when to respond, when to stay silent, and when to seek professional help. Let me work with one hand and pray with the other, leaving justice in your hands. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Write down a hurtful remark and pray for the one who said it
Focus today on finishing one piece of work that was questioned
Agree with your team how to respond when attacked
lessons.noon: “Remember the Lord, who is great and awesome” — Lord, right now I am not afraid of mockery; I look to you.

lessons.title: Character on the Expense Claim
lessons.theme: Because we fear God, we don’t exploit the perks of authority

v: Moreover from the time that I was appointed to be their governor in the land of Judah, from the twentieth year even to the thirty-second year of Artaxerxes the king, that is, twelve years, I and my brothers have not eaten the bread of the governor.

But the former governors who were before me were supported by the people, and took bread and wine from them, plus forty shekels of silver; yes, even their servants ruled over the people, but I didn’t do so, because of the fear of God.
Yes, I also continued in the work of this wall. We didn’t buy any land. All my servants were gathered there to the work.
Moreover there were at my table, of the Jews and the rulers, one hundred and fifty men, in addition to those who came to us from amongst the nations that were around us.

Now that which was prepared for one day was one ox and six choice sheep. Also fowls were prepared for me, and once in ten days a store of all sorts of wine. Yet for all this, I didn’t demand the governor’s pay, because the bondage was heavy on this people.
Remember me, my God, for all the good that I have done for this people.

lessons.still: Take out your wallet or company card, look at it, and put it back. Say to the Lord: “Lord, the authority and resources in my hands are entrusted by you. Today let me use them cleanly, honouring you and my colleagues.”
teach: Nehemiah served as governor of Judah for twelve years, and by custom he was entitled to draw the governor’s allowance from the people. Yet he says, “I and my brothers have not eaten the bread of the governor.” His reason: “the former governors who were before me were supported by the people”, “but I didn’t do so, because of the fear of God.” He not only refused it; he provided from his own resources, with a hundred and fifty people eating at his table. Nor did he use his position to acquire property: “I also continued in the work of this wall. We didn’t buy any land.” In the end he asked only one thing of God: “Remember me, my God, for all the good that I have done for this people.”

Today’s “governor’s allowance” might be a family dinner on the company card, a personal holiday tagged onto a business trip, a “small token” from a supplier, inside information you learn early because of your role, or finding jobs in the company for relatives. Often “everyone does it”, and it may even be “within the rules”. Think of it as a load-bearing wall in a building. Normally you don’t notice it, and during a renovation you are tempted to knock it through for more space. But once it is gone, the whole building becomes unstable. A leader’s self-discipline is the load-bearing wall of a team’s trust.

Nehemiah could do this because he feared God and saw that “the bondage was heavy on this people”. 321 teaches that the self-centred see authority as privilege, while the self-emptied see it as a trust. Self-denial means living for Jesus and for others, not for ourselves. Nehemiah did not seek applause from people; he asked only to be remembered by God. That is letting Jesus receive all the glory. Self-discipline will not guarantee you more wealth, but it will let you stand firm before God and people.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Self-denial means living for Jesus and for others, not for self. When a leader lays down privilege, he lays down power and returns to his proper place. Refusing to exploit your position lets Jesus be King of your expense claims and your company card.
lessons.scene: Liheng is general manager of a building-materials company in Ipoh. At year end the company is hosting key clients for three days in Langkawi. The admin manager suggests: “Sir, why not bring your wife and children too? Flights and hotel can go on the company account. The previous GM always did.” The board won’t check closely, and colleagues think it is perfectly normal. Liheng looks at the itinerary and remembers that last month he froze his staff’s pay rises.
